reinstatement.title: Reinstatements and Probationary Licenses
reinstatement.intro: These decisions are not new discipline. They granted a petition to reinstate a surrendered or revoked license, or issued a probationary license to an applicant, and are included because they describe the conduct that led to the original action and the conditions imposed on return to practice. Each lists the offense category of that underlying conduct.

appendix.title: Appendix: Physicians Listed with Psychiatry as a Secondary Specialty
appendix.intro: The physicians in these cases list psychiatry among their specialties in public provider registries, but none was found in the American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology's certification records, and the decision itself (and in most cases the registries' primary specialty) points to another field: family, internal, emergency, addiction or laboratory medicine, or neurology. They are kept here because the conduct is still instructive.

about: These summaries describe disciplinary actions taken by state medical boards against physicians identified as psychiatrists, roughly 2021-2026, drawn from the boards' own decision documents: California (Medical Board of California: decision documents linked in its newsletter (Volumes 158-173)); Florida (Florida Board of Medicine / Department of Health: orders from the Department of Health's discipline search); Georgia (Georgia Composite Medical Board: orders bundled in its monthly Public Board Actions lists); Kentucky (Kentucky Board of Medical Licensure: each physician's current order, found through its monthly Board Action Reports); Maryland (Maryland Board of Physicians: orders linked from its Board Actions pages); North Carolina (North Carolina Medical Board: orders linked from licensees' public profiles (2021-2023 only partially available)); Nevada (Nevada State Board of Medical Examiners: orders linked from its Disciplinary Actions page); Ohio (State Medical Board of Ohio: each physician's formal-action file, found through its monthly Formal Action Reports); Oregon (Oregon Medical Board: orders attached to its monthly Board Action Reports); and South Carolina (South Carolina Board of Medical Examiners: orders from its Public Board Orders list). Each entry summarizes what happened leading up to the action, usually from the charging document attached to or recited in the order (an Accusation, Administrative Complaint, statement of charges, or notice of opportunity for hearing) or from the order's findings, followed by the board's order.

Most cases were resolved by settlement (a stipulated settlement, consent order or consent agreement), in which the physician often does not admit the allegations. Entries say the charging document "alleged" in those cases, and reserve "found" for cases where a judge, hearing officer or the board made findings (including findings the physician agreed to) and "admitted" for admissions. Allegations are not proven facts.

Physicians are not named, and case numbers are assigned for this collection only; they are not drawn from any board's records. Patients are referred to as in the original documents. Many decisions are scanned images read via OCR, so occasional details may be imperfect; consult the original decision before relying on a specific fact. Each case appears once, under the category of the conduct that most drove it, with any other categories listed beneath its heading.

Only decision documents that boards publish openly are included. New York, Illinois and Texas post only short summaries (their orders sit behind CAPTCHA- or terms-gated searches), Wisconsin's order archive blocks automated downloads, and North Carolina's 2021-2023 orders are mostly reachable only through a CAPTCHA-gated search, so those records are not covered yet. A physician counts as a psychiatrist when a public NPI Registry record carries the same state license number with a psychiatry specialty.

narrative: This decision granted a petition for reinstatement of a surrendered license; it is included because the reinstatement terms flow from earlier discipline. The psychiatrist had practiced in an academic health system, as program director at a psychiatric hospital, as medical director of an addiction treatment provider, and in private practice. In 2016 the Board filed a First Amended Accusation charging him with sexual abuse, misconduct, and relations with a patient; repeated negligent acts, including prescribing benzodiazepines to that patient, who abused alcohol; general unprofessional conduct; and gross negligence and over-prescribing involving four additional patients. He resolved that Accusation by a stipulated surrender of his license, effective November 2017. The present decision does not describe the details of the underlying conduct further.

At the 2021 reinstatement hearing before an administrative law judge, the psychiatrist admitted the sexual encounter with a patient, acknowledged it was egregious, and expressed remorse. The judge found that he had attended a 12-step program for sex and love addiction since 2012 (serving as a sponsor), had individual psychotherapy until 2018 and ongoing group therapy, had completed a professional boundaries and ethics course in 2013, had worked as a medical content writer since the surrender, had completed substantial CME, and presented supportive testimony and letters. The judge found significant rehabilitation and that reinstatement on probation would not be against the public interest; the Attorney General did not oppose reinstatement.
cases.outcome: Petition for reinstatement granted; license reinstated, revoked, revocation stayed, 3 years' probation with clinical competence assessment program (no practice until completed), total controlled-substance restriction (including no marijuana recommendations), professionalism/ethics program, psychiatric evaluation, psychotherapy, practice monitor, solo practice prohibition, third-party chaperone for female patients, and prohibition on supervising PAs/APNs.

narrative: The psychiatrist treated Patient 1, a man he diagnosed with moderate to severe major depressive disorder and unspecified anxiety, for eleven sessions from September 2014 to December 2015; the patient's wife, who had previously worked with the psychiatrist as a receptionist, had encouraged him to seek care. After an ALJ evidentiary hearing and exceptions, Disciplinary Panel A found that during treatment the psychiatrist gratuitously questioned Patient 1 about sexual positions and frequency of sex with his wife, advised him to seclude himself from his wife and children and give his wife "space," and drove to the couple's home to show off his new car, then took the wife on a one-to-two-hour ride alone, told her he had dreamed about her, and dismissed the patient's distress about the outing. The panel found he had a romantic interest in the wife well before sexual contact and that his advice was designed to estrange the patient from her. Patient 1 stopped attending without formal discharge. In June 2016, about six months after the last visit, the psychiatrist began a sexual relationship with the wife (including oral sex in his office) that continued with sexual texts and photographs until Patient 1 discovered it in December 2017. After the patient complained to the psychiatrist's employer and he was told to have no contact, he texted the couple that they "should be happy" they had damaged his future.

The ALJ had found only the text message unprofessional. The panel rejected that view and found the psychiatrist guilty of immoral and unprofessional conduct, finding he exploited knowledge gained in treatment, that Patient 1 was seriously harmed (losing 40 pounds and making a suicide attempt with a loaded rifle), and that the psychiatrist was repeatedly dishonest with the Board, including fabricating a referral to another physician.
cases.outcome: Reprimand; suspension for a minimum of 6 months (effective 30 days after the order) with MPRP enrollment and an in-person professionalism course; on MPRP endorsement, suspension to be terminated and replaced by at least 2 years' probation with continued MPRP participation; no early termination.

narrative: In the Consent Agreement the psychiatrist admitted the allegations of the May 2021 Notice of Opportunity for Hearing. The Board learned in September 2020 that the psychiatrist's employer had ordered him to stop all patient contact over allegations of an inappropriate relationship with a patient. He had treated Patient 1 from about March 2019. At the last office visit, on about March 30, 2020, he prescribed enough medication with refills to last six months. The chart contained a note dated that day saying that he and the patient had agreed to end the treatment relationship because they had social contacts in common. He did not sign the note electronically until August 2020, and he never sent the patient a written termination notice by certified mail or appropriate electronic means. In a February 2021 Board interview he admitted a sexual relationship with Patient 1 from a couple of weeks after that visit until about July or August 2020, and said he had been fired because of it. He knew the patient had a progressive brain disorder, a history of sexually and physically abusive relationships, and recent inpatient and intensive outpatient psychiatric treatment.

He had denied any sexual contact before the last visit. However, the Notice stated that the Board's investigation showed the sexual relationship began before then. The Notice also stated that he flirted with the patient and asked clinically irrelevant sexual questions, and he acknowledged finding her on Facebook and messaging her in December 2019 and sharing personal information with her. According to the Notice, the termination note was a plan he devised to falsely document a reason for ending treatment, so that their first meeting outside the office would appear innocent. The Notice also stated that he exploited the power imbalance: the patient helped him move, found him an apartment and helped pay to furnish it, and during arguments he used information she had disclosed in psychiatric sessions.
cases.outcome: License suspended indefinitely for at least two years; $20,000 fine; quarterly declarations and Board appearances; reinstatement requires a physician/patient boundaries course with a written report and a new consent agreement with probationary terms.

narrative: According to the Accusation, beginning in March 2018 the psychiatrist treated Patient 1, a 29-year-old woman with panic attacks, chronic anxiety, a history of sexual abuse by a partner, and a prior ADHD diagnosis, in an outpatient practice with weekly in-person therapy he described as cognitive behavioral therapy. He allegedly did not obtain prior records, validate the ADHD diagnosis, or document an adequate history; prescribed diazepam routinely and continued as-needed methylphenidate without documented informed consent, rationale, effectiveness review, or CURES check; later added quetiapine for insomnia without documented reasoning; and kept notes that made it hard to tell what therapy was delivered. He also reviewed the patient's social media, including photographs, and discussed it in sessions. By mid-2018 he charted her transference attraction and his own countertransference, a curbside consult, and a referral to a therapist that she declined, but he continued treating her. Text messages, his interview with Board investigators, and her complaint allegedly showed escalating boundary violations: calling himself a 'pick-up artist,' saying they would 'probably be hooking up' if both were single, continuing therapy after learning she was the person he had been chatting with in a sexually provocative way in an online game chat room, asking her during a video session to show her breasts, and making a sexually explicit remark.

In a January 2019 in-person session, by the patient's account, he unzipped her dress, breathed along her back, neck, and inner thighs, touched her, and kissed her forehead; he told investigators he traced her exposed skin with his lips and face. He charted a 'clear significant boundary violation' without details, yet kept contacting her by text, video, and in person after purportedly referring her elsewhere, calling her his 'favorite patient.' The Accusation charged sexual misconduct, gross negligence, unprofessional conduct, and inadequate records. He did not admit the allegations but agreed a prima facie case or factual basis could be established.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 7 years' probation with 40 hours/year education, medical record keeping course, professionalism (ethics) program, and professional boundaries program (the latter three already satisfied), psychiatric evaluation, psychotherapy, practice monitor, prohibition on accepting new female patients (with patient notification log), probation disclosure to patients under B&P 2228.1, prohibition on supervising PAs/APNs, and probation monitoring costs.

narrative: The psychiatrist formally treated an adult woman with severe psychiatric disorders from 2014 to early 2016, and also treated a family member of hers with whom she lived (billed 2014-2015, then pro bono until 2019). In mid-2017, after meeting her by chance at a pharmacy, he got her cell phone number from her medical records and invited her to dinner. According to the Consent Order's findings, from 2017 to December 2020 he provided what he labeled 'informal courtesy treatment as a friend free of charge,' calling in refills every few months, including a benzodiazepine, and the state prescription monitoring report showed he prescribed controlled substances to her from 2014 to 2020. He never checked the monitoring program for her or for the family member, and he discussed the family member's care with her. By 2018-2019 they met every week or two and talked or texted daily. He told the Board he was in love with her, hoped the relationship would become romantic, and kissed her briefly on the lips in 2018-2019. In November 2019 he paid for a four-day international trip (airfare about $2,410 and hotel about $730) on which they shared a hotel room and slept in the same bed while she was taking medications he prescribed. In 2020, after she had COVID-19 and became severely depressed, he prescribed several antidepressants, paid her rent and groceries, and transferred $5,200 to her.

The matter came to light when the psychiatrist he had referred her to for therapy reported that she disclosed a sexual relationship with him; she later denied this to the Board, and he also denied any sexual relationship. The Consent Order found the facts above without finding intercourse, and concluded that he was guilty of immoral and unprofessional conduct and violated the Board's sexual misconduct regulations, which cover romantic kissing and sexual or romantic relationships with patients, former patients, and key third parties.
cases.outcome: Reprimand; suspension for a minimum of 10 business days, followed by probation for a minimum of 2 years with enrollment in the Maryland Professional Rehabilitation Program and a professional boundaries and ethics course within 6 months; $15,000 civil fine within two years.

narrative: The Public Consent Order recited that on or about September 4, 2020, the physician resigned his hospital privileges following allegations of improper intimate contact with a patient, and that he had elected to stop practicing medicine in November 2019 in the wake of those allegations. In connection with the allegations he voluntarily underwent treatment for sexual boundary issues at a professional assessment and treatment program, which in April 2021 issued a report recommending various limitations to further his ability to practice safely. The order does not describe the patient, the contact, the clinical setting, or how the matter reached the Board, and it contains no admission or finding that the contact occurred; the physician simply waived further findings of fact. The order lifted a summary suspension that the document does not otherwise describe and placed his license on probation, with the practice restrictions and treatment-reporting requirements focused on sexual boundary issues.
cases.outcome: Summary suspension lifted; public reprimand; probation (may petition to terminate after three years) restricted to male patients only (may petition after one year with a psychiatrist's evaluation that he is safe to treat women), Board approval of workplace, quarterly practice and employer reports, quarterly psychiatrist visits with reports on sexual-boundary safety, continued psychotherapy with quarterly reports, $5,000 fine within six months, and a PBI course on prescribing opioids/pain management within one year.

narrative: The psychiatrist executed a Permanent Surrender of Certificate to Practice Osteopathic Medicine and Surgery with consent to permanent revocation, in lieu of formal disciplinary proceedings. The surrender cites the Board's rule on sexual misconduct with an adult in the course of practice as the provision under which the action was taken in lieu of proceedings. The document contains no factual allegations or findings: it does not identify the patient or patients, the setting, or what conduct occurred, and the psychiatrist made no admission beyond agreeing to surrender in lieu of proceedings on that ground. The Board ratified the surrender and entered an order permanently revoking the license; the psychiatrist is permanently ineligible to reapply in Ohio.
cases.outcome: Permanent surrender of Ohio osteopathic license; license permanently revoked; ineligible for reinstatement or any new certificate.

narrative: In August 2023 the Board issued a Notice of Proposed Disciplinary Action against the psychiatrist, proposing revocation. It charged unprofessional conduct contrary to medical ethics and dangerous to patients, and sexual misconduct. The sexual misconduct charge was framed as sexual impropriety: behavior, gestures or expressions that are seductive, sexually suggestive or sexually demeaning to a patient or the patient's family, and sexually explicit communication in person or by electronic means such as text, email or social media. The Notice also charged impairment due to a mental health condition, repeated and gross negligence, knowingly making a false statement to the Board, and failing to comply with a Board request. The Stipulated Order does not describe the underlying facts, and the Notice is not attached.

The psychiatrist neither admitted nor denied the allegations, but the Board found that the conduct described in the Notice amounted to unprofessional conduct, sexual misconduct (sexual impropriety and sexually explicit communication), negligence, and willfully making a false statement or representation to the Board. The Board made no finding on the impairment charge or on the charge of failing to comply with a Board request. The order limits the psychiatrist's practice to forensic psychiatry, medication management and administrative medicine, and bars the psychiatrist from practicing psychotherapy.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; reprimand; $10,000 civil penalty ($7,500 stayed); practice limited to forensic psychiatry, medication management, and administrative medicine; no psychotherapy; ongoing therapeutic relationship with a Board-approved provider; longitudinal intensive boundaries course; no-notice chart audits and office visits; may ask to modify or end the order after five years.

narrative: The psychiatrist surrendered a Maryland license by a Letter of Surrender while under Board investigation. The letter states only that the Board had received a complaint alleging that the psychiatrist engaged in inappropriate communication with a patient. It does not describe the content of the communications, the patient, the treatment setting, or the time frame.

The psychiatrist surrendered to avoid further investigation; no charges were issued and no hearing was held. The psychiatrist did not admit the allegations but chose not to contest them, and agreed that for all purposes relevant to medical licensure they would be treated as proven and supported conclusions that the psychiatrist was guilty of immoral and unprofessional conduct in the practice of medicine and had violated the Board's sexual misconduct regulations. The surrender is not permanent, but any petition for reinstatement would be considered as if the license had been revoked.
cases.outcome: License surrendered (reinstatement only on petition, treated as if revoked); surrender of state controlled dangerous substance registration.

narrative: Patient A, an adult woman with OCD, panic disorder, and ADHD who reported recent thoughts that suicide might be the only way to stop her panic, began outpatient treatment with the psychiatrist in October 2019 while another physician was prescribing her alprazolam, Adderall, and carisoprodol. According to the Accusation, the psychiatrist replaced alprazolam with lorazepam and took over and increased Adderall without contacting the other prescriber, never obtained or documented releases to coordinate with her other providers, did not document informed consent for controlled substances, and gave a "courtesy fill" of a progestin-only contraceptive based on the patient's report of her gynecologist's advice without reviewing the gynecologist's labs. In spring 2020 the patient told him she was sexually attracted to him, which he did not document. In June 2020 emails, when she asked whether she should transfer care because she wanted a sexual relationship with him, he acknowledged a "connection/tension" and encouraged her to continue treatment; when she asked him to write a sexual fantasy about her, he replied that he was happy to do so. None of these emails were in the chart.

The Accusation further alleged that on July 3, 2020, without prior notice, he discharged her (citing a clinic closing) with a three-month supply of medications and told her they could be friends; a sexual relationship began within days by her account (late July by his, as he acknowledged to Board investigators) and continued through the summer. In September 2020 he wrote her further prescriptions for Adderall, fluoxetine, and lorazepam. Her subsequent therapist documented treatment for the effects of the relationship and worsening of her conditions. Charges included sexual misconduct, sexual exploitation, gross negligence (including improper termination), repeated negligent acts, inadequate records, and unprofessional conduct. The psychiatrist did not contest that a prima facie case could be established and surrendered his license; no findings were made.
cases.outcome: License surrender accepted; not eligible for reinstatement under the statutory bar for surrender based on sexual misconduct/exploitation; cost recovery of $94,244.00 payable before any new or reinstated license.

narrative: Patient A, a 45-year-old woman with a history of treated ADHD who reported stress related to work and a recent marriage, began treatment with the psychiatrist in July 2020; he diagnosed ADHD and prescribed Adderall 20 mg. She was seen by phone, video, and in person through December 2022, and over that time discussed marital difficulties and separation from her husband. According to the Accusation, during multiple visits she asked for his private email address and made flirtatious comments (including that she fantasized about being with a doctor and suggesting a sexualized nickname for him); at one visit she tried to sit on his lap; and at another she intentionally exposed her breasts, to which he responded "those are nice." On or about August 31, 2022, during a clinical visit, he and the patient exchanged sexually explicit emails. He documented none of these events, did not refer her elsewhere, and continued treating her.

The matter surfaced when the patient's husband saw the email exchange and complained to the psychiatrist's employer. At a December 2022 visit the psychiatrist charted only that the husband was accusing her of liking her doctors, and then recommended she transfer to a female psychiatrist and seek psychotherapy. The Accusation charged sexual misconduct with a patient, gross negligence through multiple inappropriate sexual interactions, and failure to maintain adequate records. In the stipulated settlement the psychiatrist admitted only that a prima facie case could be established; no findings were made.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 5 years' probation with patient disclosure of probation status, 40 hours/year education, medical record keeping course, professionalism program (ethics course), professional boundaries program, psychiatric evaluation, psychotherapy, practice monitor, solo practice prohibition, third-party chaperone for female patients; prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; cost recovery of $24,869.00.

narrative: After a three-day formal hearing, an Administrative Law Judge found, and the Board of Medicine adopted the findings, that the psychiatrist, who owned an outpatient psychiatric clinic and mainly did medication management, touched the breasts of three young adult female patients under the guise of a physical check during routine follow-up visits in his office with the door closed. In June 2019 he told Patient E.L., treated since age 19 for bipolar I disorder with lithium and bupropion, that he wanted to take her blood pressure, something he had never done before; he then counted down her ribs until his hand was inside her bra and touched her breast and nipple. In November 2020 and October 2022, he told Patients A.B. (25 at intake, treated for major depressive disorder and panic disorder) and D.D. (27, treated for ADHD, depression and anxiety) that he needed to check their hearts, placed a stethoscope under their shirts and bras, touched and rubbed their breasts and nipples, and pulled their clothing away to expose their breasts. The Administrative Complaint further alleged that in a police-controlled call afterward he commented on D.D.'s breasts.

The matters came to light through E.L.'s therapist's mandatory report to the Department and through A.B.'s and D.D.'s same-day reports to police. D.D.'s report led to his arrest for misdemeanor battery; that charge was dismissed after he completed pretrial diversion. The judge found the three unconnected patients credible, found the psychiatrist not credible, and noted that he kept refilling E.L.'s and D.D.'s medications for months after they refused to return, had bought an insurance policy from A.B. and given her $200 cash during a visit, and signed many visit notes months or years late. Both parties' experts agreed that touching a patient's breast is outside the scope of psychiatric practice. The Board denied his exceptions and revoked his license.
cases.outcome: License revoked (Board accepted the ALJ's recommended penalty, which also proposed a $15,000 fine and costs); ruling on the Department's motion to assess costs deferred to a later meeting.

narrative: The psychiatrist, who had a history of alcohol use disorder with relapse, entered a Consent Order in which he made admissions and the Board made findings. In July 2024 the Board received a complaint about his relationship with Patient A, whom he had treated on and off from 2016 until about July 2021. In August 2021, after formal termination of treatment, he began a sexual relationship with Patient A that lasted about eight months; he admitted that several sexual encounters took place at the office after hours and described the relationship as part of an alcohol relapse, while stating he never practiced while intoxicated or drank on duty. An outside expert also found his care of Patient B below the standard. Patient B, a 54-year-old man, came to him in March 2021 after his previous psychiatrist died, carrying a bipolar disorder diagnosis and taking aripiprazole 10 mg and bupropion XL 300 mg daily, having been on aripiprazole for years. The psychiatrist took no detailed mood history and accepted the diagnosis from the prior provider, although Patient B's intake questionnaire reported no bipolar symptoms; the antipsychotic was continued and Patient B developed tardive dyskinesia. His documentation was found inadequate to support the diagnosis, and his use of multiple medications may have increased the risk.

Patient C, who had harassed providers he supervised and been discharged from the practice, complained to the Board in March 2022. On the evening of August 2, 2021, after learning of her threatening messages to his supervisee, he phoned her and, when she said she was alone in a parking lot allegedly drinking, went to meet her and asked that her husband be present. She reported that he arrived about 9:30 p.m. with a beer that he drank, talked with her in her car for about two hours, and shared his own substance-abuse problems with her husband. He made no record of the encounter, saying its purpose was her safety rather than clinical care. After a Board-ordered North Carolina Professionals Health Program (NCPHP) examination in July 2024, NCPHP could not support his safety to practice; neuropsychological testing found him in need of treatment for boundary-violation behavior and alcohol use disorder. He signed a five-year NCPHP contract, inactivated his license at the Board's request in September 2024, and acknowledged unprofessional conduct and inability to practice with reasonable skill and safety.
cases.outcome: License indefinitely suspended (may apply for reinstatement any time after the order); obey all laws, attend investigative interviews and provide compliance information on request. License had already been inactivated at the Board's request (September 19, 2024); a five-year NCPHP monitoring contract was signed in August 2024, outside the order.

narrative: The psychiatrist, licensed since 1990 and whose license had expired unrenewed in 2021 after he retired, surrendered it without admitting the charges, agreeing only that the Board could establish a factual basis for the Accusation's charges of gross negligence and general unprofessional conduct.

According to the Accusation, the psychiatrist had treated Patient A, an adult man with paranoid schizophrenia, for at least a decade in a hospital-employed position, including regular alprazolam prescriptions from about 2017 to 2020. By 2020 the patient was significantly impaired and unable to care for himself; his wife was his caregiver and accompanied him to appointments, and in March 2020 the psychiatrist noted that she had been told she would need to seek a conservatorship because he was gravely disabled. While still treating Patient A, the psychiatrist became romantically and sexually involved with the wife (in 2020 by his account, or late 2019 by hers). In August 2020 he self-reported the relationship to his employer, which opened an investigation, informed the patient, and transferred his care to another physician; the psychiatrist retired days later. In a 2024 Board interview he admitted the sexual relationship. The Accusation, citing APA and AMA ethics guidance on romantic or sexual relationships with key third parties, alleged that a sexual relationship with the spouse and caregiver of a current patient was an extreme departure from the standard of care.
cases.outcome: License surrender accepted; costs of $47,002 payable before any new or reinstated license; any reapplication treated as a petition for reinstatement with the Accusation's allegations deemed admitted.

narrative: In August 2024 the Board opened an investigation after receiving credible information that the psychiatrist had failed to provide the standard of care in psychiatry, had engaged in unprofessional conduct by behaving in a way that a patient could reasonably construe as sexually suggestive and non-therapeutic, and had engaged in conduct contrary to recognized standards of medical ethics. In July 2025 he entered an Interim Stipulated Order withdrawing from practice and placing his license on inactive status pending the investigation. The order does not describe the patient(s) or the specific behavior.

In the Stipulated Order he neither admitted nor denied the matter, but the Board found that he engaged in unprofessional or dishonorable conduct contrary to recognized standards of medical ethics and conduct that does or might constitute a danger to a patient's health, repeated acts of negligence, and gross negligence in the practice of medicine.
cases.outcome: Reprimand; retired Oregon license while under investigation and agreed never to reapply in Oregon; July 2025 Interim Stipulated Order terminated.

narrative: This file contains two recent actions. In a February 2022 Consent Agreement, the psychiatrist admitted that from 1985 to 2002 he had a sexual relationship with someone he was concurrently treating as a psychiatric patient for depression and anxiety. He also admitted that he had an ethical duty not to have a sexual relationship with a current patient, while stating that he had never had sexual contact with any other current or former patient. He further admitted that after an approximately 20-minute telephone appointment on or about March 23, 2021, his office billed two different codes to the patient's insurer for the same visit. As a result, the patient paid two deductibles and the psychiatrist received two payments. He admitted that the visit should not have been billed this way and described it as a one-time coding error. The Board treated this conduct as a violation of the AMA code of ethics and reprimanded him, with probation until he completed courses.

In January 2026 he signed a Permanent Surrender, with consent to permanent revocation, in lieu of formal proceedings under the same code-of-ethics provision. The new matter related to not properly conducting examinations on patients before prescribing medications to treat them. The surrender gives no further facts (patients, medications, or time period) and contains no admission of underlying facts. Earlier history: in 1998 he was reprimanded under a consent agreement for failing to respond to a Board continuing-medical-education audit. The Board acknowledged that he had in fact completed the required CME.
cases.outcome: 2022: reprimand; probation with quarterly declarations and Board appearances until completion of courses in medical billing/coding and professional ethics/boundaries (with written reports). 2026: permanent surrender accepted; license permanently revoked.

narrative: This Order of Emergency Suspension was issued by the State Surgeon General without a hearing as an interim action pending formal proceedings. The emergency order stated that the psychiatrist, in an outpatient practice, provided medication management by Zoom to two adult women. Patient S.A., 29, treated for major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder and OCD from 2020 to 2024, disclosed body-image concerns in a September 2024 session. He asked to assess her body to suggest exercises, had her change into a two-piece bathing suit, directed her to bring the camera close to parts of her body and show her pelvic bones, and asked her to email weekly photographs of her body from every angle; she sent six, and he later emailed asking for updates. At a December 2024 session he again had her change into a bathing suit, commented that her breasts looked larger, proposed using her breasts as the marker of change, and, when she asked whether he wanted her to show her bare breasts, replied yes if she was comfortable. She refused and stopped seeing him.

Patient C.B., 33, treated for four years for bipolar II disorder, ADHD and depression, said that after her psychologist left, the psychiatrist lengthened sessions to an hour and began examining her body, telling her, as someone underweight, that she had to be at a certain weight to take certain medications. He progressively asked her to wear less clothing, to remove her top and to lower her shorts so he could inspect her pelvic area, and in June 2025 told her to send weekly photographs in underwear or a bikini with her weight written on them. She stopped treatment. The order found no bona fide medical purpose for the examinations or photographs and concluded that he posed an immediate serious danger to the public.
cases.outcome: License immediately suspended by emergency order (interim action without a hearing); formal disciplinary proceedings to follow.

narrative: This Amendment to Public Consent Order modified the physician's 2022 Public Consent Order (Case 187), which the amendment describes as entered because of alleged 'improper intimate contact with a patient' on or about September 4, 2020. The 2022 order had restricted his practice to male patients and allowed him to petition, after one year, with a psychiatrist's evaluation that he was 'safe to practice medicine with a female population.' The amendment found that on or about November 30, 2023 he underwent a full evaluation by a psychiatrist who deemed him safe to practice with female patients and documented his compliance with the psychotherapy and treatment the 2022 order required, and that in September 2025 the same evaluator wrote to the Board confirming continued compliance and continued safety to treat women. He admitted these findings. The amendment adds no new facts about the original conduct and imposes no new sanction; it replaces the male-only restriction with a chaperone requirement and leaves all other terms of the 2022 order in force.
cases.outcome: Male-patients-only restriction replaced: may treat female patients only in the presence of a Board-pre-approved chaperone, documenting in each female patient's record that a chaperone was present and naming the chaperone, with records produced on request; all other terms of the 2022 probation remain in effect.

narrative: The psychiatrist practiced in a private office setting. Patient A, a 33-year-old woman, was referred to him for diagnostic testing for attention deficit disorder. While she waited on a couch in his private office to hear the results, he sat beside her, although other seating was available, close enough to make her uncomfortable, and rubbed her back and touched her leg as he discussed the results. When she left, visibly upset, he followed her and put his hand on the wall near her, effectively blocking her exit. In her car she was shaking and crying; she said she felt violated and compared his touch to that of a romantic partner. The Board noted similar earlier complaints: in 2014 a minor patient's mother said he sat so close to her child that their legs touched and put his hand on her own shoulder; in 2017 a patient said he commented on her attractiveness and offered her 'a bite off his banana' while eating one; in 2018 a patient said he called her 'a good-looking lady' and held her wrists; and in 2021 and 2022 patients reported comments on their attractiveness, fitness and 'girlish figure,' one after he asked her to move so he could sit beside her and put his hand on her shoulder. Staff also complained of rude or belittling communication.

The Board had twice asked him to take CME on communication; despite multiple hours of CME on boundaries and sexual misconduct, his behavior did not change, and in a 2025 subpanel interview he blamed patients for being 'too sensitive.' A Board-ordered forensic fitness-for-duty evaluation found no cognitive deficits but poor self-regulation, impulsivity and limited awareness of professional boundaries; it judged him safe to practice with monitoring, recommended no physical contact with patients unless medically necessary and no banter, and warned that further credible similar complaints should be grounds for surrender. In the Consent Order the psychiatrist made admissions and the Board found that his conduct was unprofessional conduct, a departure from the ethics of the profession.
cases.outcome: One-year suspension with 60 days active (November 1 - December 31, 2026), the remainder stayed on conditions: trained, Board-certified chaperone present and documented for all female patient encounters; CPEP ProBE ethics course within six months; compliance with all recommendations of the fitness-for-duty evaluation; summary suspension on probable cause of noncompliance.

narrative: According to the Accusation, the psychiatrist, in solo private practice, began treating a patient in 2007 in connection with a workers' compensation claim for severe anxiety, possible PTSD, and selective mutism, and provided psychotherapy until about 2018. When the patient became embroiled in civil litigation with her neighbors, the psychiatrist signed numerous declarations under penalty of perjury in the patient's support (2017-2018), identifying herself as the patient's doctor and asserting as fact that the neighbors had harassed, bullied, sexually harassed, and illegally recorded the patient, that they had caused the patient's anxiety disorders and were liable for future treatment estimated at about $68,000, and offering opinions that particular neighbors were not credible, had a history of drug use, or were paranoid, although she had never examined them. She attached her bills for the patient's care, including a $7,900 bill for "room and board" when the patient stayed in her home, and sent a letter to opposing counsel claiming power of attorney to speak for the patient. The Accusation alleged that she acknowledged the patient wrote the declarations and that she signed them without knowing whether the contents were true, because she thought it would help the patient's case, and that she had a friendship with the patient alongside treatment: they traveled together (including to visit her family out of state), dined and shopped together, and each stayed in the other's home. She produced a certification that she had no medical records for the patient.

The Accusation charged gross negligence and repeated negligent acts for crossing doctor-patient boundaries and for submitting declarations presenting a patient's accounts and opinions about unexamined third parties as fact, plus inadequate records. It also cited prior discipline in 2012 (stayed revocation with probation) for false statements in a workers' compensation psychiatric report and billing and a misdemeanor conviction for prescribing hydrocodone by fraud. The psychiatrist surrendered her license, agreeing that the complainant could establish a factual basis for the charges; no findings were made.
cases.outcome: License surrender accepted; any future petition for reinstatement to be treated as a petition for reinstatement of a revoked or surrendered license, with all Accusation allegations deemed true.

narrative: The psychiatrist began treating Patient 1, a 29-year-old woman, in October 2014 for psychiatric symptoms following a motor vehicle accident, including anxiety, insomnia, fatigue, cognitive complaints, and back and neck pain, with a significant family psychiatric and substance-use history. According to the Accusation, he prescribed zolpidem regularly from June 2015 to March 2022, at average daily doses in 2016 (22.6 mg) and later years above the recommended maximum, and alprazolam regularly from February 2016 to March 2022, with average doses ranging from about 2 mg to 9 mg per day. CURES showed several early refills only five to six days after prior fills in late 2018 and early 2019, yet the records indicated he did not query CURES until March 2020, despite the mandate that took effect in October 2018, and then not again until December 2021.

The Accusation further alleged that in November 2018, while still treating Patient 1 and prescribing her alprazolam and zolpidem, the psychiatrist purchased a home jointly with her (by his account, he paid 80 percent and she 20 percent), compromising his objectivity and effectiveness as her psychiatrist. These were charged as repeated negligent acts: failure to properly monitor controlled-substance treatment and entering a joint real-estate purchase with an active patient. In the stipulated settlement the psychiatrist did not admit the allegations but agreed that the Board could establish a factual basis for them and gave up his right to contest them. The public reprimand was expressly issued for an improper business transaction with a patient and inappropriate monitoring after prescribing controlled substances.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand; education course (40 hours); cost recovery of $12,861.57.

narrative: The psychiatrist, who practiced psychiatry in North Carolina, entered a Consent Order in which he stipulated to findings made by the Board. In July 2023 the chief executive officer of his employer notified the Board of a change in his staff privileges based on allegations of professional boundary violations and substandard prescribing. He had hired Person A as his scribe and paid her salary and health insurance personally; Person A complained that he crossed professional boundaries. He acknowledged that, in addition to employing her, he treated Person A as a patient for psychiatric issues and gave her ketamine injections at her apartment. The investigation also found that he treated another former employee and prescribed her diazepam for anxiety. His employer terminated him and summarily suspended his privileges pending an ad hoc committee's investigation.

In May 2024 the Board ordered him to the North Carolina Professionals Health Program (NCPHP), which recommended a comprehensive evaluation; an outside assessment program evaluated him in late May 2024 and made treatment recommendations. In July 2024 NCPHP told the Board that he had chosen not to follow its recommendations and would close his practice and retire. The Board concluded that his conduct was unprofessional conduct, and the order inactivated his license.
cases.outcome: License inactivated by consent order (physician retiring after declining NCPHP-recommended treatment); obey all laws, investigative interviews and compliance information on request; in effect until the Board orders otherwise.

narrative: After investigating the psychiatrist's care of Patient A, the Board issued a Public Letter of Concern, which it states is not a disciplinary action; the psychiatrist signed a consent to its issuance. According to the letter, Patient A, a 49-year-old man who was a licensed mental health worker with extensive experience in the therapeutic use of ketamine, recruited the psychiatrist in October 2021 into a ketamine-assisted psychotherapy program alongside the psychiatrist's existing clinic-based ketamine practice. The two were colleagues and became personal friends, and the friendship continued after Patient A became a patient. In December 2021 Patient A, who had a history of anxiety, asked for ketamine treatment at the clinic; the psychiatrist approved him and he received intramuscular ketamine injections in December 2021 and in May and June 2022, reporting improvement. In August 2022, when Patient A asked for ketamine at home, the psychiatrist prescribed 20 ketamine 200 mg troches and 90 ketamine 50 mg tablets "as needed for mood and pain relief," and on Patient A's request on September 13 prescribed refills of both, which were filled on September 15 and 26. Patient A died by suicide on September 27, 2022; the letter notes it is unknown whether ketamine use, or the factors that led him to seek home ketamine, contributed.

An independent expert reviewer found the care may have fallen below the standard of care, criticizing the failure to maintain appropriate boundaries, including relying on Patient A's own experience and knowledge to guide his ketamine treatment; documentation lacking a detailed history, psychosocial assessment, consideration of comorbidities or alternative diagnoses, a rationale for ketamine, alternatives, or a risk-benefit discussion; and prescribing home ketamine without an in-person visit, without documenting the course of treatment, and without communicating with Patient A's other providers. The Board stated its concern and noted with approval that the psychiatrist had already taken substantial steps to address it.
cases.outcome: Public Letter of Concern (expressly not disciplinary); agreed to complete at least 8 hours of Board-approved Category I CME on maintaining professional boundaries within six months.

narrative: The psychiatrist, board-certified in psychiatry, ran her own practice and was medical director of a transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) center. In March 2024 a provider treating Patient 1 at a psychiatric facility reported boundary concerns. Patient 1 had come to the psychiatrist around 2017 with disabling depression and anxiety; from about 2019, while still in treatment, the psychiatrist maintained a personal relationship with her. They exchanged hundreds of personal texts and emails in which the psychiatrist told Patient 1 she loved and missed her, used affectionate nicknames, and discussed her own grief over a family member's death. They exchanged gifts (clothing, gift cards, items for a dog the psychiatrist had encouraged Patient 1 to adopt); the psychiatrist gave Patient 1 a $1,300 check for rent, drove her to and from medical appointments, and, after Patient 1 went on disability, arranged her placement as a volunteer and later part-time employee in a charitable program the psychiatrist had set up within a non-profit.

In an under-oath interview the psychiatrist also admitted providing psychotherapy and prescribing controlled substances to people with whom she had close personal or financial ties: an immediate family member (34 Schedule II and IV prescriptions from 2019 to 2024 in non-emergency situations); four current or former employees, including physician assistants (one former PA received 102 prescriptions from 2020 to 2024, and another employee received ten prescriptions in 2019 with only one note in her chart); and a friend and business partner (20 prescriptions, 2020 to 2024). The Consent Order, agreed to after charges and a case-resolution conference, contains these findings, cites APA and AMA ethics guidance on exploitation and on treating family, colleagues, and acquaintances, and concludes she was guilty of unprofessional conduct.
cases.outcome: Reprimand; probation minimum 2 years with enrollment in and compliance with the Maryland Professional Rehabilitation Program; courses in professional boundaries, medical ethics, and prescribing within 6 months; $10,000 civil fine within 6 months; no early termination.

narrative: The psychiatrist worked as a child and adolescent psychiatrist, in part for an organization providing mental health treatment to youth in foster care. According to the Accusation, Patient 1 began treatment with him at age 14 in 2017; she had a history of neglect, sexual abuse, and trauma by caregivers, and was diagnosed with ADHD and oppositional defiant disorder (rule out bipolar disorder and PTSD). He continued prescribing for her after she turned 18. He allegedly texted her on his personal cell phone, remarked that he might have to come over and spank her when she forgot her medication, took her to a birthday dinner, bought gifts for her and her child, and followed her on social media. In June 2021 he arranged a Sunday "appointment" outside the office: he picked her up, hugged her, took her to lunch and a shopping center he frequented personally, held her hand, repeatedly touched her lower back, said he wanted to spoil her, and ended by having her join him in the back seat of his car, where she lay in his lap while he massaged her shoulders, head, and face. His chart note described only medication issues. The patient texted him that she felt uncomfortable and ended treatment with him. He told investigators the touching was supportive and therapeutic and denied many of her allegations.

The Accusation also alleged that over about five years beginning in 2015 he treated Patient 2, a teenage foster youth with a history of sexual abuse and suicidal behavior, while texting her on his personal phone, including her in outings with his family, and giving her gifts (including an emotional support dog), continuing after agency staff counseled him about boundaries in 2018. The charges were gross negligence (boundary and ethics violations) and repeated negligent acts; no sexual misconduct offense was charged. The case was resolved by stipulated settlement in which the psychiatrist did not contest that a prima facie case could be established.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 7 years' probation with 90 days' actual suspension, 40 hours/year of education in boundaries/professionalism, professionalism (ethics) program, professional boundaries program before resuming practice, practice monitor; solo practice prohibited; telehealth only (no in-person practice) and no treatment of female patients, with required patient notification log; prohibited from supervising PAs/advanced practice nurses; cost recovery of $66,389.75.

narrative: The psychiatrist's license had been under emergency suspension since 2018 (the file includes the March 2018 Emergency Order of Suspension, a July 2018 amended order, and the Complaint and Amended Complaint). According to the stipulated facts, in June 2017 FBI and DEA agents executed a search warrant at his practice. He was seen putting a fast-food bag into a trash can and taking two thick envelopes from a credenza; the envelopes held cash, checks and a list of patient names and amounts, and the bag held marijuana. In 2018 he was indicted in state court for felony tampering with physical evidence and for marijuana possession, and in federal court for conspiracy to distribute Schedule II, III and IV controlled substances and 25 counts of distributing Schedule II and III drugs without a legitimate medical purpose and outside the usual course of professional practice. He did not renew his license after February 2020.

In about February 2021 he pleaded guilty to distributing and dispensing Schedule II, III and IV controlled substances without a legitimate medical purpose; the other charges were dropped. In the plea he admitted prescribing high doses and large quantities, giving early refills, continuing to prescribe to patients he knew were addicted or whose drug tests were negative for the prescribed drugs, prescribing controlled substances in return for sexually graphic photos and videos, prescribing drugs contraindicated by patients' medical conditions or not typically associated with psychiatric complaints, and prescribing dangerous combinations. He was sentenced to 60 months in prison and three years of supervised release. In the Agreed Order of Permanent Surrender the parties stipulated to these facts and to conclusions that his conduct violated the Medical Practice Act.
cases.outcome: Permanent surrender of the Kentucky license; the Board will never consider reinstatement or modification; costs of $875.

narrative: The psychiatrist, a board-certified geriatric psychiatrist employed as a staff psychiatrist in a state correctional psychiatric inpatient program who also had a part-time private geriatric practice, was the subject of an Accusation based on a misdemeanor criminal conviction. After a hearing, an administrative law judge found that in 2018 police responded to a domestic violence call at the psychiatrist's home after his wife reported that he had pushed her down a flight of stairs during an argument about her plan to travel abroad with their toddler; officers observed abrasions on her shins. The psychiatrist first told officers he had not touched her and that she slipped, then admitted he had touched or tapped her shoulder while telling her to get out, but denied that this caused the fall. He was arrested, charged with felony corporal injury to a spouse, and pled no contest to misdemeanor battery on a spouse; he was placed on three years of court probation with a work-alternative program, community service, a 52-week anger management course, and fines. In a later Board interview he again initially attributed the fall to his wife's emotional state before acknowledging touching her.

The judge found that the battery and the inconsistent statements about his culpability constituted unprofessional conduct and that the conviction was substantially related to the duties of a physician, rejecting the argument that it was a purely personal matter. In mitigation, the judge found that he had completed the anger management course, stress management, couples counseling, and an ethics and professionalism course, had complied with criminal probation, had excellent work evaluations with no evidence of misconduct at work, and had a single conviction. The judge found a deviation from the disciplinary guidelines (which call for at least stayed revocation and five years' probation) warranted.
cases.outcome: Public reproval (public reprimand); no probation imposed.

narrative: The psychiatrist was charged in an Accusation with dangerous use of alcohol, a substantially related criminal conviction, and general unprofessional conduct arising from a 2017 single-vehicle crash; in the stipulated settlement he admitted the truth of every charge and allegation. According to the Accusation, at about 1:40 a.m. highway patrol officers found his car against a large pole at a freeway off-ramp with major front-end damage and deployed airbags. A passenger said they had been driving home from a bar or nightclub. The psychiatrist had red, watery eyes, slurred speech, and a strong odor of alcohol; he admitted driving and drinking two 16-ounce beers, failed field sobriety tests, and gave breath samples of about 0.13%. He was arrested, and a blood sample drawn shortly afterward measured 0.175%. He was found to have a broken back and underwent surgery the next day; the car was totaled.

He was charged with misdemeanor driving under the influence and driving with a blood alcohol level of 0.08% or more, with an enhancement allegation of 0.15% or more, and in 2019 pleaded no contest to driving at 0.08% or above. He was sentenced to four days in jail, three years of court probation, a three-month DUI program, and fines. In a 2020 Board interview he acknowledged having had a glass of wine at dinner and about two to three beers and a Jell-O shot at the bar in the hours before the crash.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 3 years' probation with abstention from alcohol and controlled substances, biological fluid testing, professionalism (ethics) program, psychiatric evaluation, psychotherapy if recommended, and probation monitoring costs.

narrative: After a hearing at which the psychiatrist did not appear (he was incarcerated and his attorney declined to attend), an administrative law judge found that in 2021 he was convicted in federal court, on his guilty plea to one count of a 23-count indictment, of illegally importing a firearm, specifically a silencer shipped in packaging labeled as a motorcycle fuel filter. In his plea agreement he admitted importing at least 13 firearms into the country by similar methods. He was sentenced to 18 months in prison and a $10,000 fine, with a mental health evaluation, evaluation for residential drug treatment, and three years of supervised release requiring drug testing, substance abuse treatment, alcohol abstinence, and mental health treatment. His license had been suspended in late 2021 because of the conviction. The First Amended Accusation further alleged that federal agents searching his homes had found 13 suppressors, 18 firearms (some loaded, including assault weapons), and a substance that field-tested positive for methamphetamine next to a handgun and rifle.

The judge also found that, during the Board investigation that began with a 2020 complaint, he agreed to physical and psychiatric examinations. He reported taking buprenorphine for chronic back pain and Adderall without an ADHD diagnosis, yet his witnessed urine screen was negative for both. The Board's psychiatric evaluator concluded that his trauma history and stressors required monitoring, a year of weekly psychotherapy, substance abuse treatment, random drug screens, and second opinions on the need for Adderall and opioids. The judge found cause for discipline both for a substantially related conviction and because his psychological condition required restrictions to practice safely, and, with no mitigation or rehabilitation evidence presented, concluded that public protection required revocation.
cases.outcome: License revoked; payment of $4,446.25 in investigation and prosecution costs is a condition of any reinstatement.

narrative: The psychiatrist, who practiced adult and child psychiatry in North Carolina, entered an Interim Non-Practice Agreement with the Board after being criminally charged in federal court. According to the agreement's findings, on or about June 21, 2022, he was charged with one count of knowingly possessing, and accessing with intent to view, material containing child pornography, between about August and September 22, 2021, transported by means of interstate commerce including by computer. He pleaded not guilty and was granted pretrial release on June 27, 2022. The agreement does not describe the underlying facts beyond the wording of the charge, and makes no finding that the conduct occurred.

The psychiatrist acknowledged only that the conduct alleged in the criminal charge, if true, would constitute unprofessional conduct and grounds for the Board to suspend, revoke, or limit his license. This was an interim, agreed measure pending the criminal case, not a final disciplinary decision. It was later amended to continue indefinitely after a superseding indictment (Case 195), and the license was revoked after his felony convictions (Case 196).
cases.outcome: Interim agreement not to practice medicine, effective until the criminal charge was resolved or December 31, 2022, whichever came first (unless extended); notify the Board of any change of residence; noncompliance would be unprofessional conduct.

narrative: The psychiatrist, who practiced adult and child psychiatry in North Carolina, had agreed in July 2022 not to practice while a federal charge of possession of child pornography was pending (Case 194); that agreement was to end when the charge was resolved or on December 31, 2022. This Amended Interim Non-Practice Agreement recites that on November 15, 2022, he was charged with additional counts, including one count of production and one count of transportation of child pornography. The government moved to revoke his bond; he was arraigned on the superseding indictment on November 18, 2022, pleaded not guilty, and the court denied the bond-revocation motion. His trial was continued from January to March 2023 on his unopposed motion. While awaiting trial he was supervised by federal pretrial services, wore an ankle monitor, was under house arrest, and had his electronic devices monitored.

As in the original agreement, the psychiatrist acknowledged only that the conduct alleged in the criminal charges, if true, would constitute unprofessional conduct; the agreement makes no finding that the conduct occurred. This was an interim, agreed measure that replaced the time-limited non-practice term with an open-ended one. His license was later revoked after his felony convictions (Case 196).
cases.outcome: Interim agreement not to practice medicine until permitted by the Board President; meanwhile may not supervise any advanced practice provider or own or operate any business that practices medicine; an ex parte probable-cause finding of noncompliance is grounds for summary suspension; obey all laws; report address changes; in effect until the Board orders otherwise.

narrative: The psychiatrist, licensed since 1998 and representing himself, admitted the truth of every charge and allegation in the Accusation and surrendered his license. The Accusation alleged that he owned and operated a drug treatment center offering detoxification, partial hospitalization, intensive outpatient, and outpatient services. In September 2020 he waived indictment and pleaded guilty in federal court to a felony count of conspiracy to pay illegal remunerations for referrals to recovery homes. In May 2022 he was sentenced to 15 months in federal prison and three years' supervised release and ordered to pay $493,104.35 in restitution; he reported to prison in August 2022. He did not report the felony charge or conviction to the Board within 30 days as required.

The Accusation also described two drunk-driving arrests. In April 2020 highway patrol stopped him for driving about 90 mph in a 65 mph zone; he admitted drinking, failed field sobriety tests, and had breath alcohol results of 0.15 and 0.16 percent. In February 2021 a witness identified him as the driver who struck a parked car outside a hotel and left; officers found him in the lobby smelling of alcohol and unsteady, and he could not complete sobriety tests and refused breath and chemical testing. In October 2021 he was convicted of misdemeanor DUI offenses arising from both arrests and placed on five years' summary probation. The Accusation noted a 2010 DUI conviction, a 2015 reckless driving conviction, and a 2018 Board public reprimand for alcohol use, a substantially related conviction, and unprofessional conduct.
cases.outcome: License surrender accepted; costs of $8,459.25 payable before any new or reinstated license; allegations deemed admitted in any reinstatement petition or other California health licensing application.

narrative: An administrative law judge found, after a contested hearing, that the psychiatrist, licensed in late 2019 and then a psychiatry resident, was convicted on a nolo contendere plea of misdemeanor driving with a blood alcohol content of 0.08 percent or more. In June 2021, after a morning shift, he attended a party hosted by an attending physician, drank several glasses of champagne without food, and drove home alone. Feeling impaired, he tried to exit the freeway but lost control of the car and struck a concrete divider on the off-ramp. Responding police noted an odor of alcohol and red, watery eyes; he performed poorly on field sobriety tests, and breath tests about 90 minutes later showed a blood alcohol content of about 0.19 percent. He admitted at hearing that he had not been candid with the officer, saying he had drunk one hard seltzer. The court imposed 36 months' summary probation, fines, a first-offender alcohol program, and a victim impact program, all of which he completed. The judge found cause for discipline for a substantially related conviction, use of alcohol in a manner dangerous to himself and the public, and unprofessional conduct.

The judge also found substantial rehabilitation: an addiction medicine evaluation concluded he did not have an alcohol use disorder, he had abstained since the arrest with 335 negative monitored breath tests, he attended AA and therapy, and supervisors and colleagues testified to his clinical skill and the absence of any alcohol concerns at work. Because he rebutted the presumption that he was a substance-abusing licensee, the judge concluded that probation would be unduly harsh and that a public reprimand was sufficient. Costs were reduced by 75 percent in light of his income and student debt.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand; cost recovery of $4,345 (reduced from $17,383.75) payable within six months.

narrative: According to the Accusation, in March 2021 police saw a car driven by the psychiatrist going the wrong way on a one-way street at high speed and running stop signs. Officers lost sight of it, then found it parked with two passengers inside and the driver's seat empty; the passengers said the driver had parked and fled on foot. The psychiatrist returned soon afterward, said he had been driving, and denied drinking. Officers noted the odor of alcohol, watery and unfocused eyes, slurred speech, and an unsteady gait. He performed poorly on field sobriety tests, would not blow into the preliminary alcohol screening device, and was arrested. At the hospital where a warrant-authorized blood draw was attempted, he repeatedly pulled the needle out, flailed, and yelled, and staff could not obtain blood after three attempts. At the jail he cried and made threats against himself, and was placed in a padded safety cell.

He was charged with misdemeanor DUI and with resisting or obstructing an officer. In March 2022 he pleaded no contest to DUI, with a stipulated blood alcohol concentration of 0.08%; the resisting count was dropped. He was sentenced to three years' supervised probation, two days in jail, a three-month alcohol education program, and fines. The Accusation charged conviction of a substantially related crime, use of alcohol in a manner dangerous to himself and the public, and unprofessional conduct. In the stipulated settlement he did not contest that the complainant could establish a prima facie case; he made no admissions and no findings were made.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 3 years' probation with abstinence from controlled substances and alcohol, biological fluid testing, professionalism (ethics) program, notification of hospitals/facilities/insurers, and prohibition on supervising PAs/APNs; cost recovery $10,045.00.

narrative: According to the Accusation, on a November 2021 afternoon (about 3:15 p.m.) the psychiatrist was in a motor vehicle collision while under the influence of alcohol, and the other driver was injured. He was arrested at the scene for DUI causing injury. About three and a half hours later, two breath tests at the detention center showed blood alcohol concentrations of 0.26% and 0.263%, more than three times the legal limit. He was released the next day.

In March 2022 the prosecutor filed misdemeanor charges of driving under the influence and driving with a blood alcohol level of 0.08% or more. In April 2022 he pleaded no contest to the 0.08% count and was placed on three years' summary probation with 180 hours of community service and a nine-month first-offender alcohol and drug education and counseling program. The Accusation charged conviction of a substantially related crime and use of alcohol in a manner dangerous to himself or others, or impairing his ability to practice safely. It did not describe his practice or any patient care issue. In the stipulated settlement the psychiatrist admitted the truth of every charge and allegation in the Accusation.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 4 years' probation with waiver of right to seek early termination, abstinence from controlled substances and alcohol, psychotherapy, notice to employers/supervisors, biological fluid testing, substance abuse support group meetings, worksite monitor, notification of hospitals/facilities/insurers, and prohibition on supervising PAs/APNs; cost recovery $14,400.50.

narrative: The psychiatrist's license was revoked by an Entry of Revocation after he was convicted in federal district court of three felonies: possession of child pornography through interstate commerce by computer; employing, using, persuading, inducing, enticing, and coercing a minor to engage in sexually explicit conduct for the purpose of producing child pornography; and transportation and shipping of child pornography. Under North Carolina law a felony conviction results in automatic revocation unless the physician requests a hearing within 60 days of notice. The Board served its Notice of Revocation by certified mail on March 16, 2024, received no request for a hearing, and revoked the license by operation of law on May 28, 2024.

The Entry of Revocation contains no findings about the underlying conduct beyond the names of the offenses, and does not say whether any minor involved was a patient. Before the convictions, the psychiatrist, who had practiced adult and child psychiatry, had agreed not to practice while the charges were pending (Case 194, amended in Case 195).
cases.outcome: License revoked by operation of law after felony convictions (no hearing requested).

narrative: The physician's North Carolina license was revoked by an Entry of Revocation after he was convicted in federal district court in New Hampshire of one count of health care fraud, a felony. Under North Carolina law a felony conviction results in automatic revocation unless the physician requests a hearing within 60 days of notice. The Board served its Notice of Revocation by certified mail on February 6, 2024, and also served his counsel, who signed for it on March 22, 2024. Having received no request for a hearing, the Board revoked the license by operation of law on June 28, 2024.
The Entry of Revocation gives no facts about the fraud beyond the offense of conviction, and does not describe the physician's practice or specialty.
cases.outcome: License revoked by operation of law after a felony conviction for health care fraud (no hearing requested).

narrative: In October 2022, at about 11 p.m., highway patrol officers responded to a witness report of a possibly impaired driver who had been drifting between freeway lanes, nearly stopping on a freeway transition with no traffic ahead, forcing other drivers to brake or swerve, and nearly hitting another car after exiting. Officers located the vehicle weaving and straddling the double yellow line and stopped it; the driver was the psychiatrist. He had red, watery eyes, a strong odor of alcohol came from the vehicle, he walked with an unsteady gait, admitted drinking beer earlier, and failed field sobriety tests. He refused voluntary breath or blood testing, and a warrant blood draw taken about three hours after the witness's observations showed a blood alcohol concentration of 0.29 percent. In June 2023 he pleaded no contest to a misdemeanor count of driving with a blood alcohol level of 0.08 percent or more and was sentenced to three years' summary probation, including a nine-month first-offender alcohol and drug program and a hospital-and-morgue program.

The Accusation charged conviction of a substantially related crime, use of alcohol in a manner dangerous to himself or the public, and unprofessional conduct. No patient care was implicated. In the stipulated settlement the psychiatrist admitted the truth of each charge and allegation in the Accusation.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 5 years' probation with abstention from controlled substances and alcohol, biological fluid testing, substance abuse support group meetings, worksite monitor, psychiatric evaluation, psychotherapy, professionalism (ethics) program, 100 hours of free community service, employer notification; prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; cost recovery of $17,504.00.

narrative: This case arose from a criminal prosecution in a California superior court. According to the Accusation, in August 2022 the psychiatrist was convicted of two misdemeanors: prescribing, dispensing, or furnishing dangerous drugs without an appropriate prior examination and a medical indication, and failing to maintain adequate and accurate records relating to the provision of services to patients. The Board charged the psychiatrist with conviction of crimes substantially related to the qualifications, functions, or duties of a physician, conviction of a statute regulating dangerous drugs or controlled substances, and violation of the Medical Practice Act. The Accusation describes only the convictions themselves; it does not identify the patients, medications, or circumstances underlying the criminal case.
In the stipulated settlement, the psychiatrist admitted the truth of each and every charge and allegation in the Accusation.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; two years' probation with 40 hours/year of education courses, prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, professionalism (ethics) program, and practice monitor (or professional enhancement program); cost recovery of $15,452.00.

narrative: The psychiatrist was indicted by a county grand jury in October 2021. That indictment charged one count of engaging in a pattern of corrupt activity and five counts of trafficking in drugs, with forfeiture specifications. A second indictment in April 2024 charged another corrupt-activity count, nine counts of money laundering, and 136 counts of trafficking in drugs. On May 1, 2025, he pleaded guilty to three felony counts of Trafficking in Drugs, one with a forfeiture specification, and to Attempted Engaging in a Pattern of Corrupt Activity and Attempted Money Laundering. After the prosecutor reported the pleas, the Board issued a Notice of Immediate Suspension and Opportunity for Hearing in June 2025. That notice suspended his license at once under the statute that requires suspension after a guilty plea to a drug-trafficking felony.

He did not request a hearing. A Hearing Examiner reviewed the documentary evidence, and the Board adopted the Hearing Examiner's findings that the guilty pleas were a plea of guilty to a felony. In explaining why he recommended the maximum sanction, the Hearing Examiner wrote that, according to the indictments, from 2019 to 2021 the psychiatrist ran a pill mill. He described the drugs as buprenorphine and buprenorphine/naloxone, distributed for profit, with large sums subject to forfeiture. The order itself rests on the felony pleas; the document contains no clinical findings about individual patients.
cases.outcome: Immediate suspension (June 2025) upon guilty plea; after no hearing was requested, license permanently revoked and $20,000 fine.

narrative: According to the Second Amended Accusation, in October 2022 the psychiatrist sideswiped the concrete center-median wall of a highway while driving home in the evening. A highway patrol officer responding to the crash noted a strong odor of alcohol; the psychiatrist said another car had cut him off and denied drinking, but he had an unsteady gait, stumbled on the walk-and-turn, and was unable to complete field sobriety tests. He was arrested, and two breath tests showed blood alcohol concentrations of 0.19% and 0.18%. He was charged with misdemeanor driving under the influence and driving with a blood alcohol level of 0.08% or higher, with an excessive-blood-alcohol enhancement, and in January 2024 he pleaded no contest to the 0.08% count. The criminal court imposed three years' probation, a three-month first-offender DUI program, an ignition interlock device, and fines. No patient care issues were alleged.

The Second Amended Accusation charged conviction of a substantially related offense and use of alcohol in a manner dangerous to himself or others. The matter was resolved by stipulated settlement in which the psychiatrist did not admit the allegations but agreed that the Board could establish a factual basis for the charges at a hearing.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 5 years' probation with abstention from alcohol and controlled substances, random biological fluid testing, professionalism (ethics) program, psychiatric evaluation, psychotherapy, medical evaluation and treatment; prohibited from supervising PAs/advanced practice nurses; cost recovery of $18,289.80.

narrative: This is an Order of Emergency Suspension issued by the State Surgeon General without a hearing, an interim action pending formal disciplinary proceedings.
