The emergency order found only that in October 2025 the psychiatrist was arrested for attempted lewd and lascivious battery on a minor, using a computer or other device to solicit or attempt to solicit a minor for unlawful sexual activity, using a computer service or device to solicit certain illegal acts, and engaging in or attempting to engage in human trafficking of a minor for commercial sexual activity. The criminal case was pending at the time of the order. Florida law requires the Department to issue an emergency suspension order for any health care practitioner arrested for these categories of offenses, and the order stated that the suspension was mandated on that basis. The order describes no patient care or clinical conduct.
cases.outcome: License immediately suspended by emergency order (interim action without a hearing, mandatory upon arrest); formal disciplinary proceedings to follow.

narrative: The psychiatrist owned and operated a solo office practice. In February 2025 a federal indictment charged her with seven counts of distributing and dispensing controlled substances outside the usual course of professional practice and not for a legitimate medical purpose, and one count of maintaining her practice as a drug-involved premises. In May 2025 she pleaded guilty to one count of distributing and dispensing alprazolam, amphetamine-dextroamphetamine, and buprenorphine, and stipulated to a statement of facts: between at least January 2019 and June 2022 she prescribed these drugs to out-of-state 'customers,' including FBI undercover agents who recorded their visits; prescribed the combinations without warning of the risks of combining them or of mixing alprazolam with alcohol; kept prescribing after customers said they were selling their excess supply; prescribed buprenorphine to customers who did not claim opioid addiction; let customers choose their doses; provided no therapeutic services; did not check readily accessible databases for prescriptions from other physicians; rarely performed urinalysis; called in prescriptions without seeing the customer and had cash left under her office door; and advised customers how to split prescriptions among pharmacies. She was sentenced to 15 months in prison, two years of supervised release, and a $10,000 fine.

The Attorney General petitioned for revocation under the provision requiring revocation after conviction of a crime of moral turpitude. In a written response the psychiatrist did not contest the plea, admitted that her prescribing was improper and unlawful, and asked for a consent order allowing a reinstatement petition after one year, citing remorse and life stressors. The disciplinary panel found the facts above, held that mitigation was not a permissible issue in this proceeding, concluded the offense was a crime involving moral turpitude, and revoked the license as the statute requires.
cases.outcome: License revoked (mandatory revocation after conviction of a crime involving moral turpitude); request for a consent order permitting a reinstatement petition after one year declined.

narrative: The psychiatrist, board-certified in pediatrics, psychiatry, and child and adolescent psychiatry, worked for more than 20 years at an outpatient mental health clinic serving children who had experienced trauma, including community and domestic violence and sexual abuse. The clinic terminated her in August 2020 and filed a mandated 10-day report citing an escalating number of complaints from patients' caregivers and her disclosure of protected health information. After a two-day evidentiary hearing, an Administrative Law Judge found, and the Board panel adopted the findings, that on July 31, 2020, the day after the clinic asked her to undergo a fitness evaluation and stop seeing patients, the clinic discovered she had emailed protected health information of nine patients, including names, dates of birth, mental health diagnoses, and medications, to her two adult sons, who were not employed by the clinic or involved in the patients' care. She explained that she panicked about losing her job and that her sons were physicians. On August 6, while on leave, she requested and received confidential patient information, which she said she wanted for two research projects. She admitted both at the hearing.

The panel also relied on conduct she admitted from the caregiver complaints: routinely answering phone calls during patient sessions; telling a patient's caregiver that schools focused too much on slavery; and difficulties hearing and using the electronic record that the panel found affected patient care. Several caregivers had asked for their children to be transferred. The panel gave little weight to other complaints she did not address, such as remarks about birth control and about a patient's deceased parents, and declined to hold her responsible for reviewing a sexual-abuse history in front of a grandmother without a release, because obtaining consent forms was the front desk's job. It found that the conduct as a whole was unprofessional and that her disclosures violated the confidentiality rule of the medical profession.
cases.outcome: Reprimand; probation (no early termination; may petition after the Maryland Professional Rehabilitation Program finds her safe to practice without monitoring) with MPRP enrollment and compliance, and courses in implicit bias, patient confidentiality, and professional boundaries within 6 months; $5,000 civil fine within one year.

narrative: The psychiatrist was employed at a behavioral health organization. In the Consent Agreement, which the Board entered in lieu of formal proceedings, she admitted that in about December 2024 and/or March or April 2025 she accessed and printed the charts of two patients who were not under her care. She had no medical purpose and no consent from the patients or their families. The agreement records that she believed she was acting in good faith because she was concerned about patient safety. The Board treated the conduct as a violation of a national professional code of ethics.
cases.outcome: Reprimand (permanent); probationary terms including quarterly declarations and appearances on request; professional ethics/boundaries course within nine months with a written report; $3,000 fine.

narrative: The psychiatrist, board-certified in psychiatry and employed as a staff physician at a hospital, was the subject of an August 2025 complaint alleging that he had inappropriately accessed the medical records of a member of his family. The family member had raised the concern with the hospital, whose internal investigation determined that he had accessed her record without authorization on at least two occasions, viewing information that included her name, date of birth, phone number, medical record number, diagnosis, medications, dates and locations of service, and providers' names. The hospital issued him a written warning and required corrective action. In an interview with Board staff, the psychiatrist admitted that he had accessed the family member's record and that he had also prescribed medication to her on multiple occasions; the order does not identify the medications.

The matter was resolved before any charges issued, by a Consent Order in which the disciplinary panel found these facts, citing the federal HIPAA rules on use and disclosure of protected health information, and concluded that his conduct, 'including but not limited to, prescribing medication for a Family Member,' was unprofessional conduct in the practice of medicine.
cases.outcome: Reprimand (no probation or other terms).

narrative: The Board received a complaint alleging that the psychiatrist mismanaged a patient's care and then, upon learning of the patient's death, falsified the patient's medical records. The Board opened an investigation, and before any charges issued the psychiatrist submitted a Letter of Surrender, stating that he was surrendering his license to avoid further investigation and prosecution of the allegations and because he had retired. The letter does not describe the patient, the clinical situation, or the nature of the alleged falsification.

The psychiatrist did not admit the allegations as such, but agreed in the letter that for all purposes relevant to medical licensure they would be treated as proven and that they support a conclusion that he willfully made a false report or record in the practice of medicine, failed to meet appropriate standards for the delivery of quality medical care, and failed to keep adequate medical records. He waived his right to a hearing; the surrender, once accepted by Disciplinary Panel A, became a public final order and disciplinary action.
cases.outcome: Surrender of Maryland medical license accepted by Disciplinary Panel A (to be treated as a revoked licensee if reinstatement is ever sought); Controlled Dangerous Substances registration to be surrendered.

narrative: The psychiatrist applied for an unlimited Oregon medical license in April 2022. In September 2023 the Board issued a Notice of Intent to Deny License, proposing to deny the application because he had not established good moral character, and, as discipline, to refuse the license, impose a $10,000 civil penalty and assess costs. The Notice charged misrepresentation in applying for a license, knowingly making a false statement or representation on a matter, and failing to comply with a Board request during an investigation, including the duty to respond truthfully to the Board's inquiries. The Notice is not attached, so the misrepresentation itself is not described.

In the Stipulated Order he neither admitted nor denied the matter, but the Board found that he failed to qualify for licensure on good-moral-character grounds and that he engaged in the conduct described in the Notice, which violated each of those provisions.
cases.outcome: Reprimand; license application denied; agreed never to reapply for an Oregon medical license; must obey all laws pertaining to the practice of medicine.

narrative: In September 2020 the Board issued a Complaint and Notice of Proposed Disciplinary Action proposing sanctions up to the maximum allowed, including revocation and civil penalties, for unprofessional or dishonorable conduct (conduct contrary to recognized standards of medical ethics, or conduct, practice or condition that does or might adversely affect a physician's ability to practice safely and skillfully) and for impairment. The Notice is not attached, so the nature of the impairment and any related events are not described.

In the Stipulated Order the psychiatrist neither admitted nor denied the matter, but the Board found that she engaged in the conduct described in the Notice and that it violated both provisions. She was already participating in the state's Health Professionals' Services Program under an agreement with that program.
cases.outcome: Reprimand; must remain enrolled and in good standing in the Health Professionals' Services Program per her agreement; must obey all laws pertaining to the practice of medicine.

narrative: In October 2019, while living out of state, the psychiatrist was stopped by police for driving erratically at up to 105 miles per hour on an interstate highway; when the officer approached, she sped off and reached about 115 miles per hour before the officer ended the pursuit. Warrants issued for this and a similar incident two days earlier. After being taken into custody she was ordered to undergo a competency evaluation and was hospitalized at a state psychiatric hospital for about three weeks, where on admission she claimed hit men were trying to kill her; she was diagnosed with bipolar I disorder, recent manic episode, and found competent to stand trial. In August 2020 she was found guilty after a bench trial of two counts of felony eluding and two counts of misdemeanor reckless driving. The Board's license had already been suspended by an interim suspension order in January 2021.

At the Board's request, a psychiatrist evaluator reviewed complaints to the Board, a prior employer's reports of unusual behavior, court records, and hospital records, and interviewed her by videoconference in October 2020. He found her restless, not always rational, and delusional (she explained the speeding by saying a police officer was trying to kill her), with severely impaired judgment: she did not acknowledge boundary violations in allowing a patient she was treating to live on her boat and dine at her house, insisted she had to keep treating a patient after realizing she had a prior sexual relationship with him, and rejected psychiatric treatment for herself. He diagnosed bipolar I disorder, presently hypomanic, and narcissistic personality disorder, and concluded there were no terms under which she could safely practice. She did not file a notice of defense, and the Board, acting by default, found all allegations of the Accusation true: mental illness affecting her ability to practice safely, conviction of substantially related crimes, and unprofessional conduct.
cases.outcome: License revoked (default decision); any reapplication to be treated as a petition for reinstatement.

narrative: The physician, who had psychiatry/addiction training and a long history of opioid addiction, worked full time at an urgent care clinic while also treating his own cash-only psychiatric and Suboxone patients there. A 2018 complaint from a nurse practitioner alleged that he threatened staff with a firearm, bullied staff, and was impaired on duty; according to the Accusation, coworkers described him carrying a handgun at work, drinking from a flask, and once placing a gun on his desk and making a threatening remark. The administrative law judge found that two urine tests (2018 and 2019) were positive for buprenorphine, and the first also for clonazepam, alcohol, and cannabis, with no matching active prescriptions in CURES; loose pills were found on him during a 2019 search. He admitted obtaining his own buprenorphine for years from an out-of-state prescriber under an assumed name, paying cash, and treating 35 to 40 Suboxone patients. He had prior discipline in two other states, including a guilty plea to narcotic possession after obtaining Demerol through his position as a county medical examiner, and an indefinite suspension after prescribing Suboxone to his partner and diverting it.

After a three-day hearing, the judge found the Board's evaluating psychiatrist persuasive and unrebutted: she diagnosed severe opioid use disorder, mild alcohol use disorder, cannabis use disorder, and antisocial personality disorder, citing deceit, lack of insight, prescribing controlled substances to his partner and diverting the partner's clonazepam, socializing with addiction patients, keeping their charts unsecured, and practicing outside his training. He denied current substance abuse and disputed the diagnoses. The judge found by clear and convincing evidence that his ability to practice safely was impaired by mental illness and that his use of controlled substances was dangerous and impaired his practice; he was already under an interim suspension order.
cases.outcome: License revoked.

narrative: According to the Accusation, in October 2019 the psychiatrist saw a child for psychiatric treatment, accompanied by his mother, and arrived late with heavy-lidded eyes and slurred speech, was significantly confused about the patient's condition (referring to the child by the wrong gender and discussing the efficacy of a medication he was not taking), and the mother reported that she was under the influence. Two months earlier she had been arrested for driving under the influence after poor driving; her blood tested positive for multiple controlled substances, two of which she had prescribed to other members of her household, and bottles of controlled substances she had prescribed to her husband were found in her car, although she admitted to police taking only one medication. CURES data for 2017-2020 showed she prescribed to an employee and relatives the same substances found in her blood, and multiple pharmacies raised concerns about her co-prescribing of opioids and benzodiazepines and prescribing to family members; at least one refused to fill her future prescriptions. In her Board interview she denied illicit or recreational drug use and disclosed no substance treatment.

A Board-appointed psychiatrist noted that she prescribed large amounts of controlled substances to family members and an employee for the same drugs she used, received prescriptions for many of the same opioids and benzodiazepines herself, sought unauthorized refills, used medications without appropriate medical oversight, and lacked insight; the evaluator diagnosed opioid use disorder and sedative, hypnotic, or anxiolytic use disorder that, untreated, impaired her ability to practice safely. The Accusation charged impairment, dangerous use of drugs, dishonest false statements to the Board investigator, and practicing while impaired. Her license was already under an interim suspension order. She did not admit the allegations but agreed that the Board could establish a factual basis for the charges and surrendered her license.
cases.outcome: License surrendered; may not petition for reinstatement for two years, and the Accusation's allegations will be deemed admitted in any reinstatement or future licensing proceeding.

narrative: The Accusation in this case is brief and was brought solely as an action for mental impairment. According to the Accusation, during a Board investigation (whose origin is not described) the psychiatrist voluntarily underwent a psychiatric evaluation by a Board-approved evaluator, who reviewed her mental health records and investigation materials and examined her in person. In a June 2020 report, the evaluator opined that she suffers from a mental illness that impairs her ability to practice safely and that she was then unable to practice safely: she was only beginning to be stabilized and treated for an illness she had most likely had for several years, if not most of her adult life. During the evaluation she admitted to having an inappropriate relationship with a patient, among other admissions related to her mental health. The evaluator found that she did not understand doctor-patient boundaries, which could seriously affect a psychiatric patient's mental condition, and concluded that she needed ongoing psychiatric treatment and psychotropic medication, monitoring by a psychiatrist for depression and anxiety in addition to her bipolar disorder, and courses on HIPAA, boundary violations, and ethics. The Accusation does not describe the nature of the relationship with the patient.
The psychiatrist did not admit the allegations; she agreed that a prima facie case could be established at hearing and gave up her right to contest the charges.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 5 years' probation with 40 hours/year education (HIPAA, professional boundaries, ethics), professionalism program, professional boundaries program (no practice until completed), psychiatric evaluation (no practice until found mentally fit), psychotherapy, practice monitor, prohibition on supervising PAs/APNs, and probation monitoring costs.

narrative: The Accusation alleged that the psychiatrist, licensed since 1974, might be unable to practice medicine safely because of a medical condition. In August 2021 the Board received a complaint that the psychiatrist might be suffering from a medical condition affecting the ability to practice safely, and in January 2022 the psychiatrist asked the Board to accept surrender of the license, which had expired at the end of 2021 and had not been renewed. The document does not describe the nature of the condition or any patient care issue.

In the stipulated surrender, the psychiatrist admitted the truth of each charge and allegation in the Accusation (that is, the inability to practice safely due to a medical condition) and surrendered the license.
cases.outcome: License surrender accepted; costs of $1,118.75 payable before any new or reinstated license; any reapplication treated as a petition for reinstatement with the Accusation's allegations deemed admitted.

narrative: The file for this case contains only the psychiatrist's earlier Ohio discipline; the August 2022 Consent Agreement itself is not included, so what is known about the 2021-present action comes from the Board's own listing. According to that listing, the psychiatrist admitted that his history of, and treatment for, substance abuse constituted impairment of his ability to practice because of habitual or excessive use of drugs, alcohol or other substances, and that he violated the Board's rules on entering a Board-approved monitoring program after treatment and the conditions of limitation placed on his license. The listing gives no detail about the substance, the circumstances of relapse or treatment, or how the matter came to the Board's attention. His license was indefinitely suspended for at least 90 days and remained subject to the 2018 Board Order; a December 2023 Consent Agreement reinstated it with at least five years' probation.

The 2018 Board Order in the file followed a hearing. The Board found that the psychiatrist, a child and adolescent psychiatrist at a community mental health agency, had an 18-month sexual relationship (about October 2013 to early 2015) with Patient 1, a case manager at the same agency, and during that time prescribed her non-controlled medications (an oral contraceptive, Augmentin, fluconazole and bupropion) without examining her or keeping a record. The Hearing Examiner also noted that, after she became pregnant, he disclosed her pregnancy and her consideration of an abortion to co-workers and a relative without permission. He had self-reported the relationship in March 2015. That order suspended his license for at least one year, with ethics and boundaries courses and at least one year of probation after reinstatement.
cases.outcome: Indefinite suspension of at least 90 days; license remains subject to the 9/12/2018 Board Order's reinstatement conditions and probationary requirements (per Board listing). Reinstated by Consent Agreement effective 12/13/2023 with at least 5 years' probation.

narrative: The physician had a long Board history related to a confidential medical condition: a 1996 non-public agreement that he violated, surrenders of his license in 1996 and 2003 after violating monitoring requirements, and reinstatement in 2016 on probation with monitoring by a confidential program, to which he agreed to remain subject for as long as he held an active license. In 2020 he was reprimanded and fined $500 for signing patient discharge forms at a facility with names other than his own, including 'Donald J. Trump' and 'I am Ironman.'

According to the Order for Summary Suspension, he was hospitalized in March 2022 after self-injurious behavior unrelated to the monitored condition, and again on July 13, 2022 after further self-injurious behavior. While a patient at the second hospital he prescribed controlled dangerous substances to several patients. On July 16 the monitoring program's medical director told him not to practice until cleared, but he continued to prescribe controlled substances to patients. He was discharged on August 10, and the medical director concluded that he was not currently capable of practicing medicine safely. These are investigative findings that the panel had 'reason to believe' were true, issued without a prior hearing; the panel concluded that his medical condition and demonstrated impaired judgment posed a substantial risk of serious harm and that emergency action was required. This was an interim action; he surrendered his license permanently the next month (Case 177).
cases.outcome: License summarily suspended (interim) pending a post-deprivation hearing set for August 24, 2022; option to request an evidentiary hearing before an ALJ.

narrative: This is a Permanent Letter of Surrender following the August 11, 2022 Order for Summary Suspension (Case 176), which is attached to it. That order stated that the physician, who had a long history of Board actions tied to a confidential monitored medical condition, was hospitalized twice in 2022 after self-injurious behavior, prescribed controlled dangerous substances to several patients while himself a hospital inpatient, and kept prescribing after the monitoring program's medical director told him on July 16, 2022 not to practice until cleared. The medical director concluded that he was not currently capable of practicing safely, and the panel found that his medical condition and impaired judgment posed a substantial risk of serious harm.

In the letter the physician acknowledged the investigation and summary suspension and surrendered his license permanently to avoid charges and further prosecution. He did not contest the allegations and agreed that, for all purposes related to licensure in Maryland, the findings in the summary suspension order would be treated as proven and would support conclusions that he engaged in unprofessional conduct in the practice of medicine and was professionally, physically, or mentally incompetent. He agreed never to reapply for a Maryland license, and the summary suspension was terminated as moot.
cases.outcome: Permanent surrender of license accepted (public, disciplinary); may not reapply for Maryland licensure; CDS registration surrendered; summary suspension terminated as moot.

narrative: This was not a disciplinary action against an existing license but a Stipulation for a Probationary License with a physician applying for an initial California physician's and surgeon's license. The applicant had submitted the application in January 2022 and reported to the Board that he had taken a leave of absence from training. The stipulation does not describe the underlying events. It states only that the Board may act where an applicant's ability to practice safely is impaired by mental illness, for unprofessional conduct, and for use of dangerous drugs or alcohol in a manner dangerous to the licensee or others, and that these grounds supported denial of the license. Instead of denying the application, the Board's Chief of Licensing and the applicant agreed that a license would be issued on probation. The applicant waived a Statement of Issues and hearing. No findings were made and nothing was admitted beyond the stipulation itself.

The probation terms show that the Board's concern was substance use and mental health. They include random observed biological fluid testing, weekly substance abuse support group meetings, a worksite monitor for a substance-abusing licensee, complete abstinence from controlled substances and alcohol, and ongoing psychotherapy with quarterly reports. The applicant was allowed to start at the second-year testing frequency because he had met the regulatory criteria for previous testing and sobriety.
cases.outcome: Probationary license issued; three years' probation with biological fluid testing, weekly substance abuse support group meetings, worksite monitor, abstinence from controlled substances and alcohol, psychotherapy, solo practice prohibition, notification of employers/hospitals/insurers, and prohibition on supervising PAs and advanced practice nurses.

narrative: The psychiatrist surrendered his license to resolve an Accusation alleging that he could not practice safely because of a mental or physical illness affecting competency. He agreed that the Board could establish a factual basis for the charge but did not admit it. According to the Accusation, he was in a motorized bicycle accident in July 2019 and suffered multiple traumatic injuries requiring hospitalization, and he had a stroke while in the hospital. About three weeks later the Board received an anonymous complaint that he was incapacitated and that his medical corporation was operating without a current medical director. He was interviewed and voluntarily agreed to an evaluation.

In May 2021 a clinical neuropsychologist performed a full neuropsychological evaluation and diagnosed major vascular neurocognitive disorder secondary to the stroke. The impairments were in the moderate to severe range and included loss of executive functions such as sustained attention and concentration, new learning, sequencing, visual scanning, and abstract thinking, along with distractibility. The neuropsychologist concluded that he was not able to practice medicine safely. The Accusation alleged no patient-care deficiencies; the only ground was impairment from illness.
cases.outcome: License surrender accepted; costs of $7,991.25 payable before any new or reinstated license; any reapplication treated as a petition for reinstatement with the Accusation's allegations deemed admitted.

narrative: This decision granted a petition for reinstatement after a hearing, and the administrative law judge's findings describe the history. The psychiatrist had a solo private practice and hospital staff work. He had depression and misused controlled substances, mainly stimulants, from his residency in the mid-1990s. The judge found that he snorted crushed Adderall and Ritalin tablets that patients had returned to him. After residential treatment in 2007 and about five years of sobriety, he relapsed. In May 2014 his nurse practitioner found him passed out in the office after he took stimulants and then Saphris to counteract them, and she reported him to the Board. A 2015 Accusation for dangerous use of controlled substances was settled with five years' probation starting March 2016. He then failed to report for testing, tested positive for a controlled substance, and did not cooperate with the testing program. These violations led to two cease-practice orders and a petition to revoke probation, and he surrendered his license in July 2017.

The judge also found that a January 2017 altercation with a former girlfriend led to a no-contest plea to misdemeanor domestic battery. He violated that criminal probation by using alcohol and drugs in December 2017; the conviction was later dismissed. In treatment after that incident, a sex and love addiction was identified as driving his relapses. The judge found him sober since January 2018, with negative tests apart from one in January 2018, and active in AA. He had opened a substance-abuse treatment center in which he did not act as a physician. The judge concluded that he had shown rehabilitation by clear and convincing evidence. Because of his relapses and earlier failure on probation, the judge required a long probation, a psychiatric evaluation before practice, and a solo-practice prohibition.
cases.outcome: License reinstated, immediately revoked, revocation stayed; seven years' probation with psychiatric evaluation before resuming practice, abstinence from controlled substances and alcohol, biological fluid testing, substance abuse support group meetings, worksite monitor, solo practice prohibition, professionalism (ethics) course, and prohibition on supervising PAs and advanced practice nurses.

narrative: The psychiatrist had prior Ohio discipline for impairment: a January 2013 Step I Consent Agreement in which he admitted taking more of his prescribed narcotic medication than prescribed, leading to an emergency at his workplace in June 2012, and prescribing Adderall to a family member and sometimes using that prescription himself. He completed treatment and five years of probation and was released in November 2018. In August 2022 the Board summarily suspended his license, and the Notice of Summary Suspension stated that in a May 2022 interview with a Board investigator he admitted that, despite his history of impairment, he had resumed drinking occasionally after his release from probation, most recently in March 2022. On December 15, 2020, after consuming two vodka drinks (and taking a third home), he crashed his car; he attributed the dizziness and blackout to cardiac medications. He did not self-report the relapse within 48 hours as Board rules require, did not disclose the pending OVI charge or the relapse on his May 13, 2021 renewal application, and pleaded guilty to OVI six days later. The Board had no information that he had entered treatment or an aftercare contract after the relapse.

In the February 2023 Step I Consent Agreement he admitted the factual and legal allegations of the Notice, which constituted impairment of ability to practice due to habitual or excessive use of alcohol or drugs and a violation of the Board's licensee reporting rule. In August 2023 a Step II Consent Agreement reinstated his license after he completed treatment, entered aftercare, and was found capable of practice by two assessors; a January 2024 superseding agreement transferred his monitoring to an outside monitoring organization.
cases.outcome: Summary suspension (8/10/2022); then indefinite suspension of at least 120 days with $4,500 fine, total abstinence from alcohol and unprescribed drugs, random toxicology screens at least four times a month, 12-step/Caduceus attendance three times weekly, quarterly declarations and appearances; reinstatement conditioned on at least 28 days of inpatient/residential treatment, aftercare, and two addictionologist assessments. Reinstated 8/9/2023 with at least 5 years' probation; monitoring transferred to an approved monitoring organization 1/10/2024.

narrative: The psychiatrist signed a Permanent Surrender/Retirement of her Ohio certificate to practice medicine and surgery, with consent to permanent revocation, in lieu of further investigation. The investigation was under the provision covering inability to practice according to acceptable and prevailing standards of care because of mental or physical illness. The agreement says only that the surrender was related to her personal decision to retire from medicine to focus on her personal well-being. The document contains no charging document, allegations, findings, or admission, and it does not describe any illness, patient care, or other conduct. The Board ratified the surrender and permanently revoked the license.
cases.outcome: Permanent surrender/retirement accepted; license permanently revoked (permanently ineligible to reapply in Ohio).

narrative: The listed 2024 action is a Superseding Consent Agreement, effective January 10, 2024. It amended a prior Board Order only to move probationary monitoring from the Board to a newly approved monitoring organization. That agreement is not in the file. The file contains the 2018-2019 impairment proceedings that produced the prior order.

In April 2018 the Board ordered the psychiatrist, who had recently resigned from a community clinic, to attend a 72-hour inpatient chemical-dependency evaluation. The order cited a 2016 incident: arrest on domestic violence and drunk-driving charges, a breath-alcohol level of 0.276 after a car crash, and guilty pleas to OVI and disorderly conduct. An evaluation after that incident found too little evidence for a substance use disorder but advised re-evaluation if another alcohol incident occurred. The order also cited a December 2017 domestic-violence arrest in which he was allegedly intoxicated. He did not attend the June 4, 2018 evaluation, saying he could not pay its roughly $5,000 cost, and the Board summarily suspended his license. At a remand hearing he testified that severe depression had left him unable to function. After the missed evaluation he was hospitalized from July 31 to August 21, 2018, with diagnoses of recurrent severe major depressive disorder and severe alcohol use disorder. He then left a partial hospitalization program against clinical advice. He denied having an alcohol problem. The hearing examiner found that depression was at least part of the reason he missed the evaluation. On January 9, 2019, the Board amended that finding to say he had not shown circumstances beyond his control. Under Ohio law, this made the missed evaluation an admission of impairment from alcohol or drug use. The Board suspended his license indefinitely under its standard impairment terms.
cases.outcome: 2024 Superseding Consent Agreement moved probationary monitoring from the Board to an approved monitoring organization. Underlying 2019 Board Order: indefinite suspension with interim monitoring (drug and alcohol abstinence, random toxicology screens at least four times a month, recovery meetings three times a week, continued psychiatric treatment with reports). Reinstatement requires at least 28 days of inpatient treatment, an aftercare contract, and two independent fitness assessments, followed by at least five years' probation with a monitoring physician.

narrative: On April 25, 2024, the psychiatrist signed a Permanent Surrender of Certificate to Practice Medicine and Surgery, consenting to permanent revocation of the Ohio license. The psychiatrist stipulated that the surrender was made in lieu of formal disciplinary proceedings under Ohio's provision on inability to practice according to acceptable and prevailing standards of care by reason of mental or physical illness, and the document states that this was related to the psychiatrist's cancer diagnosis, which made it difficult to practice medicine.

The file contains no Notice of Opportunity for Hearing, no allegations of misconduct, and no findings; the only stated basis is the illness-related inability to practice. The Board ratified the surrender and entered an order permanently revoking the license on May 8, 2024.
cases.outcome: Permanent surrender accepted; license permanently revoked; permanently ineligible to apply for reinstatement or any new Ohio certificate.

narrative: In a public letter of concern, the Board stated that on January 28, 2024, after drinking an excessive amount of alcohol, the physician was in a single-vehicle collision and was taken for his injuries to a hospital in the same system that employed him. He was cited for driving while impaired, and a blood test showed a blood alcohol content above the standard for gross impairment. While being treated in his hospital room he was seen using the room's computer; the Board's investigation confirmed that he signed into the hospital system, accessed several patient records, co-signed clinical notes and modified one patient record. The Board noted that these actions appeared to be within his normal duties and that no patient was harmed, but stated that it was inappropriate to access patient records and perform any duties while under the influence. The Board declined formal proceedings and does not consider the letter disciplinary; the physician consented to it.
cases.outcome: Public letter of concern (non-disciplinary); no formal proceedings.

narrative: This is an Order for Summary Suspension, an interim action taken without a prior hearing; its investigative findings state facts the disciplinary panel had 'reason to believe' were true, not findings after a hearing. The psychiatrist, board-certified in psychiatry, practiced at a hospital. In July 2024 the Board received an anonymous complaint about an alleged health condition of the psychiatrist 'which is putting both staff and patients in dangerous situations,' describing several specific incidents. The Board obtained the psychiatrist's hospital personnel file and medical records, interviewed three hospital staff members, received a written statement, and referred the psychiatrist to a Board-approved program for a fitness-to-practice evaluation.

According to the order, the psychiatrist suffered a workplace injury in June 2023, after which hospital staff observed several concerning behaviors that placed staff and patients at risk. On July 24, 2024 a specialist noted a potential health condition and ordered further testing; on July 31 an evaluating physician concluded the psychiatrist was currently unable to perform the essential duties of a psychiatrist; on August 20 another specialist found the psychiatrist not fit to continue in the hospital position; and on September 6 the program's evaluator concluded the psychiatrist was 'not currently competent to practice psychiatric medicine.' The order deliberately withholds the nature of the condition and the specific behaviors. The panel concluded that the public health, safety, or welfare imperatively required emergency action. About two weeks later the psychiatrist permanently surrendered the license (Case 50), which ended the suspension as moot.
cases.outcome: License summarily suspended pending a post-deprivation hearing (set for October 9, 2024), with the right to request an evidentiary hearing before an ALJ; superseded by permanent surrender (Case 50).

narrative: The psychiatrist permanently surrendered a Maryland license by a Permanent Letter of Surrender about two weeks after the Board summarily suspended the license on September 30, 2024 (Case 49), an interim order based on a health condition that several evaluators had found prevented the psychiatrist from safely practicing at a hospital. The letter acknowledged that the Board had received a complaint alleging the potential existence of a health condition affecting the psychiatrist's ability to practice medicine safely, that the Board had investigated, and that the license had been summarily suspended. It does not describe the condition or any patient care.

The psychiatrist surrendered to avoid further investigation and prosecution and because of the psychiatrist's current health condition and retirement. No charges were issued and no hearing was held. The psychiatrist did not contest the allegations and agreed that, for licensure purposes, they would be treated as proven and supported a conclusion under the provision covering a physician who is professionally, physically, or mentally incompetent. On acceptance of the surrender, the summary suspension order was terminated as moot.
cases.outcome: Permanent surrender of license (no right to reapply); surrender of state controlled dangerous substance registration; summary suspension terminated as moot.

narrative: In November 2024 the Board opened an investigation after receiving credible information about the psychiatrist's possible inability to practice medicine safely and competently; the cause is redacted in the public order. The order does not describe patients, prescriptions, or specific conduct.

In the Stipulated Order he neither admitted nor denied the matter, but the Board found that he engaged in unprofessional or dishonorable conduct, violated the Medical Practice Act's impairment provision (the accompanying description is redacted), and prescribed controlled substances without a legitimate medical purpose, without following accepted procedures for examination of patients, or without following accepted procedures for record keeping.
cases.outcome: Retired Oregon license while under investigation; may not reapply for at least two years and must demonstrate medical competency on any reapplication; must obey all laws pertaining to the practice of medicine.

narrative: The psychiatrist, licensed since 2011 and co-owner of a psychiatric group practice, did not contest that the Board could establish a prima facie case on the Accusation's charges of failing to comply with a Board-ordered mental and physical evaluation and of impairment due to mental illness affecting competency; she made no admissions.

According to the Accusation, the case began with her September 2022 arrest on felony charges of inflicting corporal injury on a spouse and making criminal threats; prosecutors ultimately did not file charges. The arrest report contained allegations that she had assaulted and threatened her husband, vandalized her in-laws' home, and threatened to kill herself; her husband told police that her mental health had declined rapidly after the birth of their third child, that she had been diagnosed with bipolar disorder and borderline personality and had stopped taking her escitalopram and lamotrigine, and he raised possible drug use and erratic behavior such as climbing onto the roof. After a Board investigator's interview in February 2023 she declined a voluntary mental and physical evaluation, and the Board ordered one in July 2023. At the medical evaluation she declined, citing protected health information, to disclose her medical history, medications, or drug and alcohol use, or to release records, so the examiner could not determine whether she had an impairing physical condition. The Board-appointed psychiatrist, also denied access to her records, found a picture consistent with compulsive personality type and a possible underlying mood, posttraumatic, anxiety, or adjustment disorder, and concluded she could not practice safely without restrictions, monitoring, and psychiatric care.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 5 years' probation with professionalism (ethics) program, psychiatric evaluation and medical evaluation with no practice until found fit, psychotherapy, medical treatment as required, practice monitor (or professional enhancement program), notification of facilities/insurers; prohibited from directly supervising PAs/APNs; costs of $45,128.

narrative: The psychiatrist, an osteopathic physician whose specialty is psychiatry, was hired by an outpatient behavioral health practice that in February 2025 reported to the National Practitioner Data Bank that it had terminated his clinical privileges because he could not practice safely by reason of psychological impairment. The report, quoted in the order, described a little over a month of employment in which he appeared confused throughout training, needed substantial help with technology, could not give his date of birth or Social Security number, wandered the halls, stammered, microwaved a debit card at the office, confused patients and medications when discussing cases, and gave a patient instructions unrelated to the session, such as directions to a nonexistent internal pharmacy. Through counsel he denied the allegations but reported that, after his brother's death caused significant depression, he had started brexpiprazole (Rexulti) samples five days before his first day of work and stopped them the day after, and that the medication caused shaking, confusion and atypical behavior that took ten days to resolve. He stopped practicing pending neurological and neuropsychological testing.

In April 2025 the Board's Inquiry Panel, finding probable cause to believe he had a condition that might impede competent practice, ordered a neuropsychological evaluation. He scheduled it for May 19, 2025, but on May 16 told the Board through counsel that he wished to retire his license instead, and he did not attend. The panel found the failure was not due to circumstances beyond his control. Under Kentucky law, failing to submit to an ordered examination constitutes an admission that the physician has a condition making continued practice dangerous and a default, so the panel entered this final order without a hearing.
cases.outcome: License indefinitely restricted from any practice of medicine until further order of the Panel; no request to resume practice will be considered until he completes the ordered neuropsychological evaluation and the Board receives the evaluator's report; burden of persuasion on the licensee.

narrative: The psychiatrist, licensed since 2011, settled the Accusation without admitting it, agreeing only that the Board could establish a prima facie case for impairment due to mental illness, dishonest or corrupt acts, and general unprofessional conduct. The charges arose from conduct outside clinical practice rather than patient care.

According to the Accusation, in January 2023 police investigating a residential burglary found that the psychiatrist had used a previously provided key to enter her ex-boyfriend's apartment and remove property; the next day she pulled a building fire alarm when he would not answer his phone. After Miranda warnings she admitted the entry, the taking of property, and the false alarm; stolen property was recovered from her car, and a felony first-degree burglary complaint was filed. Later that month she left a threatening voicemail for a local elected official and was placed on a 72-hour psychiatric hold after a disturbance that frightened a former employer; she had a prior bipolar disorder diagnosis with hospitalizations in 2013-2014, was diagnosed with bipolar I disorder, manic episode, and was discharged on lithium, aripiprazole, lamotrigine, and other medications. In February 2023 she left another threatening voicemail, was again hospitalized on a hold after a community disturbance, and on discharge (with residual grandiose delusions noted) was taken into custody, served with a restraining order, and later charged with two misdemeanor counts of annoying telephone calls. A Board-ordered psychiatric evaluation in July 2023 concluded that her ability to practice was impaired by bipolar I disorder and PTSD, citing periodic manic psychotic episodes with risk of loss of control. The Accusation does not state the outcome of the criminal charges.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 3 years' probation with waiver of early termination, abstention from ketamine with biological fluid testing, professionalism (ethics) program, psychiatric evaluation, psychotherapy, biweekly psychiatric treatment with quarterly reports, notification of employers/insurers; prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; costs of $46,952.

narrative: The psychiatrist, licensed since 1972, surrendered the license without admitting the charge, agreeing only that the Board could establish a factual basis for it. The Accusation, which contained a single cause for action, alleged only that the psychiatrist's ability to practice medicine safely was impaired because his competency had been affected by a mental condition, a physical condition, or both. The document gives no further details about the nature of the condition, how it came to the Board's attention, or any patient care.
cases.outcome: License surrender accepted; any reapplication treated as a petition for reinstatement with the Accusation's allegations deemed admitted. No cost recovery ordered.

narrative: This case was decided by the Florida Board of Osteopathic Medicine after a hearing before an Administrative Law Judge, whose findings the Board adopted. In November 2023 a longtime friend and physician colleague reported the psychiatrist, who practiced telemedicine, to the state's impaired practitioner program after she had shown about two years of escalating paranoid delusions: that her former telehealth employer was retaliating against her as a whistleblower, that cameras were planted in her home, that her devices were hacked, that she was being followed, and that her telemedicine patients were actors. She refused his urging to seek care. The program could not reach her and referred the matter to the Department, to which she sent emails investigators found incoherent and paranoid. In a Department-ordered evaluation in April 2024, a psychiatrist diagnosed unspecified psychosis, noted she had been prescribed Adderall 20 mg three times daily since 2021 and that a stimulant-induced psychosis needed to be ruled out (she did not complete the required toxicology testing), and concluded she could not practice safely; he recommended residential assessment and monitoring, which she never pursued.

In August 2024, after colleagues noticed she believed her patients were FBI agents, she was involuntarily hospitalized under the Baker Act, where Adderall was stopped and paliperidone started; her discharge diagnoses were delusional disorder, persecutory type, and substance-induced psychotic disorder. The judge found that her delusions persisted through a December 2024 deposition, March 2025 texts and her own testimony at the August 2025 hearing, and that the Department proved by clear and convincing evidence that she was unable to practice with reasonable skill and safety because of a mental condition. The Board denied her exceptions and adopted the recommended penalty.
cases.outcome: License suspended until she demonstrates ability to practice with reasonable skill and safety, including an evaluation by the impaired practitioner program (PRN) and an appearance before the Board, which retains jurisdiction to impose probation on reinstatement; costs of $42,898.61 payable within 24 months of reinstatement.

narrative: The psychiatrist had a prior history of chemical dependency: in 2014, as a resident, he took benzodiazepines and oxycodone from patients' pill bottles in an emergency department and used some during shifts, leading to revocation of his Ohio license in 2015 and a felony plea to attempted theft; after treatment and documented sobriety he was granted a new license in 2018 under a probationary consent agreement. In September 2025 the Board received information about his possible impairment at work and referred him to the Ohio Professionals Health Program (OhioPHP) for its confidential monitoring program. According to the December 2025 Notice of Summary Suspension and Opportunity for Hearing, an OhioPHP well-being screening in October 2025 found him impaired in his ability to practice because of a mental health condition and a substance use disorder, including a positive test for buprenorphine, norbuprenorphine, amphetamine, hydrocodone and norhydrocodone. To remain eligible for confidential monitoring he was required to enroll in treatment by October 24 and begin by November 5, 2025, and to notify OhioPHP within two days of choosing a facility; he did none of these, and OhioPHP reported him to the Board as impaired and ineligible.

The Board summarily suspended his license on December 10, 2025, finding clear and convincing evidence of impairment due to substance use disorder and of inability to practice due to mental or physical illness, and that his continued practice posed a danger of immediate and serious harm. In January 2026 he signed a permanent surrender of his license in lieu of further proceedings, expressly admitting the allegations in the Notice; the Board ratified it and permanently revoked the license.
cases.outcome: Summary suspension (12/10/2025); permanent surrender of Ohio osteopathic license with consent to permanent revocation, ratified 2/11/2026; permanently ineligible for reinstatement or any new Ohio license.

narrative: After a hearing the psychiatrist did not attend, the hearing examiner made findings that the Board adopted. In November 2024 the psychiatrist was referred to the Ohio Professionals Health Program (OhioPHP) for possible confidential monitoring. The psychiatrist missed a December 2024 screening, citing safety concerns, and then refused the rescheduled January 2025 screening after hiring counsel. A more comprehensive evaluation was scheduled but never attended, and OhioPHP referred the matter to the Board. In an April 2025 interview by video, the psychiatrist said an unidentified stalker was the reason for repeatedly changing phone numbers and email addresses and for moving abroad without plans to return. The investigator testified that the psychiatrist was still caring for about 200 patients of an outpatient practice, called the records 'a shambles,' and was still prescribing controlled substances according to OARRS. Five subpoenaed patient charts were never produced.

In July 2025 the psychiatrist had a medical emergency at an airport after taking meclizine, carisoprodol and clonazepam, which the psychiatrist said were bought without a prescription abroad. The psychiatrist was carrying numerous unidentified pill bottles. The urine drug screen was positive for THC and clonazepam, and later presumptively for carisoprodol. Hospital diagnoses included lithium toxicity (with a report of self-prescribing), probable substance-induced psychosis, and benzodiazepine and cannabis use disorders. The psychiatrist arrived at a Board-ordered 72-hour evaluation carrying medication bottles with the labels scratched off and was self-prescribing lithium and lamotrigine. The evaluator concluded the psychiatrist could not practice safely because of an unspecified mood disorder with psychotic features, unprescribed medication and cannabis abuse, and worsening delusional beliefs. The Board summarily suspended the license on October 8, 2025. It concluded that the psychiatrist was unable to practice because of mental illness. Because the psychiatrist was outside the country, had not sought treatment, and could not be monitored, it revoked the license rather than suspending it.
cases.outcome: Summary suspension (October 8, 2025), then revocation after hearing (not permanent); no fine. The hearing examiner encouraged reapplication if the psychiatrist returns to Ohio and obtains treatment.

narrative: The psychiatrist, trained in general and child and adolescent psychiatry, had admitted in a 2012 Step I Consent Agreement to amphetamine dependence: after her own prescriber stopped Adderall in 2009, she obtained it for herself by writing prescriptions in the names of two patients and a family member and by having a patient fill a prescription and give her the drug, and she initially gave the Board false information and documents. She completed residential treatment and five years of probation, ending in 2018. In 2021, without telling a new treating psychiatrist (chosen out of her area) about her history of amphetamine dependence, she was prescribed Mydayis, an extended-release amphetamine, which continued through August 2025.

In September 2025 Board investigators interviewed her about an allegation that she was inappropriately prescribing extended-release stimulants; the Board found she had difficulty answering questions, went on tangents, had marked hand tremors and was not transparent about the controlled substance she was taking. She was referred to the Ohio Professionals Health Program, but two well-being screenings were cancelled because she would not complete the required paperwork and releases. When investigators served a Board order for a 72-hour inpatient examination in December 2025, she became agitated and made suicidal statements, prompting a police wellness check. She did not appear for the examination, and the Board summarily suspended her license. After a hearing, the Board found her failure to appear was not due to circumstances beyond her control, which under Ohio law constitutes an admission of impairment due to mental illness and to substance use; she also acknowledged that a self-arranged evaluation found her impaired.
cases.outcome: Summary suspension (December 2025); then license suspended indefinitely with interim monitoring through OhioPHP, psychiatric assessment and treatment, drug/alcohol assessment and treatment, abstinence, toxicology screens and self-help meetings; reinstatement requires two assessments of fitness; at least 5 years' probation after reinstatement with a ban on prescribing or possessing controlled substances without Board approval and a supervised practice plan with a monitoring physician. Reinstated 8/12/2026 subject to those probationary terms (per Board listing).

narrative: According to the Accusation, in November 2016 the psychiatrist telephoned a community pharmacy with a prescription for an antibiotic and diazepam in the name of a fictitious patient, intending to obtain the medications for her own use. The pharmacist noticed that the "patient" had recently filled diazepam (making this an early refill) and, when the psychiatrist arrived to pick it up, recognized her voice as that of the prescribing doctor and refused to fill it. An altercation followed, and sheriff's deputies who located her nearby reported that she refused commands, pulled away and kicked during handcuffing, kicked the patrol-car window, and showed poor balance, slurred speech, dilated pupils, and droopy eyelids; a blood sample drawn the next morning was positive for opiates and benzodiazepines. The Accusation further alleged that over roughly nineteen months (April 2015 to November 2016) she wrote about 19 prescriptions to herself under variants of the fictitious name, including clonazepam, lorazepam, triazolam, phentermine, and zolpidem, with zolpidem quantities in early 2016 consistent with 20 mg per day, double the maximum recommended dose, without any documented justification. She also prescribed clonazepam, amphetamines, and zolpidem to Patient A, a former private-practice patient living abroad, while keeping no medical records for Patient A or for herself.

The Accusation charged that writing prescriptions in a false name, prolonged self-prescribing of controlled substances when other physicians were available, the absence of any records, and excessive dosing constituted gross negligence, repeated negligent acts, dishonest and corrupt acts, self-use of drugs in a dangerous manner, and inadequate records. The case was resolved by stipulated settlement in which the psychiatrist did not contest that a prima facie case could be established; no findings were made.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 3 years' probation with prohibition on ordering, prescribing, dispensing, or possessing controlled substances except as approved by another physician (worksite monitor may review), controlled substance log, abstention from controlled substances and alcohol, prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, professionalism (ethics) program, psychotherapy, biological fluid testing, worksite monitor, employer notification, and prohibition on supervising PAs/APRNs; probation monitoring costs.

narrative: In February 2021 the Investigative Committee of the Nevada Board filed a Complaint alleging one violation of the Medical Practice Act provision that makes it grounds for discipline to violate the statutes and regulations of the Nevada State Board of Pharmacy. The Complaint itself is not attached to the Settlement Agreement, and the agreement gives no facts: it does not say which pharmacy statute or regulation was involved, what medication or prescriptions were at issue, or how the matter came to the Board's attention. In the Settlement Agreement the psychiatrist stated generally that she was not admitting that the claims had merit and was settling to avoid the cost of a hearing, but then specifically admitted Count I, the violation of the pharmacy statutes and regulations, and agreed that the Board could enter an order finding conduct that is grounds for discipline. The Board approved the agreement on March 5, 2021. This was the first of three actions against the same physician; a later summary suspension (Case 214) and settlement (Case 215) concerned failure to comply with a Board order granting her license with conditions.
cases.outcome: Public Letter of Reprimand; $500 fine; costs of $653.69; remaining claims dismissed.

narrative: A Medical Disciplinary Panel heard the charges in a Formal Complaint dated September 4, 2018, and the Board adopted the Panel's Certified Report in full after a Final Order hearing, so the facts below are findings after a hearing. The psychiatrist prescribed medications to a partner in his own medical practice (called "Partner" in the order) without an appropriate physician-patient relationship. As an example, in March 2016 Partner presented to a local pharmacist a prescription signed by the psychiatrist for 60 tablets of Norco (hydrocodone). On further investigation the State found that from 2009 through February 2016 he had prescribed to Partner more than 50 times, including lorazepam, clonazepam, zolpidem, trazodone, Topamax, escitalopram, Dexilant, benazepril-hydrochlorothiazide and pravastatin.

The Panel found that he kept insufficient records of these prescriptions, a point he "more or less conceded," and that the benzodiazepine doses he wrote exceeded FDA guidelines, especially for an older patient such as Partner; it treated the excessive doses, together with the lack of a proper physician-patient relationship, as an exacerbating circumstance. Before the Panel he admitted that the hydrocodone prescription was "ill-advised" and that he never checked SCRIPTS, the state prescription monitoring database, before writing controlled-substance prescriptions for Partner. The Board concluded that he failed to maintain adequate patient records and failed to establish a physician-patient relationship before prescribing, which by statute requires personally taking and documenting a history and physical examination, making a diagnosis and treatment plan, discussing risks and benefits, and ensuring availability for follow-up. In setting the sanction it cited the years-long prescribing and the multiple controlled substances, including very high benzodiazepine doses, and noted that a physician can hardly keep the objectivity needed to treat a medical partner.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand; must complete a Board-approved narcotic prescribing course and a record keeping course within six months of the order.

narrative: According to the Accusation, from about January 2014 through December 2015 the psychiatrist treated two of her own family members and regularly prescribed them high amounts of opioids and benzodiazepines in combination. Patient A, a 69-year-old female relative, complained of pain and anxiety attributed to trauma from prior cancer treatment; CURES records showed recurring prescriptions for hydrocodone/acetaminophen, oxycodone/acetaminophen, promethazine with codeine, alprazolam (escalating from 0.5 mg to 1 mg, #90 monthly), and clonazepam. Patient B, a 49-year-old male relative with orthopedic knee pain, received hydrocodone/acetaminophen, buprenorphine/naloxone (8/2 mg, #90 monthly), alprazolam, clonazepam, zolpidem, and eszopiclone, often several of these concurrently. The Accusation alleged that for both relatives she failed to perform or document an adequate history and physical examination (including an orthopedic exam for Patient B) or a full mental status examination, did not coordinate care with the treating oncologist or orthopedist or consult pain management, did not review or document review of CURES, did not obtain a controlled-substance agreement, did not timely refer the patients to other providers, and practiced over an extended period in areas (oncology, orthopedics, pain management) for which she lacked adequate training.

The Accusation charged gross negligence, repeated negligent acts, violation of the Medical Practice Act, and general unprofessional conduct. The case was resolved by stipulated settlement in which the psychiatrist did not contest that a prima facie case could be established on each charge; no findings were made.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 3 years' probation with 40 hours/year of education courses, prescribing practices course, professionalism (ethics) program, psychiatric evaluation, practice monitor (or professional enhancement program), prohibition on prescribing controlled substances to family members or herself, and prohibition on supervising PAs/APRNs; probation monitoring costs.

narrative: According to the First Amended Accusation, the psychiatrist provided long-term outpatient care to three older women and prescribed benzodiazepines and other controlled substances for years without adequate examination, substance-use assessment, coordination with co-prescribers, or documentation. Patient 1, born in 1944 and treated since 1988 for anxiety, depression, and insomnia, received diazepam on 32 occasions and triazolam on 18 occasions between January 2011 and August 2013 without examination; refills were authorized after phone calls in which she reported being stable, and the faxed renewals were lost. He knew another physician was concurrently prescribing her hydrocodone/acetaminophen and methadone but never contacted that physician. In August 2013 he gave an early refill of diazepam 10 mg #120 with four refills; she died at home in October 2013 of acute mixed drug intoxication (methadone and benzodiazepines). Patient 2, a psychologist born in 1944 and treated since about 1995 for PTSD, depression, panic, and insomnia, received clonazepam for over 20 years plus phentermine and trazodone while drinking alcohol regularly, receiving opioids from an internist, and developing incontinence, word-finding difficulty, balance problems, and MRI findings consistent with dementia; he issued clonazepam and phentermine with multiple refills after a cancelled visit and first checked CURES in November 2018. Patient 3, born in 1941 with major depression, a history of opioid dependence, and a family history of alcohol use disorder, received methylphenidate, alprazolam, zolpidem, and other sedative-hypnotics, and benzodiazepines were continued after a November 2018 psychiatric hospitalization for suicidal ideation at which severe obstructive sleep apnea was diagnosed.

The Accusation charged prescribing without appropriate examination or indication, gross negligence, incompetence (including in dual-diagnosis care and psychopharmacology), repeated negligent acts, failure to document informed consent, and illegible, incomplete records. It noted prior Board probation imposed in 2002. The psychiatrist agreed in a stipulated settlement that a prima facie case could be established, without admitting the allegations; no findings were made.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 5 years' probation with patient disclosure of probation status, 40 hours/year of education in psychopharmacology and neuroscience, medical record keeping course, practice monitor (or professional enhancement program), and prohibition on supervising PAs/APRNs; probation monitoring costs.

cases.type: Public reprimand / public letter of reprimand
narrative: According to the Board's Public Letter of Reprimand, an investigation by the Medical Board revealed that the psychiatrist did not follow the set requirements for dispensing controlled substances in an office setting, failed to discuss (or failed to document having discussed) the risks, benefits, and alternatives of psychotropic medications with patients or their guardians, and failed to obtain signed medication consent from patients or guardians. The letter characterizes these actions as violations of the medical records and unprofessional conduct provisions of the Business and Professions Code.
cases.outcome: Public Letter of Reprimand; required to complete a prescribing practices course and a medical record keeping course.

narrative: The Board opened its investigation after a March 2020 complaint from a person with a personal relationship to the psychiatrist (whose board certification in psychiatry had lapsed in 2016), alleging that she had prescribed "dangerous drugs" to the complainant with no labs, consultation or records, leaving the complainant "an addict and suicidal." A PDMP query showed at least 27 controlled-substance prescriptions (including refills) from 2015 to 2019. In the Consent Order, Disciplinary Panel A found that from at least 2014 to 2019 the psychiatrist diagnosed the complainant with a chronic medical condition and provided non-emergent treatment with controlled and other prescription-only drugs while in an inappropriate dual relationship. She told the complainant to fill prescriptions at different pharmacies and not to tell other treating providers, then had the filled medications handed back to her, kept them in a lockbox and dispensed them according to her own assessment of need. She kept no medical record (saying the complainant asked her not to), ordered no laboratory studies, including for a medication she acknowledged required them, did not check the PDMP, did not assess co-morbidities, did not coordinate with other treaters, and engaged in conduct that undermined treatment of the condition.

In March 2019 she obtained a court order resulting in the complainant's involuntary hospitalization; the evaluating physician found admission unwarranted and discharged the complainant, and told Board staff the psychiatrist had appeared intoxicated, with slurred speech and heavy sedation. When the Board subpoenaed records, she supplied none for her own care. In her interview she acknowledged she "probably should have checked" the PDMP. The panel concluded she was guilty of unprofessional conduct (treating a person where her judgment and objectivity were compromised); she agreed to the findings and waived any right to contest them.
cases.outcome: Reprimand; minimum 1 year probation with enrollment in the Maryland Professional Rehabilitation Program (MPRP) and compliance with its rehabilitation agreement and plan; professional ethics/boundaries course within 1 year; $5,000 civil fine.

narrative: According to the Administrative Complaint, the psychiatrist treated Patient C.S., a man who first presented in February 2011 with opiate withdrawal, anxiety, depression and sleep disturbance, for more than seven years (through August 2018). During that time she prescribed Suboxone, Subutex, Adderall, Xanax, Valium, Ambien and tramadol in various quantities and doses. The Complaint alleged that she never appropriately diagnosed or documented ADHD, insomnia or obsessive-compulsive disorder (she prescribed tramadol specifically for OCD); did not assess whether the controlled substances were appropriate; prescribed without a treatment plan or a signed treatment contract and then did not follow the contract once signed; saw the patient infrequently and erratically; gave refills and changed doses without office visits and based solely on the patient's requests; prescribed Adderall in excessive quantities; did not obtain a medical history or pharmacy profile, coordinate with other treating providers, offer psychosocial treatment, or monitor for illicit drug use, relapse and diversion; and kept prescribing despite evidence of ineffectiveness, tolerance, dependence and abuse. It also alleged that she failed to maintain appropriate physician-patient boundaries with the patient.

The Complaint further alleged that, although trained only in psychiatry, she treated the patient's non-psychiatric conditions beyond her competence: Linzess and Amitiza for gastrointestinal complaints, podofilox for genital warts, Valtrex for genital blisters and shingles, Cialis for Peyronie's disease, anastrozole for depression, buprenorphine for acute pain, and the antibiotics azithromycin and clindamycin without documented justification. It also alleged inadequate records. In the Settlement Agreement adopted by the Board's Final Order, the psychiatrist neither admitted nor denied the allegations.
cases.outcome: Reprimand; $10,000 fine; costs of $6,778.18; medical records course; 5 hours CME in boundaries; 5 hours risk-management CME; restricted from prescribing or ordering Schedule I-II controlled substances until the Board lifts the restriction; 1 year probation with indirect supervision by a monitor who reviews all records of patients treated with controlled substances.

narrative: According to the Administrative Complaint, the psychiatrist worked at a two-location pain management clinic in 2011-2013, where he treated five adult patients (T.B., C.D., I.K., J.K. and J.M.) for chronic back and neck pain, each for roughly four months to a year and a half. The Complaint alleged that he prescribed inappropriate or excessive quantities of opioid and benzodiazepine combinations to all five: oxycodone (Roxicodone) with clonazepam or Xanax for most, oxycodone, Dilaudid and Valium for I.K., and Roxicodone, methadone and clonazepam for J.M. It alleged that he did not perform or document complete histories and physical examinations, did not consult prior providers or appropriate specialists, and treated pain exclusively with large doses of controlled substances rather than alternative modalities. He repeatedly documented diagnoses of lumbar myelopathy and radiculopathy for every patient without exam findings to support them, and recorded a PTSD diagnosis for J.K. without any supporting history. For I.K., whose records showed a history of intravenous drug abuse and depression, he allegedly kept prescribing opioids and Valium without referring the patient for detoxification, addiction counseling or psychiatric care, or considering less-addictive alternatives.

The Complaint charged medical malpractice, inadequate medical records, and prescribing controlled substances other than in the course of professional practice for each patient. In the Settlement Agreement adopted by the Board's Final Order, the psychiatrist neither admitted nor denied the allegations, and the agreement states that the disposition is not a finding of guilt for any other purpose.
cases.outcome: Reprimand; $20,000 fine; costs of $12,806.24; laws and rules course, medical records course, drug prescribing course, and 5 hours risk-management CME, each within one year.

narrative: The psychiatrist, board-certified in psychiatry and licensed since 1971, had a solo private practice and later worked part-time at a clinic. In 2019 the daughter of Patient 4 complained to the Board about the benzodiazepines the psychiatrist prescribed. The Board subpoenaed records for nine patients, and two psychiatrist peer reviewers concluded that care fell below the standard for four patients (Patients 2, 3, 4 and 8) and that records were inadequate for one. According to the Charges, the deficiencies included using benzodiazepines as first-line treatment for panic disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, and major depression; prescribing excessively high doses and long-term use; failing to coordinate with other clinicians who were prescribing benzodiazepines to the same patients at the same time; prescribing a high quantity to a patient with concerns of abuse and diversion; not using urine toxicology monitoring; and not checking the state prescription monitoring database (CRISP).

In her Board interview she said she did not use drug contracts and did not repeat urine screens for her private patients because they were 'normal working people' whose lives did not suggest drug use. She acknowledged that for several years she gave Patient 1 three prescriptions at a time with two left undated for the patient to fill in. When Patient 4's husband reported that she had taken two weeks' worth of clonazepam within days, the psychiatrist, unsure who was telling the truth, prescribed another week's supply. The Charges also alleged failure to cooperate with the investigation: after certifying that she had produced complete records, she later submitted more than 3,000 additional pages for five patients. She surrendered her license to avoid prosecution, agreeing that the charges would be treated as if proven for licensure purposes.
cases.outcome: Surrender of license accepted (public, treated as a disciplinary action); CDS registration surrendered; any reinstatement petition to be treated as if the license had been revoked.

narrative: In December 2019 the Board opened an investigation after receiving credible information about the psychiatrist's prescribing and monitoring practices for controlled substances. The order does not identify patients, medications, doses, or the source of the information.

In the Stipulated Order, signed by the psychiatrist in July 2021, he neither admitted nor denied the matter, but the Board found that he failed to meet the standard of care and prescribed controlled substances without following accepted procedures for examination of patients or for record keeping.
