cases.outcome: Retired Oregon license while under investigation; may not reapply for at least two years; must obey all laws pertaining to the practice of medicine.

narrative: The psychiatrist, board-certified in addiction medicine and psychiatry, ran a general and addiction psychiatry practice and was medical director of an addiction counseling facility. After a patient's mother complained in 2020 about medications he prescribed, two addiction-psychiatry peer reviewers found that his care fell below the standard for four of ten patients, all with substance use disorders treated with buprenorphine alongside stimulants and/or benzodiazepines. In the Consent Order, the Board panel found that for Patient 1, a woman in her late 20s with severe opioid and sedative use disorders, he started Vyvanse and later Adderall XR 30 mg based on a self-report ADHD survey without a comprehensive ADHD assessment, replaced 'stolen' Subutex without verification and authorized an early Adderall refill, and did not document counseling on combining opioids and sedatives until she relapsed on heroin in 2019; in 2020 she told him she had been selling her Adderall. For Patient 4 he prescribed lorazepam long term together with Zubsolv/Suboxone, and for Patients 6 and 9 he made frequent, poorly documented medication changes, prescribed stimulants without a full ADHD assessment, and kept prescribing benzodiazepines and stimulants through relapses, misuse, and alcohol use. In his written response he agreed with many of the reviewers' criticisms.

The panel also found that he prescribed to two family members (Patients 11 and 12) over several years, including Schedule IV controlled substances and, in March and April 2020, hydroxychloroquine, azithromycin, zinc, and ivermectin to keep on hand in case they contracted COVID-19. In his interview he admitted these COVID prescriptions were not clinically appropriate and said he would no longer prescribe for family. The panel concluded that he failed to meet the standard of quality care and engaged in unprofessional conduct. He signed the Consent Order and waived any right to contest its findings.
cases.outcome: Reprimand; probation for a minimum of 6 months with courses in ethics and in prescribing controlled dangerous substances within 6 months; $1,000 civil fine within 6 months.

narrative: The psychiatrist, a board-certified psychiatrist in long-standing solo private practice, had previously been on three years' Board probation (2016-2019) for prescribing large quantities of pain medications to an out-of-state family friend without an examination; that probation prohibited him from prescribing opiates. In January 2017, while on that probation, he prescribed hydrocodone-homatropine cough syrup to Patient 1, a long-time patient with schizophrenia who lacked a primary care physician, without a physical examination, calling it a 'bridge' and a 'minor lapse' and saying he did not connect that it violated his probation. In January 2019 he advised Patient 2 to taper off citalopram from 20 mg to 10 mg for a week and, to help, took a bottle from a cabinet of medications in his office that bore another patient's name label, told her the pills were expired but fine, and poured them into her pill dispenser, without documenting the dispensing. Uncomfortable, she did not take them and filed an online complaint with the Board. A 2020 search of his office found dozens of expired samples, some many years old, mixed with unexpired samples, and two expired medications prescribed to another patient.

After a hearing, an administrative law judge found, based on the persuasive and unrefuted opinion of the Board's psychiatrist expert, one simple departure (prescribing cough syrup without an examination) and three extreme departures: prescribing an opioid while prohibited by probation, dispensing expired medication returned by another patient, and failing to document the dispensing. The psychiatrist admitted the conduct but justified it as helping patients. The judge concluded that, despite prior probation and recent prescribing, recordkeeping, and professionalism courses, he showed a lax attitude toward prescribing, possessing, dispensing, and documenting medications and lacked insight, warranting five years' probation rather than the letter of reprimand he requested.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 5 years' probation with controlled-substance record log and inventory access, 40 hours/year education, prescribing practices course, professionalism (ethics) program, clinical competence assessment followed by professional enhancement program, practice monitor, solo practice prohibition, prohibition on supervising PAs/APNs, and probation monitoring costs.

narrative: The psychiatrist was charged in an Accusation concerning three adult outpatients with opioid use disorder to whom he prescribed buprenorphine-naloxone (Suboxone) together with other controlled substances. According to the Accusation, Patient A, who also had ADHD and sedative-hypnotic-anxiolytic dependence and had been in his care since 2008, received recurring prescriptions from 2014 onward for Suboxone, amphetamine salts, alprazolam, and diazepam, and for several months phenobarbital. Patient B, with anxiety and sedative dependence, received Suboxone, amphetamine salts, clonazepam, and diazepam from 2017 to 2020. Patient C, with anxiety, received Suboxone, diazepam, and alprazolam from 2017 to 2020. After California's mandatory CURES-consultation requirement took effect in October 2018, the Accusation alleged he did not check CURES at all for Patients A and C through March 2020, and checked it only once for Patient B.

The Accusation further alleged that his records were missing progress notes for multiple encounters with Patient A, did not document the basis for prescribing amphetamines, benzodiazepines, or Suboxone, did not document an ADHD assessment for Patient B, and contained inconsistent statements about patient evaluation. It charged gross negligence (inadequate records for Patients A and B; failure to review CURES for Patient C), repeated negligent acts, failure to consult CURES, and inadequate records. The Accusation did not separately allege that the prescribing itself was excessive. The psychiatrist did not contest that a prima facie case could be established and made no admissions.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 4 years' probation with 40 hours/year of additional education, prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, and practice monitor; prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; probation monitoring costs.

narrative: The psychiatrist, in solo outpatient practice, was charged in an Accusation covering seven patients; he did not contest that the complainant could establish a factual basis for the charges and made no admissions. The central allegations concerned Patient A, a young woman recently out of residential substance-abuse treatment, whom he resumed seeing in 2017 and immediately prescribed Adderall XR 60 mg/day plus Xanax and bupropion without a history, mental status examination, ADHD evaluation, or prior records. According to the Accusation, the day after the first visit her mother reported an overdose with alcohol, cocaine use, and doctor-shopping; CURES showed Adderall from three other prescribers, yet he never checked CURES again or contacted the other prescribers. Over roughly two years, while the mother and a therapist sent repeated reports of whole bottles of Xanax and Adderall consumed, Klonopin taken with alcohol, a drug-induced psychosis, psychiatric hospitalization, police involvement, self-harm, and binge-purging, he did not respond or document any review, and continued, at times escalated, stimulants (up to 75 mg/day of Adderall XR, later Vyvanse 70 mg), benzodiazepines, and bupropion despite the seizure risk. Many progress notes were blank or a few words long.

Similar patterns were alleged for other patients: multiple concurrent benzodiazepines for a man also receiving opioids from his primary care physician (who later died of a cardiac dysrhythmia), benzodiazepines, stimulants, and hydrocodone without documented rationale for a patient with alcohol use disorder, high-dose Adderall with escalating Xanax and temazepam for a patient with insomnia, and about 20 blank progress notes for one patient. He was also alleged to have prescribed Adderall, Vyvanse, and Strattera for years to two of his own children without any evaluation or records. He told the Board investigator he was unfamiliar with the CURES-review requirement and did not always check it.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 5 years' probation with proof of CURES registration, additional education course, prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, professionalism (ethics) program, and practice monitor; prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; probation monitoring costs.

narrative: In December 2020 the psychiatrist self-reported to the Board that he had entered into an agreement with the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration concerning his DEA controlled-substance registration. The Public Consent Order found that between December 31, 2018 and April 21, 2020 he wrote six prescriptions for himself: clonazepam 2 mg, quantity 180, on December 31, 2018 and again on July 20, 2019; clonazepam 2 mg, quantity 40, in December 2019 and quantity 90 in January 2020; diphenoxylate-atropine 2.5/0.025 mg, quantity 10, in March 2020; and clonazepam 2 mg, quantity 90, in April 2020 (580 clonazepam 2 mg tablets in about 16 months). Both drugs are controlled substances, and there was no documented emergency on any of those dates. The order found that this conduct departed from minimum standards of acceptable practice and was unprofessional conduct under the Board's rules. The psychiatrist agreed to the findings of fact. The order does not describe the terms of the DEA agreement, any clinical reason for the prescriptions, or any finding of impairment.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand; $5,000 fine within 30 days; mini-residency on appropriate prescribing of controlled substances within six months, in addition to renewal CME.

narrative: The psychiatrist, in private practice, was charged in an Accusation concerning two patients; he did not contest that a prima facie case could be established and made no admissions. According to the Accusation, Patient A, a woman with depression, fibromyalgia-related chronic pain and gastrointestinal disease, was receiving opioids from a neurologist; when the neurologist stopped practicing in 2015, the psychiatrist took over without a pain assessment, physical examination, prior records, or pain agreement. Over about three and a half years he prescribed oxycodone 10 mg at roughly 240 to 279 tablets a month (after earlier fentanyl and OxyContin), plus Klonopin and Zanaflex. He kept prescribing despite repeated insurer notices of early refills, CURES fills from other prescribers, a reported theft, prescriptions handed to her spouse when she was not present, a hospitalization for delirium and hypotension, and reduced kidney function, with no documented discussion of opioid-benzodiazepine risk or naloxone; he ended care only after CURES showed opioids from another prescriber. The Accusation alleged resulting harm including sedation, cognitive decline, colitis flares, hypotension with syncope, and opioid-induced hyperalgesia.

For Patient B, who had bipolar disorder, PTSD, dissociative identity disorder and borderline personality disorder, the Accusation alleged he prescribed about 75 mg/day of Adderall XR and 4 to 6 mg/day of Klonopin from 2015 to 2018, raised Klonopin in response to PTSD symptoms, did not check CURES, and did not consider whether the stimulant was causing her insomnia. When she called in 2017 agitated and suicidal, he prescribed olanzapine by phone without a documented suicide risk assessment or timely follow-up. Records for both patients repeatedly lacked mental status examinations, diagnoses, and treatment plans.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 3 years' probation with 30 hours/year of additional education, prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, and practice monitor (or professional enhancement program); prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; probation monitoring costs.

narrative: In October 2018 the Board received a complaint that the psychiatrist kept prescribing alprazolam (Xanax) to patient C.D. although he knew the patient had a history of prescription drug abuse. A Board-approved peer reviewer then evaluated his care of three outpatients and concluded that his diagnosis, treatment and/or records fell below minimal standards. C.D. was treated from about September 2015 to January 2019 for opiate dependency and an anxiety disorder, and between February 2017 and January 2019 received Suboxone 8 mg or alprazolam 1 mg prescriptions thirty times. The reviewer cited no documented comprehensive initial psychiatric assessment, no documented diagnosis correlating with the Xanax, continued buprenorphine plus benzodiazepine prescribing without a documented plan to reduce the benzodiazepine or a trial of non-addictive medications first, and no corroborating history from a friend or family member. J.N., seen from 2014 to 2019 for anxiety, depression and pain, received opioid medications together with high-dose benzodiazepines and other psychotropics; the reviewer called Xanax 6 mg a day with concurrent opioids unusually high and beyond the maximum dose for anxiety disorders, and noted little if any recommendation of psychotherapy, no attempts to taper the benzodiazepines, and no routine urine drug screens or outside records to corroborate the reported back pain.

H.K., treated from June 2017 to August 2018 for opiate dependency, anxiety and insomnia with buprenorphine-naloxone and benzodiazepines, kept receiving controlled medications after inconsistent confirmatory urine drug tests. Suboxone was continued after a confirmatory screen showed relapse to heroin, morphine and hydromorphone, with no documented discussion of the results; Xanax frequency was increased after a documented failure to follow the treatment plan; and concurrent oxycodone use interspersed with Suboxone was not addressed. The psychiatrist admitted these findings of fact in the Public Consent Order.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand; within six months, a Board-approved mini-residency on appropriate prescribing of controlled substances and a Board-approved medical record documentation course, both in addition to renewal CME.

narrative: The Board opened an investigation after receiving credible information that the psychiatrist was self-prescribing controlled substances under a fictitious name. By the time of the order she was no longer practicing in Oregon; her license had become inactive in October 2021 and lapsed in January 2022. The order does not name the drugs, the time period, or how the prescriptions came to light.

In the Stipulated Order she neither admitted nor denied the matter, but the Board found that she engaged in unprofessional or dishonorable conduct, defined as conduct, practice or condition that does or might adversely affect a physician's ability to practice safely and skillfully, and that she prescribed controlled substances without a legitimate medical purpose.
cases.outcome: Surrendered Oregon license while under investigation; may not reapply for at least two years; must obey all laws pertaining to the practice of medicine.

narrative: In May 2022 the Board issued a Second Amended Complaint and Notice of Proposed Disciplinary Action against the psychiatrist, proposing revocation. It charged unprofessional conduct that did or might endanger patients or the public, repeated acts of negligence, gross negligence, and prescribing controlled substances without a legitimate medical purpose or without following accepted procedures for examination or record keeping. The Stipulated Order does not describe the underlying facts, and the Notice is not attached. The order's remedial terms point to the areas of concern: older patients, diagnostic workup, and prescribing of stimulants and benzodiazepines. These terms require CME in the diagnosis and medical management of geriatric mental health, a documentation course, and a practice mentor. The mentor must review the psychiatrist's treatment of every patient over 65 each month and report on diagnostic workup, prescribing with special attention to stimulants and benzodiazepines, and other needs identified in a February 2020 CPEP assessment.

The psychiatrist neither admitted nor denied the allegations, but the Board found that the conduct described in the Notice violated the cited provisions. The order also requires the psychiatrist to follow published prescribing and monitoring standards for all controlled substances. For opioids these include risk assessment before starting treatment, urine drug screens, PDMP checks and pain contracts.
cases.outcome: Reprimand; $5,000 civil penalty; 30 hours of Board-approved CME in geriatric mental health diagnosis and management and a documentation course within six months; monthly practice mentor review of all patients over 65 with quarterly reports; adherence to published controlled-substance prescribing and monitoring standards (risk assessment, urine drug screens, PDMP checks, pain contracts); no-notice chart audits and office visits.

narrative: The psychiatrist did not contest that the Board could establish a prima facie case on the Accusation, which alleged gross negligence, repeated negligent acts, inadequate records, and unprofessional conduct in the long-term outpatient care of two patients, largely between 2014 and 2019. Patient 1, a woman treated for depression, possible bipolar disorder, and panic disorder with a past history of cocaine use, was prescribed alprazolam, later clonazepam (up to 4 mg/day), and carisoprodol, a muscle relaxant the Accusation said had no psychiatric indication, with no documented informed consent and no contact with her psychologist or other treaters. According to the Accusation, she attempted suicide by alprazolam overdose in 2014, was detoxified from clonazepam and carisoprodol in 2017, and developed delirium in 2018 before a month-long residential detoxification and a diagnosis of sedative, hypnotic, or anxiolytic use disorder. Despite this history, the psychiatrist resumed clonazepam (eventually up to three times daily) and added suvorexant in 2019. On two occasions in 2017, when told by phone that she was oversedated, slurring, confused, or possibly hallucinating, he advised medication changes rather than ensuring emergency evaluation.

Patient 2 had been treated since 2001 with an ADHD diagnosis that the Accusation alleged lacked a clinical basis, while his depression, anxiety, and insomnia went unaddressed; he received amphetamine products together with alprazolam at doses up to 1 mg four times daily (90-day supplies of 360 tablets), plus antipsychotics without stated indication, despite falls, balance problems, and a pharmacy warning about excessive sedative use. Records for both patients were described as inconsistent and nonchronological, with handwritten notes on medication lists and memo pads, unsigned or misdated entries, missing pages, two differing "certified" versions of one chart, and an after-the-fact summary apparently meant to support the ADHD diagnosis in a disability claim.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 4 years' probation with 40 hours/year education course, prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, professionalism (ethics) program, and practice monitor; prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; cost recovery $4,227.50.

narrative: The psychiatrist gave up the right to contest that the Board could establish a prima facie case on the First Amended Accusation, which alleged gross negligence (two patients), repeated negligent acts, clearly excessive prescribing, and inadequate records in the outpatient care of three patients between 2016 and 2020. Patient L, a 25-year-old man with paraplegia, panic disorder, and ADHD, was continued on Adderall 60 mg daily (above the maximum recommended dose, without documented rationale or vital signs) and started on alprazolam 1 mg, zolpidem 10 mg, and paroxetine without documented informed consent or a CURES check. One week later the psychiatrist tripled alprazolam to 3 mg daily with an early refill and no office visit, then raised it to 3.5 mg and 4 mg daily even after the patient admitted taking more than prescribed, without addressing possible misuse or diversion.

Patient B, a 24-year-old woman with schizophrenia and ADHD, reported command auditory hallucinations to harm herself in 2018 and again in 2020; according to the Accusation, no suicide risk assessment was done, antipsychotics were left at low doses despite persistent psychosis, and stimulants were continued and even increased after she admitted overusing methylphenidate. Benzodiazepine and stimulant changes were made without visits, prescriptions issued in 2019 were not documented, and CURES was not checked until months into treatment, with no note that she was receiving oxycodone and hydrocodone elsewhere. Patient S, a 42-year-old man with persistent depression and ADHD, was given lorazepam and later alprazolam while receiving opioids and carisoprodol from other prescribers, with no documented opioid-benzodiazepine risk discussion, no suicide risk assessment despite repeated reports of worsening depression, and lorazepam issued twice after the chart said it had been stopped.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 4 years' probation with controlled-substance log, 30-hour/year education course, prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, professionalism (ethics) program, and practice monitor; prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; cost recovery $4,960.

narrative: The psychiatrist did not contest that the Board could establish a factual basis for the charges in the First Amended Accusation, which alleged the following. Between May 2016 and September 2017, the psychiatrist treated Patient 1 in an outpatient practice, through in-person and telephone sessions and text messages, for depression and anxiety. At intake the psychiatrist diagnosed major depression and prescribed Cymbalta, added Klonopin (clonazepam) as needed for anxiety and sleep, and a few weeks later added an ADHD diagnosis and Adderall based on the patient's report of lifelong difficulty organizing tasks. The Accusation alleged that none of these diagnoses was supported by a documented history, mental status examination, psychiatric or medical history, or substance use history, even though the intake form listed polysubstance abuse and the patient disclosed past and ongoing alcohol and GHB use. Over the following year the psychiatrist learned the patient missed an appointment while intoxicated, was drinking to console herself, and once offered a large jar of marijuana in lieu of payment, yet conducted no substance use assessment, did no monitoring or testing, and documented no discussion of the risks of combining alcohol or GHB with a benzodiazepine.

The psychiatrist wrote monthly prescriptions for 90 tablets each of Klonopin and Adderall, far more than the instructed doses, and in June 2017 issued two prescriptions of each, explaining to investigators that she wanted the patient to have extra medication on hand. The patient's condition deteriorated (a work "meltdown," disability leave, appearing at work intoxicated) without any change in the treatment plan. In August 2017 the patient stopped her medications on her own, developed suicidal thoughts and severe anxiety, and was treated at a detoxification facility for sedative-hypnotic withdrawal and a severe sedative-hypnotic use disorder. Notes were allegedly brief and sometimes misdated, with no prescribing rationale or documented informed consent.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 3 years' probation with clinical competence assessment program, education course (CME hours later corrected by nunc pro tunc order), prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, professionalism (ethics) program, and practice monitor; prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; cost recovery $4,500.

narrative: The psychiatrist settled an Accusation charging gross negligence, repeated negligent acts, inadequate records, and violation of the Medical Practice Act in the care of one patient. He did not contest that a prima facie case could be established. Patient A, a 26-year-old woman, came to him in June 2014 for poor concentration. At the first visit he diagnosed ADHD and prescribed Adderall 20 mg twice daily. According to the Accusation, he did not document six or more symptoms, onset before age 12, or symptoms in two settings. He knew she drank alcohol but did not ask about past substance use, treatment, or family history of substance use. Over the next five years he raised Adderall to 30 mg twice daily, above the 40 mg/day maximum recommended dose, without documenting a rationale. He issued two 90-tablet Adderall prescriptions a week apart in April 2015 without recognizing this as a warning sign. From 2015 he added alprazolam 0.5 mg, and from 2017 Ambien 10 mg, the higher dose rather than the 5 mg recommended for women. He did not record these prescriptions in the chart until 2017 and documented no diagnosis or assessment to support them.

The Accusation alleged that he never checked CURES, never took vital signs, never discussed the risks of combining a stimulant, a benzodiazepine, and a hypnotic, and went months between visits while continuing prescriptions. It alleged that he did no ongoing suicide risk assessment. A 2018 suicide attempt was not reflected in his records, and he told investigators he learned of it only after her death. CURES showed fills at about eight pharmacies and six controlled-substance prescriptions from three other providers. Patient A died by suicide in July 2019, and her toxicology was positive for cocaine, THC, benzodiazepines, and amphetamines. He told investigators he never found her to have suicidal ideation.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; five years' probation; prohibited from prescribing controlled substances (except Schedule V) until completing a prescribing practices course and from issuing cannabis recommendations; 40 hours/year of education, medical record keeping course, clinical competence assessment program, practice monitor, prohibition on supervising PAs and advanced practice nurses, and cost recovery of $3,500.

narrative: The psychiatrist, licensed since 1966, surrendered the license after agreeing that the Board could establish a factual basis for the charges in the Accusation, without admitting them. The Accusation alleged gross negligence, repeated negligent acts, excessive prescribing, furnishing drugs to an addict, prescribing without appropriate examination or indication, and inadequate records in the treatment of two women for ADHD through 2019. Patient 1, about 30, was treated intermittently from 2007, partly through email exchanges, and from 2016 to 2019 received high-dose Adderall prescriptions and refills with no documented rationale; the psychiatrist sometimes contacted pharmacies and insurers to obtain exceptions for the doses. She had reportedly once been taken to an emergency room after overdosing on 30 Adderall tablets, yet there were no drug screens, pill counts, or CURES checks. Of hundreds of chart pages, only about five were progress notes; the rest were emails to non-secure addresses, and there was no recorded diagnosis, risk assessment, suicidality assessment, or treatment plan. He stopped treating her abruptly in 2019 without a referral.

Patient 2, about 38, was treated from 2011 to 2019 for ADHD without an adequate documented diagnosis or plan and was prescribed Adderall, clonazepam, quetiapine, risperidone, and escitalopram. In 2012 she reported drinking to blackout two to four times a month and taking her mother's Xanax, and she had a history of bipolar disorder, but the Accusation alleged that the psychiatrist documented no concern about substance use or bipolar illness, took no monitoring steps, and continued high-dose controlled substances, including a stimulant-benzodiazepine combination the Accusation said raised her cardiac risk.
cases.outcome: License surrender accepted; costs of $19,692.50 payable before any new or reinstated license; any reapplication treated as a petition for reinstatement with the Accusation's allegations deemed admitted.

narrative: The psychiatrist, by then retired from a private outpatient practice and with an expired license, surrendered the license after agreeing that the Board could establish a factual basis for the single charge of gross negligence in the Accusation, without admitting it. According to the Accusation, Patient A first came to the psychiatrist in December 2003 wanting to stop OxyContin (80 mg/day) while also taking Valium 30 mg/day. Over the next several years the psychiatrist successfully tapered the opioid and diazepam and treated the patient's chronic depression and anxiety, and the patient left care in 2008 on diazepam 10 mg. He returned around 2011 after a back injury, again taking 50 mg of diazepam daily, and by the last in-person visit in October 2012 he had also resumed OxyContin. The psychiatrist agreed to prescribe diazepam with a plan to taper, but declined to prescribe OxyContin.

CURES showed that from August 2014 to October 2017 the psychiatrist kept prescribing diazepam 10 mg, 75 tablets every 14 days, with no follow-up visit of any kind. The charged period was November 2015 to October 2017. The psychiatrist reportedly trusted the patient to say when he had found a new psychiatrist. The Accusation alleged that the standard of care calls for follow-up every one to three months (face-to-face, telephone, or video) for benzodiazepine prescribing, with closer monitoring for patients with a substance use history. It alleged that two years of prescribing without monitoring, to a patient on high-dose benzodiazepines who was also taking opioids and had no accountability for tapering, was gross negligence.
cases.outcome: License surrender accepted; costs of $1,877.50 payable before any new or reinstated license; any reapplication treated as a petition for reinstatement with the Accusation's allegations deemed admitted.

narrative: The psychiatrist surrendered his license and agreed that the allegations, if proven, would establish a factual basis for the charges. The First Amended Accusation charged gross negligence, repeated negligent acts, and inadequate records in the care of one patient. He did not admit them. Patient A, a 52-year-old woman, was hospitalized in September 2013 with severe depression, suicidal ideation, and overuse of Norco and Klonopin. She had a history of alcohol abuse, past heroin and methadone use, prior overdoses, and a 2010 DUI on prescription medications. She was diagnosed with bipolar II disorder and benzodiazepine dependence. The psychiatrist followed her from a partial hospitalization program in October 2013 and then as an outpatient through at least September 2019. According to the Accusation, he prescribed clonazepam throughout, usually about 3 mg a day, while she was also taking opioids. She repeatedly reported taking more than prescribed, up to 6 mg a day. Her family said she was overmedicated, and she had falls, a fractured ankle, psychomotor slowing, and excessive daytime sleepiness. He recorded that she seemed overly intoxicated and stumbled.

CURES records cited in the Accusation showed that from late 2014 on, another physician prescribed her large monthly quantities of Norco, oxycodone 30 mg, and carisoprodol, and other prescribers also supplied clonazepam. An insurer faxed the psychiatrist that she was getting clonazepam elsewhere, but he did not run CURES, document the alert, or discuss it with her. His medication lists left out the oxycodone and carisoprodol and repeatedly listed drugs he had planned to stop. The Accusation alleged that it was grossly negligent to continue long-term clonazepam in a patient with a substance use history who was overusing it and taking opioids. It also faulted him for failing to connect reports of sedation with the drug combination and for failing to investigate her substance use history. It cited a prior public reprimand.
cases.outcome: License surrender accepted; costs of $7,747.50 payable before any new or reinstated license; any reapplication treated as a petition for reinstatement with the Accusation's allegations deemed admitted.

narrative: The psychiatrist did not contest that the Board could establish a prima facie case on the First Amended Accusation, which alleged gross negligence, repeated negligent acts, and inadequate records in the care of four middle-aged women at an outpatient psychiatric clinic between 2015 and 2021. Each patient had been taken over from another clinician, and the psychiatrist continued long-term benzodiazepines (alprazolam or clonazepam) while the patients were receiving opioids from other physicians, without eliciting or documenting their opioid use, pain, cognition, or memory, and without documented informed consent for long-term benzodiazepine use or for combining benzodiazepines with opioids. Clinic staff recorded CURES reports as "approved" or "printed," but the psychiatrist never referred to them in her notes, never checked CURES herself, and one chart entry wrongly stated she was the only prescriber. Notes were largely copied forward with minimal clinical content, and no laboratory testing was obtained.

According to the Accusation, Patient 1, a kidney-transplant recipient later treated for esophageal cancer, received clonazepam 1 mg daily while on a fentanyl patch and Percocet four times daily; the psychiatrist's response was to tell her not to take pain medication at night, without contacting the pain prescribers, and a planned taper was not carried out for months. Patient 2 received about 1,071 clonazepam 0.5 mg tablets over 488 days while on OxyContin and Percocet. Patient 3 received alprazolam 2 mg nightly for more than three years alongside Norco and codeine, with advice only to take them at different times, even after a car accident and pneumonia. Patient 4, with bipolar disorder and panic disorder, stayed on clonazepam 2-3 mg daily through tramadol and Percocet courses after knee surgery and was told to separate the doses by four hours.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 3 years' probation with controlled-substance log, prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, and professionalism (ethics) program; solo practice prohibited; prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; cost recovery $8,000.

cases.type: Public reprimand / public letter of reprimand
narrative: The Board issued a one-page Public Letter of Reprimand stating that its investigation revealed that the psychiatrist deviated from the standard of care by self-prescribing medications, in violation of the general unprofessional-conduct and repeated-negligence provisions of the Medical Practice Act. The letter does not identify the medications or give any other details.
cases.outcome: Public Letter of Reprimand; no additional terms stated.

narrative: The respondent was an osteopathic physician whose specialty, the Board's pleadings state, is psychiatry. According to the Amended Emergency Order of Restriction, on December 15, 2022 a search warrant executed at the psychiatrist's residence recovered a baggie of a white substance consistent with methamphetamine, bags of the ADHD drug Vyvanse, and scales, pipes, a container and baggies with residue, and he was arrested on state charges of first-offense trafficking in a controlled substance, first-degree possession of a controlled substance and possession of drug paraphernalia. The Inquiry Panel Chair restricted his license the next day, and the Panel ratified that order when it issued a Complaint in February 2023. On May 25, 2023 a federal grand jury indicted him on four counts of knowingly distributing and dispensing amphetamine, a Schedule II drug, outside the scope of professional practice and not for a legitimate medical purpose. The Panel Chair then issued the Amended Complaint and the Amended Emergency Order of Restriction, stating there was probable cause to believe his practice endangered patients and the public; under Board regulation a felony indictment involving controlled substances is treated as an immediate danger. These were probable-cause findings for interim action, not findings after a hearing.

The file also contains the later resolution. In an Agreed Order of Surrender filed September 19, 2024, the parties stipulated that in March 2024 he pleaded guilty to one federal distribution count, admitting that during six undercover visits by a DEA task force officer to his clinic (April-September 2022) he prescribed Ritalin after the officer asked for a 'kick in the britches,' then switched to Adderall and planned dose increases without explanation, performed no examinations beyond cursory blood-pressure and lung checks, did not ask about medical need, and took no action when the officer skipped ordered blood work five visits in a row. While on pretrial release he tested positive for unprescribed methamphetamine and was detained; he was sentenced to 32 months in prison.
cases.outcome: Interim restriction: prohibited from prescribing, dispensing or otherwise professionally using controlled substances until the hearing panel resolves the Amended Complaint after the criminal case. (Later, by Agreed Order of Surrender filed 9/19/2024: license surrendered in lieu of revocation; no petition for at least two years and until the criminal sentence is completed and $562.50 costs paid; any return would require a clinical skills assessment, a 96-hour inpatient impairment evaluation, a permanent controlled-substance restriction and 2-5 years' probation.)

narrative: The psychiatrist, licensed since 1981 and in outpatient private practice, settled without admitting the allegations, agreeing only that the Board could establish a prima facie case. According to the First Amended Accusation, in February 2014 he took over care of Patient 1, a man with a history of OxyContin and heroin abuse who said another psychiatrist had been prescribing him Subutex, Xanax, and Celexa for panic attacks. Without obtaining the prior psychiatrist's records or calling him, checking CURES, or doing a drug screen, and without a documented mental status examination, he diagnosed opioid and heroin abuse, recurrent major depression, panic disorder, and generalized anxiety disorder and prescribed Subutex 8 mg twice daily, Xanax 2 mg twice daily, and Celexa 20 mg daily. He followed the patient only monthly, never prescribed naloxone, and documented no suicide risk assessment. Over two years most notes read only "stable, same meds," several visits had no note at all, and when the patient was taking more Xanax than prescribed the dose was raised in 2016 to 2 mg three times daily with no documented reason. CURES showed Xanax 2 mg prescriptions in rapid succession without chart entries (for example, #80 on January 22, #15 on January 27, #25 on January 28, and #80 on February 9, 2016).

The Accusation further alleged that in 2016 a pharmacist called to verify a Xanax prescription the psychiatrist had not issued; the patient admitted faxing it himself using the psychiatrist's credentials. The psychiatrist discharged him by text message and referred him to rehab but continued Subutex until late October 2016. After providing the Board a summary of the chart, he destroyed the original record. Separately, CURES showed he prescribed testosterone, a controlled substance, to himself four times between 2017 and 2018.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 3 years' probation with controlled-substance log, 40 hours/year of education (treating patients with opioid/drug/alcohol abuse histories), prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, professionalism (ethics) program, and practice monitor; prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; costs of $16,000.

narrative: The psychiatrist, in outpatient practice, did not contest that the Board could establish a prima facie case. The Accusation concerned long-term medication management of three women, with handwritten, poorly legible records that did not track prescriptions, and almost no CURES checks or drug screens. Patient 1, followed from 2007 to 2019 for rapid-cycling bipolar I disorder and alcohol use disorder, had more than 20 hospitalizations, mostly after suicide attempts, and received over 70 different medications. He continued clonazepam, lorazepam, and temazepam despite documented ongoing drinking, a three-car accident, cannabis use, and repeated nonadherence, and in 2018 added tramadol for pain without evaluation while another provider was also prescribing opioids. He documented self-harm or suicidality on at least six visits without a suicide risk assessment. The Accusation alleged she suffered numerous overdoses on medications he prescribed.

Patient 2, in her late 60s and older with prior TIAs, received lorazepam (at times with diazepam), buspirone, and trifluoperazine for years, including two lorazepam prescriptions a month, despite repeated early refills, reports of lost or stolen pills, taking more than prescribed, concurrent benzodiazepines and opioids from other prescribers, fatigue, dizziness, and frailty; she was alleged to have overdosed on benzodiazepines. Patient 3, who had been through opiate rehab, was prescribed clonazepam, zolpidem, and suvorexant together (plus trazodone) while other prescribers supplied Xanax, opioids, and benzphetamine. CURES showed duplicate clonazepam fills at different pharmacies and six months' supply in five months; in 2017 she reported taking 8 mg of clonazepam a day against 2.5 mg prescribed, yet the psychiatrist did not address possible benzodiazepine use disorder, and he made no adjustment when she turned 65. He also did no violence risk assessment after she reported being arrested for slapping her husband.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 3 years' probation with 40 hours/year of education, prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, clinical competence assessment program, and practice monitor; prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; costs of $21,659.

narrative: In September 2021 the Board received a complaint from the spouse of one of the psychiatrist's patients alleging that the spouse and 'several others' were seeing him for Suboxone only to resell it, that it was easy to get prescriptions from him, and that the Suboxone and 'pain killers' he prescribed were 'destroying lives.' The Board identified ten patients who received controlled dangerous substances from him between January 2020 and September 2021 and sent their records to two peer reviewers, one board-certified in addiction medicine and one in addiction psychiatry.

In the Consent Order, Disciplinary Panel B found that both reviewers concluded his care fell below the standard for all ten patients. The reasons included failing to use consistent compliance monitoring for any of the ten; continuing to prescribe and refill controlled substances despite noncompliant behavior such as discordant urine screens or a patient's admission of buying controlled substances illicitly (nine patients); starting or changing controlled-substance doses without sufficient diagnostic or clinical findings; prescribing combinations of opioids, benzodiazepines, and/or sedatives without clear counseling about the risks of combining them; not requiring a substance-use treatment agreement from patients receiving ongoing controlled substances; and not considering or referring for non-controlled alternatives. The reviewers also found his records inadequate for all ten patients because clinical notes were vague, inconsistent, or missing. The panel concluded that he failed to meet the standard of quality care and failed to keep adequate records. The psychiatrist signed the Consent Order and waived any right to contest its findings.
cases.outcome: Reprimand; permanent prohibition on prescribing and dispensing all controlled dangerous substances in Maryland, with transfer of CDS patients and an annual affidavit of compliance; probation for a minimum of one year with a medical recordkeeping course within 6 months.

narrative: The Accusation concerned the psychiatrist's pain management care of three patients, for which he prescribed controlled substances. Patient A, a 51-year-old man, arrived in December 2015 already taking extended-release oxymorphone 60 mg three times daily and oxycodone 20 mg three times daily. Through July 2017 he was seen about 14 times, 10 of them by the psychiatrist's nurse practitioner, and was prescribed oxycodone averaging 60 mg and oxymorphone averaging 180 mg daily (about 630 morphine milligram equivalents). The Accusation alleged that the notes said little about his pain, that CURES checks and side-effect monitoring were missing or undocumented, and that urine drug screens were not used adequately, although an early screen was negative for the oxycodone his primary care physician prescribed. Patient B, a 53-year-old woman with ADHD and bipolar disorder, received transdermal fentanyl 100 mcg, oxycodone averaging 114 mg daily, clonazepam averaging 2.5 mg daily, and carisoprodol from June 2016 to June 2017. The same monitoring gaps were alleged, and urine drug screening was alleged to be inadequate even though the psychiatrist knew of a prior DUI involving oxycodone.

Patient C, a nursing-home resident with COPD, heart failure, diabetes, depression, and chronic pain, was seen about 23 times from 2014 to 2017 and received opioids, carisoprodol, and knee steroid injections. In May 2016 she was hospitalized after a drug overdose, and her urine was positive for amphetamine, cannabis, opiates, and oxycodone. The Accusation alleged that the psychiatrist did not follow up on her methamphetamine and marijuana use, obtained no drug screens, and did not coordinate with her primary care physician, her psychiatrist, or nursing-home staff. In the stipulated settlement he did not contest that a prima facie case could be established; he made no admissions. The reprimand states that from 2015 to 2017 he failed to adequately monitor Patients A, B, and C and to coordinate Patient C's care while prescribing controlled substances.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand with 40-hour education course, prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, and clinical competence assessment program (must cease practice if not completed on time); cost recovery $51,736.25.

narrative: According to the Administrative Complaint, the psychiatrist treated Patient A.D., a woman, from March 2016 to about August 2017 for major depressive disorder and bipolar disorder. In May 2017 he changed her diagnosis from major depressive disorder to bipolar disorder without clearly documenting why. Throughout treatment he prescribed and switched among multiple benzodiazepines (alprazolam, lorazepam, temazepam, diazepam and clonazepam) and among antidepressants, mood stabilizers and antipsychotics (Wellbutrin, escitalopram, lamotrigine and Seroquel), without adequately justifying the changes in the record. In February 2017 he also prescribed oxycodone for a foot injury, which the Complaint described as outside the scope of a psychiatrist's practice, while she was also taking alprazolam that he prescribed. The Complaint alleged that co-prescribing an opioid and a benzodiazepine without sufficient justification fell below the standard of care, and that he did not document any consideration of the potential drug interaction.

The Department charged medical malpractice (the opioid-benzodiazepine combination) and failure to keep medical records justifying the course of treatment. In the Settlement Agreement adopted by the Board's Final Order, the psychiatrist neither admitted nor denied the allegations.
cases.outcome: Reprimand; $20,000 fine; costs of $15,000 (both payable within two years); CME of 5 hours in laws, rules and ethics, 10 hours in drug prescribing, 3 hours in medical recordkeeping, and 5 hours in risk management, each within one year.

narrative: In November 2023 the Investigative Committee of the Nevada Board filed a four-count Complaint alleging malpractice (Count I), two violations of the statutes and regulations of the Nevada State Board of Pharmacy (Counts II and III), and failure to adequately supervise (Count IV). The Complaint is not attached to the Settlement Agreement, which gives no facts about the patients, prescriptions, or persons supervised, or how the matter came to the Board's attention. In the agreement the psychiatrist stated generally that he was not admitting the claims had merit and was settling to avoid the cost of a hearing, but specifically admitted Counts II and III, the two pharmacy-law violations, and agreed the Board could enter an order finding conduct that is grounds for discipline. The malpractice and supervision counts were dismissed with prejudice. The required continuing education was in the proper prescribing of controlled substances. The Board approved the agreement on March 1, 2024.
cases.outcome: Public Letter of Reprimand; $2,000 fine; costs of $1,142.47; 4 hours of CME on proper prescribing of controlled substances within 180 days (in addition to licensure CME); Counts I and IV dismissed.

narrative: The Accusation concerned four outpatients to whom the psychiatrist prescribed controlled substances on a recurring basis between 2018 and 2022. It focused on two missed safeguards: checking the CURES database as state law requires (before first prescribing and at least every four months, later every six months) and seeing patients before renewing prescriptions. Patient A, a 49-year-old man with generalized anxiety, depression, insomnia, chronic pain, and a history of alcohol abuse, was also getting hydromorphone, methadone, hydrocodone, and buprenorphine-naloxone from other prescribers. The psychiatrist prescribed him clonazepam 1 mg (60 tablets a month, later 30) for almost four years. He saw the patient about seven times, once going roughly 11 months between visits while prescriptions continued, and kept writing clonazepam for more than two years after his last CURES check in June 2019. Patient B, a 25-year-old man with ADHD, received immediate- and extended-release amphetamine salts. In November 2018 the psychiatrist noted "odd dispensing" on CURES, yet the Accusation alleged he continued stimulant prescriptions for nearly a year without a visit (February 2019 to January 2020) and for about 20 months without a CURES check (August 2020 to April 2022).

Patient C, a 53-year-old woman with major depression with psychotic features, received clonazepam 0.5 mg from late 2019 to 2022; CURES was checked only once, at intake. Patient D, a 46-year-old woman with depression and panic attacks, received alprazolam 1 mg (60 tablets a month) from 2020 to 2022, and CURES was never checked. The Accusation charged repeated negligent acts, violation of the controlled-substance statute requiring CURES review, and violation of the Medical Practice Act. The psychiatrist surrendered his license, agreeing that the complainant could establish a prima facie case. He did not admit the allegations, and no findings were made.
cases.outcome: License surrender accepted; costs of $37,656.00 payable before any new or reinstated license; any reapplication treated as a petition for reinstatement with the Accusation's allegations deemed admitted.

narrative: The Board opened this matter after receiving a referral from the state Office of Controlled Substances Administration reporting concerns about the physician's prescribing of controlled dangerous substances to patients. No formal charges had been issued. The physician, who stated that he was retired, submitted a Letter of Surrender to avoid the issuance of charges and prosecution of the allegations. The letter does not describe the patients, drugs, doses, or the specific prescribing concerns.

In the letter the physician did not contest the allegations and agreed that, for all purposes relevant to medical licensure, they would be treated as proven and would support a conclusion that he failed to meet appropriate standards for the delivery of quality medical care and failed to keep adequate medical records. He also agreed to surrender his state Controlled Dangerous Substance registration.
cases.outcome: Surrender of license accepted (public, treated as a disciplinary action); CDS registration surrendered; any future reinstatement petition to be treated as if the license had been revoked.

narrative: In August 2023 the Board opened an investigation after receiving credible information regarding the psychiatrist's alleged diversion of controlled substances. The order does not identify the drugs, patients, time period, or source of the information.

In the Stipulated Order he neither admitted nor denied the matter, but the Board found that he engaged in unprofessional or dishonorable conduct contrary to recognized standards of medical ethics, violated the federal Controlled Substances Act, and prescribed controlled substances without a legitimate medical purpose or without following accepted procedures for examination of patients or for record keeping.
cases.outcome: Surrendered Oregon license while under investigation; may not reapply for at least two years; must obey all laws pertaining to the practice of medicine.

narrative: The Accusation concerned six patients the psychiatrist treated, roughly 2016 to 2022, in a practice that combined chronic pain management, interventional injections, and long-term opioid, benzodiazepine, carisoprodol, and stimulant prescribing, often in patients with psychiatric and substance-use histories. It alleged that he never (or only once) checked CURES, started controlled substances before first visits, and had controlled-substance agreements signed months or years late and never enforced. Patient S, a 42-year-old man with bipolar II disorder, ADHD, and cocaine abuse, received oxycodone, oxymorphone, carisoprodol, and Adderall; despite urine screens negative for prescribed opioids and positive for heroin and methamphetamine, a report that he sold oxycodone, a possible overdose, and suicidal ideation, average daily MME rose from about 461 in 2017 to about 1,350 by January 2021 (e.g., 600 oxycodone 30 mg tablets in one month alongside oxymorphone). When the patient appeared unannounced at the psychiatrist's home late at night saying he did not want to live in such pain, the psychiatrist did not call a psychiatric emergency team or send him to the ER, instead de-escalating over 3.5 hours. Patient H tested positive for cocaine six of seven times while repeated "three strikes" warnings went unenforced and Percocet and carisoprodol continued. Patient C received fentanyl spray (Subsys) 18 times without confirmation of malignancy, even while the psychiatrist believed he was obtaining street fentanyl, plus HIV antiretrovirals without verifying the diagnosis.

The Accusation also alleged failures in general medical care (unaddressed blood pressures above 200/90, tachypnea, a possible DVT, edema, and a stage 4 diabetic foot ulcer treated only with Percocet) and missing consent and procedure documentation for dozens of injections. Charges were gross negligence, repeated negligent acts, inadequate records, clearly excessive prescribing (Patient S), and lack of knowledge (the foot ulcer). In the stipulated settlement the psychiatrist did not contest that a prima facie case could be established; no findings were made.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 4 years' probation with controlled-substance record log, 30 hours/year education emphasizing controlled-substance prescribing, prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, professionalism (ethics) program, practice monitor, clinical competence assessment program; prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; cost recovery of $56,348.00.

narrative: The psychiatrist signed a Permanent Surrender of his Ohio certificate to practice medicine and surgery, with consent to permanent revocation, in lieu of formal disciplinary proceedings. The surrender states two grounds. The first is a violation of the American Medical Association's code of ethics "related to my inappropriate conduct toward peers in the workplace." The second is a violation of the Board's rule governing office-based treatment for opioid addiction, related to his Suboxone (buprenorphine/naloxone) prescribing practices.

The document gives no further facts. It does not describe the workplace conduct, the patients, the doses, or which requirements of the office-based opioid treatment rule were not met. There is no charging document, no findings, and no admission of underlying facts. The psychiatrist stipulated only that he was surrendering in lieu of proceedings on these grounds. The Board ratified the surrender and entered an order permanently revoking the license.
cases.outcome: Permanent surrender accepted; license permanently revoked (permanently ineligible to reapply in Ohio).

narrative: The case began with an online complaint to the Board from Patient 1, a 32-year-old woman who was a relative of the psychiatrist, concerning modafinil prescribed in her name. According to the Accusation, the investigation found that over roughly April 2018 to April 2021 the psychiatrist, who worked at an emergency psychiatry clinic, prescribed medications, including controlled substances, to three adult relatives without appropriate examinations and without keeping medical records. CURES showed four modafinil prescriptions and one lorazepam prescription for Patient 1; three zolpidem, nine modafinil, and one tramadol prescription for Patient 2 (a 36-year-old woman), who also received naproxen, atorvastatin, fenofibrate, metoprolol, and quetiapine; and 16 lorazepam, two modafinil, and one zolpidem prescription for Patient 3 (a 32-year-old man). Modafinil was prescribed off-label for ADHD, and filled prescriptions for Patients 2 and 3 were often delivered to the psychiatrist's residence.

The Accusation alleged that in a first phone call the psychiatrist told investigators she had never treated the three, then said she had treated them with antibiotics; in a later interview she acknowledged prescribing to them over several years, keeping no records, performing only an "informal examination" of Patient 3 and none for Patients 1 and 2, and that this was not appropriate. Patient 1 told investigators she had not taken modafinil, was concerned about prescriptions in her and Patient 2's names, and understood the psychiatrist herself took modafinil. The charges were inadequate records, prescribing without an appropriate prior examination and medical indication, and repeated negligent acts. In the stipulated settlement the psychiatrist did not contest that a prima facie case could be established; no findings were made.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 3 years' probation with 40 hours/year education, prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, professionalism (ethics) program, psychiatric evaluation and psychotherapy if recommended, practice monitor; practice limited to employment as an emergency psychiatrist at a specified or similar emergent psychiatric facility; prohibited from treating family members; prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; cost recovery of $23,315.80.

narrative: The psychiatrist, a child and adolescent psychiatrist treating children and adults in outpatient practice, came to the Board's attention in March 2022 when another physician reported that he was prescribing high doses of benzodiazepines together with gabapentinoids (pregabalin and gabapentin, sometimes 400 mg four times a day) to patients in their 20s and 30s who were also in addiction treatment, including methadone. A state Inspector General review of his KASPER (PDMP) data for 2020 to March 2022 found 197 of his patients with overlapping opioid and benzodiazepine prescriptions from all prescribers and 53 filling controlled substances from five or more prescribers; in 2021 he issued 5,769 benzodiazepine/sedative prescriptions (specialty average 567) and 7,133 stimulant prescriptions. A Board consultant reviewed 14 of 15 requested charts (one could not be located) and found care below minimum standards in most: notes too sparse to support the diagnoses or complex polypharmacy, no regular safety assessments or adequate mental status examinations, two benzodiazepines used together chronically, several medication changes at once, abusable medications restarted after repeated reports of stolen medication, and almost no documentation of therapy ('doing fine').

The psychiatrist conceded that documentation of his clinical thinking was 'definitely lacking' and cited the difficulty of COVID-era telehealth. Under an Interim Agreed Order he completed a clinical skills assessment in February 2024, which noted no electronic record or templates, ADHD stimulant treatment without standardized third-party ratings or testing, unexplained combinations of controlled substances including opioids with benzodiazepines, medication changes recorded only as arrows, no monitoring of weight, vital signs, AIMS or metabolic labs, and that he wrote his own prescriptions. Before the Inquiry Panel he admitted he had not done regular urine drug screens, conducted most visits by telephone, and prescribed his own (non-controlled) medications. In the Agreed Order, entered in lieu of a Complaint and Emergency Order of Suspension, the parties stipulated to these facts and to conclusions that his conduct violated the Medical Practice Act.
cases.outcome: License restricted indefinitely: no prescribing, dispensing or administering controlled substances until approved by the Panel; no telehealth; no prescribing to himself or immediate family; neuropsychological evaluation within 60 days. No request to modify until he completes 10 CME hours in child/adolescent psychopharmacology or ADHD, a medical record documentation course, an intensive controlled substance prescribing course, a DEA controlled substance prescribing course, a review of dosing and monitoring guidance, and a clinical skills re-assessment; any return to controlled-substance prescribing would require a practice monitor at least quarterly for at least one year.

narrative: From October 2018 to June 2019 the psychiatrist treated Patient 1, a 54-year-old man with opioid use disorder who had taken hydrocodone for about ten years after a car accident and then at least two years of buprenorphine maintenance; an earlier discontinuation of buprenorphine had caused severe withdrawal, depression, and suicidal thoughts. The psychiatrist continued buprenorphine (Subutex) 8 mg, 45 tablets a month, then from March 2019 tapered toward discontinuation (to 30 tablets by June 2019), after which the patient did not return. According to the First Amended Accusation, he tapered a stable patient off maintenance treatment, risking relapse to opioids; ordered no laboratory tests (no toxicology screens, liver function, hepatitis, or HIV testing), relying on a prior physician's month-old drug screen that he never dated or initialed; did not personally review CURES or document review; documented no pill counts; and prescribed buprenorphine without naloxone rather than the combination product, with no documented reason, even though he told a Board investigator he suspected the patient was abusing medications. His records were also alleged to be deficient: an undated, unsigned diagnosis, no basis for the starting dose, no session durations, and no suicide or homicide risk assessment.

The charges were gross negligence, repeated negligent acts, incompetence (lack of knowledge of current addiction-treatment standards), inadequate records, and unprofessional conduct. The Accusation also noted a 2020 public reprimand for failing to follow up on prior treatment of three patients. In the stipulated settlement the psychiatrist agreed that a prima facie case could be established and gave up his right to contest the charges; no findings were made. The public reprimand specifically cites his failure to personally review and document CURES and to perform and document random urine drug screens while treating the patient's opioid addiction.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand; 20 hours of education in addiction medicine/treatment of opioid use disorder, prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course; cost recovery of $22,334.

narrative: The Board opened an investigation after receiving credible information about the psychiatrist's prescribing practices. The psychiatrist was board-certified in psychiatry. According to the Stipulated Order, the investigation showed that the psychiatrist had been practicing as a primary care provider, outside the scope of practice for a psychiatrist. This included prescribing and monitoring antiretroviral medications, prescribing opioids to chronic pain patients, and prescribing methadone for opioid maintenance. The order also states that the psychiatrist's opioid prescribing fell outside the CDC's standard for safe opioid prescribing. The order cites the ACGME psychiatry program requirements as the measure of a psychiatrist's scope of practice.

The psychiatrist neither admitted nor denied the allegations, but the Board found violations of the Medical Practice Act. These were unprofessional or dishonorable conduct, including willfully performing medical treatment contrary to acceptable standards; gross or repeated negligence; and prescribing controlled substances without a legitimate medical purpose or without following accepted procedures for examination or record keeping. To resolve the investigation, the psychiatrist agreed to retire the Oregon license while under investigation.
cases.outcome: License retired while under investigation; must stop practicing by August 30, 2024 and may not reapply in Oregon for at least two years.

narrative: The Accusation concerned five outpatients the psychiatrist treated between 2018 and 2021. Its central allegation was a pattern of prescribing controlled substances without reviewing, or documenting review of, CURES. Patient A, treated for ADHD and recurrent major depression, was seen in August 2019 on Adderall 20 mg three times daily; the psychiatrist prescribed Adderall 20 mg four times daily, clonazepam 1 mg, and sertraline 200 mg without checking CURES and with a note lacking history of the patient's recent treatment, depression, anxiety, or the rationale for clonazepam. Three days later he wrote another Adderall prescription (120 tablets) with no documented visit or justification. About ten days after that, Patient A was found dead; the coroner attributed death to acute polydrug intoxication from methamphetamine, amphetamine, fentanyl, and clonazepam. Patient B (depression and anxiety, with a prior psychiatric hospitalization) and Patient C (a 69-year-old woman with depression, generalized anxiety, and panic disorder, on clonazepam 0.5 mg up to four times daily plus as-needed alprazolam, who fell and broke her femur during treatment) received dozens of benzodiazepine prescriptions from 2018 to 2021 with no documented CURES review. Patient E received stimulants (Adderall, then phentermine, then a 90-day supply of methylphenidate) for depression-related fatigue and poor focus without a CURES check.

The Accusation also alleged that for Patient D, a 39-year-old man with bipolar I disorder maintained on lithium 600 mg twice daily, the psychiatrist neither ordered nor documented reviewing lithium levels or kidney or thyroid function at two visits in 2018. The charges were repeated negligent acts, inadequate records, and general unprofessional conduct. In the stipulated settlement the psychiatrist did not contest that a prima facie case could be established; no findings were made.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 4 years' probation with 40 hours/year education, prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, clinical competence assessment program, notification of Decision and Accusation to hospitals/insurers; prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; cost recovery of $28,412.75.

narrative: According to the First Amended Accusation, the psychiatrist began treating Patient 1, a 39-year-old woman with depression, significant suicide/self-harm risk, and possible psychotic or dissociative symptoms, in 2015 in a county mental health system, and continued treating her after moving into private practice in 2017. He had no medical records at all for her care from August 2017 through July 2022, although pharmacy records showed he prescribed during that period amitriptyline, fluoxetine, alprazolam, clonazepam, diazepam, aripiprazole, olanzapine, and ziprasidone. He also took over prescribing carisoprodol for her reported chronic pain from lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, or fibromyalgia after another provider declined to continue it, with no documented rheumatologic history, physical examination, review of prior records, or consultation with specialists. No psychiatric evaluation establishing an indication for the medications or assessing their ongoing safety and effectiveness was documented, and notes from July 2022 onward lacked mental status or physical examination findings and medical decision-making. Gross negligence (prescribing controlled substances without medical indication, prescribing carisoprodol without adequate examination, and inadequate psychiatric evaluation) and inadequate records were charged.

The Accusation further alleged that in June 2024 the psychiatrist was indicted in federal court, with a co-defendant, on charges of conspiracy to distribute controlled substances, distribution, conspiracy to commit health care fraud, and conspiracy to obstruct justice, arising from his role as the nominal owner and clinical president of a subscription-based online ADHD treatment company alleged to have arranged prescriptions for tens of millions of stimulant pills from 2020 to 2023; he did not report the indictment to the Board within 30 days as required. The indictment was a pending charge, not a conviction. In surrendering his license, the psychiatrist agreed that a factual basis for the charges could be established at a hearing and did not contest cause for discipline; there were no findings or admissions.
cases.outcome: Stipulated surrender of license; cost recovery of $47,594.78 payable before any new or reinstated license.

narrative: The psychiatrist, licensed since 1974 and retiring after a 51-year career, surrendered the license without admitting the charges, agreeing only that the Board could establish a prima facie case for gross negligence and repeated negligent acts in the care of one patient. The case began with a complaint from the patient's ex-girlfriend about ten days after his suicide, alleging negligent care, excessive benzodiazepine prescribing, over-billing, and that the psychiatrist appeared to "nod off" and had slowed speech during online sessions.

According to the Accusation, Patient A, an attorney treated from 2003 for work stress and relationship crises, came on Valium from his primary care physician; the psychiatrist reduced the dose to 2 mg and diagnosed generalized anxiety disorder, insomnia, and panic disorder. In early 2022 his sleep worsened; trials of Klonopin 0.5 mg, trazodone 50 mg, and Cymbalta failed, the last reportedly causing mania, and he spent a night under emergency room observation in February 2022. He took a leave of absence late that month, with no suicidal ideation documented, and died by suicide on March 8, 2022; autopsy showed three different benzodiazepines in his system. The psychiatrist told Board investigators she knew he took more benzodiazepine than directed, yet prescribed 300 tablets of Valium 2 mg per 30-day prescription because "that's what" he wanted and it made him "feel safe" to have extra. The Accusation alleged that she continued benzodiazepines despite known noncompliance, did not investigate the causes of his insomnia, and made no referral for psychotherapy, second opinion, sleep study, or benzodiazepine taper before trying other drug classes.
cases.outcome: License surrender accepted effective June 1, 2025; costs of $38,474.50 payable before any new or reinstated license; any reapplication treated as a petition for reinstatement with the Accusation's allegations deemed admitted.

narrative: The Accusation concerned four long-term outpatients to whom the psychiatrist, licensed since 1970, prescribed controlled substances between roughly 2019 and 2023, largely without records. For three of the four there were no medical records at all for years of treatment (Patient A, 2017-2021; Patient B, 2019 to February 2022, apart from an illegible, undated handwritten intake form; Patient C, 2017 to mid-2021), and the notes that did exist lacked history, examination findings, diagnostic formulation, and treatment plans. Patient A, a 42-year-old woman who first came asking for medication to reduce her desire for alcohol, was prescribed amphetamine salts and dextroamphetamine (up to 30 mg), Vyvanse 60 mg, zolpidem 10 mg, and alprazolam 0.5 mg without a documented rationale for stimulants or diagnosis of insomnia. Patient B received overlapping benzodiazepines, alprazolam 2 mg (60 per month) and clonazepam 1 mg (120 per month), plus zolpidem, for years despite continuing to report debilitating anxiety, with no indication documented and no change in plan. Patient C, a 63-year-old woman, received alprazolam 2 mg, clonazepam, and zolpidem ER 12.5 mg without documented indication, monitoring for misuse, or adequate CURES review. Patient D, a 64-year-old woman with bipolar disorder and a known history of street-drug use, received alprazolam, diazepam, methylphenidate, and dextroamphetamine 30 mg, with antidepressants but no mood stabilizer, no mood monitoring for mania or depression, no CURES review, and diagnoses changed without documented basis.

The Accusation charged gross negligence and repeated negligent acts for all four patients (inadequate records, improper prescribing of controlled substances, and inadequate assessment and supervision), incompetence in managing Patient D's bipolar disorder, inadequate records, and general unprofessional conduct. In surrendering his license, the psychiatrist did not contest that a prima facie case could be established; there were no findings or admissions.
cases.outcome: Stipulated surrender of license; cost recovery of $33,532.75 payable before any new or reinstated license.

narrative: The case began in 2022 with a complaint from an outside advocacy organization raising possible Medicare fraud tied to the psychiatrist's high prescribing volume; Board investigators then pulled CURES data and reviewed six patients treated in an outpatient practice that consisted mainly of elderly patients with chronic pain and medical comorbidities. According to the Accusation, between 2016 and 2019 the psychiatrist prescribed paired sedative-hypnotics month after month to elderly women, several with dementia, Alzheimer's disease, falls, or concurrent opioids from other physicians: for example, clonazepam 0.5 mg with triazolam or temazepam, zolpidem, zaleplon, flurazepam, or lorazepam. She told patients and caregivers to take them only as needed and three hours apart, but CURES showed regular monthly fills (and early clonazepam refills that went unremarked), and the expert noted that the drugs' half-lives in the elderly far exceed three hours. She was unaware that one 90-plus-year-old patient with Alzheimer's disease, who had three falls in 14 months, was receiving codeine from another physician, used no controlled-substance agreements or toxicology screening, documented no CURES review, rarely coordinated with other prescribers, and said a urine drug screen was the primary care physician's role. That patient was also given quetiapine without documented black-box discussion or metabolic monitoring.

The Accusation also alleged that the handwritten template notes were largely illegible (the psychiatrist herself had trouble reading them in her interview), lacked patient identifiers, and that no medication-specific informed consent was documented beyond a generic intake consent signed years earlier; one patient's chart held a single progress note. Gross negligence was charged for two patients, and repeated negligence and inadequate records for all six. The psychiatrist did not contest that a prima facie case could be established; there were no findings or admissions.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand (for inappropriately monitoring patients prescribed controlled medications and inadequate records, 2016-2019) with 40 hours of education, prescribing practices course, and medical record keeping course; cost recovery of $46,282.80.

narrative: The psychiatrist owned several outpatient clinics where he practiced general medicine and psychiatry. According to the Accusation, Patient A, a 68-year-old man, had been treated since 2003 by the psychiatrist and by physician assistants he supervised. Between September 2017 and January 2018 the psychiatrist prescribed tramadol 50 mg (60 tablets) to Patient A on five occasions without documenting an initial or ongoing history, examination, evaluation, risk stratification, risk mitigation, or informed consent, and without monitoring compliance through toxicology screens, pill counts, or CURES review, despite an increased risk of negative health outcomes. The records were often absent, brief, handwritten, and sometimes unintelligible, so that it was impossible to tell from the chart which medications were prescribed, when, for what indication, and in what quantities without CURES data. The Accusation charged repeated negligent acts (improper initiation and monitoring of the opioid regimen and inadequate records), prescribing without an appropriate examination or medical indication, excessive prescribing, and failure to maintain adequate records. It also cited prior discipline as aggravation: probation and a 30-day suspension in 1995, a public letter of reprimand in 2014, and three years' probation in 2016.

In the stipulated settlement the psychiatrist did not contest that a prima facie case could be established; there were no findings or admissions. The public reprimand states that in 2017-2018 he inappropriately prescribed controlled substances to a patient without an appropriate medical examination or indication.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand with prescribing practices course and medical record keeping course (cease practice if not completed on time); cost recovery of $41,067.75.

narrative: The Board's September 2024 Notice of Opportunity for Hearing alleged that, from about 2005 to 2023, the psychiatrist failed to appropriately treat and/or document his treatment of five patients, most of whom were receiving stimulants for ADHD. Patient 1 had evidence of multiple opioid prescriptions and medications from other providers. For this patient he was alleged to have prescribed Adderall above the FDA daily maximum without supporting documentation. He kept prescribing very high doses despite evidence that the patient was misusing it. He did not coordinate care, check blood pressure, heart rate or weight, obtain urine drug screens, or respond to red flags for drug abuse. Patient 2 had major depression and ADHD and reported receiving fentanyl, Percocet, Lyrica and other drugs from outside prescribers.
