He saw this patient too infrequently, did not obtain outside records, prescribed Adderall above the FDA maximum, and continued Xanax despite multiple falls possibly caused by it.

Patient 4 had a history of strokes and known cardiovascular problems. He continued stimulants, including higher-than-recommended doses of methylphenidate and Adderall, and took a blood pressure reading only once in five years. Patient 3 had bipolar disorder, ADHD, GAD and a suspected active cannabis and alcohol use disorder. This patient was seen as infrequently as twice a year, with no vital signs after intake, no urine drug screen or OARRS check, and no consistent mental status examinations or risk assessments. Patient 5 was 4 years old at the start of treatment and was prescribed liquid methylphenidate and clonidine for nearly three years. He had only one mental status examination, no weight or vital signs, no documentation that the child was present at later visits, and no reassessment when the mother reported worsening symptoms. In the surrender, the psychiatrist expressly admitted the violations alleged in the Notice.
cases.outcome: Permanent surrender with consent to permanent revocation, in lieu of further proceedings; license permanently revoked effective September 30, 2025; no new patients during the interim period.

narrative: In October 2025 the Investigative Committee of the Nevada Board filed a Complaint alleging one violation of the statutes and regulations of the Nevada State Board of Pharmacy (Count I) and one count of unsafe or unprofessional conduct (Count II). The Complaint is not attached to the Settlement Agreement, which does not describe the underlying conduct, the patients or medications involved, or how the matter came to the Board's attention. In the agreement the psychiatrist stated generally that he was not admitting the claims had merit and was settling to avoid the cost of a hearing, but specifically admitted both the pharmacy-law violation and the unsafe or unprofessional conduct violation, and agreed the Board could enter an order finding conduct that is grounds for discipline. The terms point to the area of concern without stating facts: a 21-hour proper prescribing course, and, for the 24-month probation, a requirement to notify the Board of all international travel and, for any controlled substance he prescribes while traveling abroad, to provide records and billing documentation within 30 days showing a bona fide therapeutic relationship with the patient when the prescription was issued. The Board approved the agreement on December 12, 2025.
cases.outcome: Suspension stayed; 24 months' probation with notice to the Board of all international travel and, for any controlled-substance prescription issued while abroad, records showing a bona fide therapeutic relationship; Public Letter of Reprimand; $7,500 fine and costs of $6,879.87 (both in installments); 21-hour proper prescribing course (PBI RX-21) within six months; may petition to lift probation once terms are met.

narrative: According to the Administrative Complaint, the psychiatrist met Patient P.M. through an online dating service in January 2018 and began a romantic relationship with him. From about March 2018 through February 2022, while the relationship continued, she prescribed him controlled substances for psychiatric treatment, including dextroamphetamine-amphetamine salts (generic Adderall) and Adzenys XR-ODT (both Schedule II stimulants used for ADHD), tramadol, and diazepam. In December 2018, during this period, Patient P.M. suffered a traumatic brain injury. The complaint alleged that she never referred him to another provider for psychiatric care and failed to create medical records that justified the course of treatment.

The Department charged that the standard of care required the psychiatrist to refrain from prescribing controlled substances for psychiatric treatment to a romantic partner on an ongoing basis and to refer him to another provider, and that her failure to do so was medical malpractice; a second count charged inadequate medical records. The matter was resolved by a Settlement Agreement in which the psychiatrist neither admitted nor denied the allegations of fact, admitting only that the facts alleged, if proven, would constitute violations of Florida law. The Board of Medicine adopted the agreement in a Final Order.
cases.outcome: Letter of Concern; $5,000 administrative fine; $5,000 Department costs; 5 hours CME in laws, rules and ethics, 3 hours CME in medical recordkeeping, and 5 hours CME in risk management within one year.

narrative: The December 2024 Notice of Opportunity for Hearing alleged that from 2016 to 2022 the psychiatrist inappropriately prescribed to, failed to appropriately monitor and manage, and inadequately documented the care of eight outpatients, and in the Consent Agreement he admitted the factual and legal allegations. For nearly every patient, the diagnoses (bipolar disorder, PTSD, GAD, major depression, ADHD) were not substantiated using DSM-5 criteria; stimulants were prescribed without a substantiated ADHD diagnosis; benzodiazepines were prescribed at high doses for long periods, sometimes several at once or alongside other prescribers' opioids and muscle relaxants; informed consent for long-term use was not obtained; tapering was not documented; and OARRS reports were not checked timely or incorporated into the record. Patient 1 was ultimately on Adderall 30 mg three times daily and Valium 10 mg four times daily, without appropriate blood testing or antidepressant adjustment. Patient 3 received Xanax 1.5 mg every six hours for a panic disorder that was not among the patient's diagnoses, despite early refills, drug screens positive for amphetamines and buprenorphine, emergency visits for altered mental status and an assessed benzodiazepine overdose; antipsychotics were also given without a documented indication. Patient 4 was continued on Vyvanse 140 mg daily based solely on his report of a prior prescription, without corroboration or an initial OARRS check. Patient 5 was continued on Xanax 8 mg daily after refusing a taper, with Ambien, and with Norco and tizanidine from other providers. The Notice also alleged that in a January 2024 Board interview he acknowledged that his employer had raised concerns in 2021-2022 that he was not seeing patients often enough, and that about five patients receiving controlled substances had not been seen for over a year.
cases.outcome: License indefinitely suspended for at least 180 days; interim monitoring with quarterly declarations; controlled-substance prescribing course and medical records course with written reports; $3,000 fine; reinstatement conditioned on a further consent agreement. (A subsequent Consent Agreement reinstated the license effective August 2026.)

narrative: The Board's March 2025 Notice of Opportunity for Hearing alleged that, from about 2014 to 2024, the psychiatrist failed to appropriately treat and/or document her treatment of six outpatients. Patient 1 had schizoaffective disorder and many other diagnoses. For this patient she was alleged to have prescribed Adderall in excessive doses without a documented rationale, including after signs of misuse. She also prescribed multiple antipsychotics at the same time without considering drug interactions and without screening for involuntary movements; the patient developed tardive dyskinesia. She did not obtain informed consent for a complex, off-label regimen, did not obtain prior treatment records, and did not check OARRS (Ohio's prescription monitoring program) at the required frequency. Patients 2 and 3 received lorazepam, Adderall and Adderall XR for more than 90 days without the required OARRS reviews. For Patient 2, the medications in the narrative note did not match the medication-change section.

Patient 4 had a history of alcohol use and a diagnosis of alcohol abuse. The psychiatrist prescribed Nuvigil above 250 mg daily without a documented rationale and continued it despite symptoms possibly caused by it. She also gave early refills and did not coordinate with other prescribers, require toxicology screens, do pill counts, or obtain a controlled-substance agreement. For Patient 6 (bipolar II disorder, panic disorder, ADHD), she prescribed Lexapro, Lamictal, Seroquel, Valium, Abilify, Adderall and gabapentin without consistently documenting the rationale, diagnosed ADHD without a comprehensive evaluation, and did not order bloodwork or monitor weight. Several records lacked documentation of the actual prescriptions and follow-up appointments, and Patient 5's chart lacked a mental status examination. In the Consent Agreement she admitted the drug-selection, standard-of-care, and Board-rule violations as alleged in the Notice.
cases.outcome: Indefinite suspension, minimum 60 days; $2,500 fine; reinstatement conditioned on a controlled-substance prescribing course and a psychiatry review course (each with a written report) and compliance with interim monitoring (quarterly declarations, appearances).

narrative: The psychiatrist, board-certified in psychiatry, owned an office-based practice and also provided psychiatric and substance use disorder services through a clinic. In November 2024 the state Office of Controlled Substances Administration referred him to the Board, reporting that he was prescribing controlled-substance combinations that carry black-box warnings or could lead to abuse or diversion, specifically buprenorphine together with stimulants, benzodiazepines, and/or hypnotic sleep aids such as Ambien. He told the Board that he treated many patients with substance use disorders and comorbid psychiatric conditions, that some received buprenorphine with benzodiazepines and stimulants, and that he had previously used written agreements with Suboxone patients but no longer routinely did so.

Two board-certified psychiatrists reviewed 10 records of adults he had maintained, sometimes for years, on Suboxone often combined with benzodiazepines and/or stimulants. They found standard-of-care failures in 2 cases and inadequate records in all 10. For Patients 3 and 6 he prescribed and continued high-risk combinations of buprenorphine with benzodiazepines, stimulants, and other sedating medications without an adequate clinical rationale or risk-benefit analysis and without appropriate monitoring such as PDMP checks and urine drug testing. In all 10 records he did not adequately document his reasoning for starting and continuing the controlled-substance regimens, rarely documented any discussion of risks, benefits, or alternatives, and did not consistently document that he had requested and assessed PDMP data. These are findings of fact in a Consent Order he agreed to after charges and a case-resolution conference; the panel concluded he failed to meet the standard of care and to keep adequate medical records.
cases.outcome: Reprimand; probation until completion of a medical recordkeeping course within 6 months; no early termination.

narrative: The psychiatrist, who practiced in an outpatient medical office and held no specialty board certification, came to the Board's attention in March 2025 through a complaint from a county health department that was reviewing the overdose death of Patient 1 and reported that she had not responded to its records requests. Patient 1, who had a history of alcohol and drug abuse, had been treated by her since 2008 with Lexapro, Lamictal, gabapentin, Ritalin, Xanax, and Ambien. She told the Board that she rarely checked Patient 1's PDMP report and found the process 'tedious'; that she did not check the PDMP before starting any patient on controlled substances, although she acknowledged Maryland law required it; that she did not perform urine toxicology screening on any patient, including those with substance-abuse histories, because she trusted her patients; that she did not use treatment agreements for patients on stimulants and benzodiazepines; and that she prescribed Suboxone to about 10 patients despite having no addiction-medicine training.

Two board-certified psychiatrists with addiction subspecialty certification reviewed 10 records of adults she had kept, sometimes for years, on benzodiazepines and/or stimulants such as Ritalin and Adderall. In 7 cases they found she failed to meet the standard of care: she did not perform or document urine toxicology or PDMP checks at required intervals, did not use substance-use agreements, and did not document assessments, work-ups, diagnoses, risk counseling, compliance monitoring, or referrals justifying the controlled-substance prescribing. These are findings of fact in a Consent Order she agreed to after charges and a case-resolution conference; the panel concluded she violated the standard-of-care and PDMP-compliance provisions. The order does not attribute Patient 1's death to the prescribing.
cases.outcome: Reprimand; probation minimum 1 year; prohibited from prescribing or dispensing controlled substances to new patients (beginning 45 days after the effective date) until completing courses in controlled-substance prescribing and medical record keeping, required within 6 months; no early termination.

narrative: The physician, who completed two years of a general psychiatry residency and told Board investigators in April 2025 that she practiced psychiatry and general medicine, ran a small consulting practice that offered medical and psychiatric services. After a hearing, the Board adopted the Hearing Examiner's findings that from about October 2023 to April 2025 she treated and prescribed controlled substances to four family members, not in emergency situations. Patient 1, a young relative with complications after gunshot wounds and thoracic surgery, signed a pain management agreement and received Percocet (increased from 7.5-325 mg to 10-325 mg), tramadol and gabapentin roughly monthly from December 2023 to March 2025. Patient 2, who had liver cancer and leg fractures after a fall and had been discharged by a palliative care provider, received hydromorphone, OxyContin, gabapentin and tizanidine from August 2024 to April 2025, although she had a primary care physician and several specialists; the psychiatrist's note called the situation "emergent" but the prescribing continued for months. Patient 3 received lorazepam 0.5 mg (90 tablets) in December 2024 and March 2025 plus Trulicity; the Board found neither occasion an emergency. Patient 4 was started on phentermine 15 mg daily for weight loss, along with other drugs including warfarin, and it was stopped after she was seen in an emergency department for a pulmonary embolism.

At hearing the physician candidly admitted she knew the rule against prescribing controlled substances to family members, chose to violate it because her relatives' needs were not being met, stopped only after the Board investigator's visit, and would do so again. A separate charge that she failed to document Patient 1's controlled-substance treatment was not proven once she produced her complete records, which she had initially submitted incompletely.
cases.outcome: License revoked; $1,500 fine.

narrative: The Board entered this Consent Agreement in lieu of formal proceedings. No charging document is attached; the facts come from the psychiatrist's admission. He admitted that his practice includes prescribing controlled substances, including stimulants and benzodiazepines. He admitted that he had not checked OARRS (Ohio's prescription drug monitoring program) for all of his patients at the times and intervals required by Board rule. He also admitted that he had infrequently failed to document all of the controlled substances he prescribed, and that for some patients he had not obtained random urine screens or medication contracts. The Board treated this as a violation of its rules. The agreement names no patients, doses, or time period, and does not say how the matter came to the Board's attention.
cases.outcome: Reprimand; $2,500 fine; probation with quarterly declarations and Board appearances until completion (within nine months) of courses on controlled-substance prescribing, medical records, and OARRS, each with a written report.

narrative: The Board entered this Consent Agreement in lieu of formal proceedings. No charging document is attached; the facts come from the psychiatrist's admission. He admitted that he treated a patient for about one year with an incorrect form of dextroamphetamine. He prescribed it without reviewing the patient's prior medical records and without seeing the patient in the office, and he continued prescribing without drug screens. The Board treated this as a departure from minimal standards of care.

The agreement gives no further details, such as the diagnosis, the intended formulation, the dose, or how the matter came to the Board's attention. He stated that he was also licensed in twelve other states. He attested that he had given the Board a full and honest account and acknowledged that any later-discovered misrepresentation could lead to further discipline, up to permanent revocation.
cases.outcome: Reprimand; license permanently limited to prohibit prescribing controlled substances; $5,000 fine; required reporting to employers, hospitals, other licensing boards and the DEA.

narrative: The psychiatrist worked at a mental health facility. In December 2023 the facility's chief executive complained to the Board that she had been terminated on December 8, 2023 because of disruptive behavior and profane outbursts toward staff; the Consent Order calls these 'unsubstantiated claims' and states that she had in fact resigned by letter the day before. The Board's review of the state Controlled Substances Reporting System for December 2021 through December 2023 confirmed that she had prescribed controlled substances to five individuals for whom the facility failed to keep appropriate medical documentation. The order does not identify the individuals, drugs or quantities.

The Board ordered an examination by the North Carolina Professionals Health Program (NCPHP) in December 2023. NCPHP recommended professional coaching, a workplace monitor, personal controlled-prescription monitoring, a behavioral monitoring contract, and further evaluation to rule out an underlying impairing condition related to the prescribing and professionalism concerns. A comprehensive outside assessment in April 2024 diagnosed no disorder but recommended intensive treatment, which NCPHP disagreed with because no diagnosis supported it. She signed a three-year NCPHP behavioral monitoring contract in September 2024 and remained compliant; she completed courses in proper prescribing of controlled substances and professional ethics and a year of professional coaching, continued in her own psychiatric treatment, and returned to outpatient practice in March 2025, where her treating psychiatrist and NCPHP reported no impairment concerns. In the Consent Order she made admissions, the Board made findings, and she acknowledged that her conduct constituted unprofessional conduct, including departure from prevailing standards of practice and from the ethics of the profession.
cases.outcome: Consent Order with conditions: maintain the NCPHP contract; abstain from alcohol and all mind- or mood-altering and controlled substances unless lawfully prescribed by someone else; provide bodily fluid or tissue samples on request; obey all laws; appear for Board interviews. No suspension.

narrative: In the Consent Agreement the psychiatrist admitted the factual and legal allegations of an April 2026 Notice of Opportunity for Hearing. From at least about May 2022 to about July 2025 she ran a ketamine clinic where she administered ketamine, a Schedule III controlled substance, or authorized others to administer it. She never obtained a Terminal Distributor of Dangerous Drugs license before opening. She did not apply until April 2024, and the license was issued in May 2024. Although she was the clinic's responsible party, she employed or allowed other people to give patients ketamine when she was not in the clinic.

On about February 10, 2023, and from about April 16 through December 20, 2024, she prescribed and/or administered ketamine to a family member, sometimes weekly, without documenting any emergency. She also authorized the family member to self-administer ketamine away from the clinic. She kept a chart for the family member, but it did not always record her prescriptions or administrations. She also failed to check, or to document checking, the state prescription monitoring database (OARRS) at the times and intervals the Board's rules require before prescribing or administering ketamine to the family member.
cases.outcome: Indefinite suspension of at least 90 days beginning September 24, 2026; interim monitoring (quarterly declarations, appearances); medical ethics course within nine months with a written report; $15,000 fine; reinstatement conditioned on compliance and an application to the Board.

cases.type: Public reprimand / public letter of reprimand
narrative: According to the Board's Public Letter of Reprimand, an investigation by the Medical Board revealed that the psychiatrist's monitoring, treatment, and record keeping of a patient's bipolar disorder departed from the standard of care. The letter cites only the medical records provision of the Business and Professions Code as the violation.
cases.outcome: Public Letter of Reprimand; required to complete a medical record keeping course.

narrative: The case began with a November 2017 complaint from an emergency department psychiatrist who evaluated a minor relative of the psychiatrist (Patient A) brought in for an emergency psychiatric evaluation. He learned that the psychiatrist had started the child on nortriptyline 10 mg/day about two weeks earlier and increased it to 20 mg/day a week before the visit; she said the child's treating physician had recommended the drug and let her prescribe it, but that physician had last seen the child six months earlier, planned only annual follow-up, had no record of nortriptyline, and did not recall giving her that option. The psychiatrist, who told Board investigators she is not trained in child psychiatry, acknowledged writing the prescription and keeping no medical records for the two minor relatives involved. According to the Accusation, CURES and pharmacy records showed at least 124 prescriptions to Patient A from December 2011 to November 2019 (continuing after the emergency visit), including about 70 for guanfacine extended-release, 9 for aripiprazole, 4 for lithium, and at least 30 for immediate- and extended-release amphetamine/dextroamphetamine (about 3,360 tablets). For a second minor relative, Patient B, she wrote 17 prescriptions from 2013 to 2019, including at least 9 amphetamine/dextroamphetamine prescriptions (about 750 tablets) over roughly six months. In both cases she not only refilled other physicians' prescriptions but initiated new ones, and she prescribed controlled substances beyond any emergency.

The Accusation charged gross negligence, repeated negligent acts, failure to maintain adequate records, and general unprofessional conduct, based on establishing multi-year physician-patient relationships with family members, initiating and continuing psychotropic treatment, and prescribing controlled substances to them. In the stipulated settlement the psychiatrist admitted the truth of each charge and allegation, and she had also admitted to investigators that prescribing controlled substances to both relatives was inappropriate.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 5 years' probation with 40 hours/year of education courses, prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, professionalism (ethics) program, practice monitor (or professional enhancement program), solo practice prohibition, and prohibition on supervising PAs/APRNs; probation monitoring costs.

narrative: According to the Accusation, in October 2014 a 21-year-old woman presented to the psychiatrist with depression, alcohol abuse, mood swings, anxiety, and paranoia, and he diagnosed bipolar I disorder and alcohol dependence. He prescribed lamotrigine (Lamictal) starting at 50 mg daily for one week, then 100 mg, 150 mg, and 200 mg daily in successive weeks, reaching 200 mg by the fourth week. The Accusation noted that the manufacturer-recommended schedule, intended to reduce the boxed-warning risk of serious rash, starts at 25 mg daily for two weeks, then 50 mg daily for two weeks, 100 mg for one week, and 200 mg from week six. The patient signed an informed consent form that listed Lamictal but not its risks or side effects, and the record did not document any discussion that the starting dose and titration were more aggressive than recommended. About two weeks after starting the medication as directed, the patient developed Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis.

The Accusation charged gross negligence in failing to prescribe a sufficiently low starting dose and gradual titration and in failing to discuss and/or document the risks of the drug and of the alternative dosing to obtain informed consent. The psychiatrist did not admit the allegations; he did not contest that the Board could establish a prima facie case at hearing and agreed to a public reprimand, whose text states that he committed gross negligence by prescribing Lamictal without a sufficiently low initial dose and sufficiently gradual increase.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand, with prescribing practices course and medical record keeping course.

narrative: The psychiatrist treated Patient A, a man in his mid-60s referred by his endocrinologist in 2013 for severe recurrent depression, whose history included two prior suicide attempts, past alcohol and phentermine abuse (sober since 2005), diabetes, and possible chronic liver failure. According to the First Amended Accusation, she never obtained prior treatment records, thyroid tests, or baseline liver labs, and never conferred with his internist or endocrinologist about his liver disease. In 2014 she started Dexedrine for low energy without a detailed substance-abuse history, informed consent, or coordination with his other physicians, and escalated the dose repeatedly without documented rationale. Although he repeatedly admitted taking more than prescribed and running out early, she kept refilling, at one point authorizing up to seven tablets a day, and later documented an ADHD diagnosis without supporting DSM criteria. From 2016 to 2020 she prescribed Lexapro 40 mg daily and did not correct the dose after a pharmacy benefit manager sent several letters noting it exceeded the manufacturer's maximum (and the lower geriatric maximum); she told the Board investigator she believed 40 mg was the maximum dose. She also prescribed trazodone 150 mg for years without any mention in her notes, and from 2017 to 2020 wrote monthly Dexedrine prescriptions while documenting only about six encounters.

The Accusation charged gross negligence, repeated negligent acts, inadequate records, and incompetence, and noted a 2011 public reprimand for negligent care of two patients. In the stipulated settlement the psychiatrist admitted that the complainant could establish a prima facie case; she did not otherwise admit the allegations.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 4 years' probation with prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, professionalism (ethics) program, clinical competence assessment program, and practice monitor; prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; cost recovery of $5,555; probation monitoring costs.

narrative: The psychiatrist treated Patient 1, a 36-year-old man with generalized and social anxiety disorder, a history of passive suicidal ideation and cutting at age 18, and past drinking, from May 2016. According to the Accusation, he declined sertraline and preferred intermittent diazepam, which she prescribed (5 mg, 20 tablets with refills); over the following 16 months his use rose from about three days a week to daily amid marital problems, and she increased the quantities to 30 and then 45 tablets without documenting the reason for the first increase. At the final visit in September 2017, concerned about daily use and the dose wearing off, and noting he had recently separated from his wife, she stopped the diazepam abruptly, without a taper or a documented discussion of withdrawal, and started sertraline at 12.5 mg daily plus trazodone, with refills lasting about three months and no earlier follow-up scheduled. She declined a pharmacy's diazepam refill request two days later. About three weeks after the visit, the patient died by suicide.

The Accusation charged gross negligence (abrupt discontinuation of a benzodiazepine prescribed for 18 months in increasing amounts, and a subtherapeutic SSRI start without timely follow-up for a patient with escalating anxiety), repeated negligent acts, and inadequate records. The psychiatrist agreed that the complainant could establish a prima facie case and gave up her right to contest the charges. The public reprimand itself states the basis more narrowly: failure to document a tapering schedule to wean the patient from diazepam prescribed for over a year, and failure to document a timely follow-up visit within a month of starting an SSRI for the first time.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand; must complete a prescribing practices course and a medical record keeping course.

narrative: The psychiatrist was already on three years' probation under a 2018 stipulated settlement resolving allegations that he had prescribed benzodiazepines, stimulants, and buprenorphine to patients with addiction histories without adequate evaluation, CURES review, urine drug screening, or records. A combined Accusation and Petition to Revoke Probation then alleged new negligent care of one patient in 2019. According to the Accusation, Patient 1, a 24-year-old woman in a respiratory therapy program who complained of poor focus and had a history of a suicide attempt by overdose at age 13, was diagnosed with attention deficit disorder at her first visit based solely on a child/adolescent self-report checklist that a pharmaceutical representative had given him years earlier. He did not apply DSM-5 criteria, obtain collateral or educational history, screen for depression or anxiety, check CURES, or consider medical causes. He started Adderall at 20 mg twice daily rather than a low starting dose, offered only Adderall or Strattera without discussing risks and alternatives, and told her to exercise to exhaustion. At three monthly follow-ups he kept prescribing 60 tablets although she was taking only a quarter to half of that and was not filling monthly, did not check CURES, did not assess side effects or vital signs, and did not document mental status examinations at two visits.

The Accusation charged gross negligence, repeated negligent acts, incompetence, prescribing without indication, inadequate records, and unprofessional conduct, and the Petition alleged that this conduct violated the probation condition to obey all laws and rules governing medical practice. It also noted a 2020 citation for late quarterly probation declarations. The psychiatrist admitted that the complainant could establish a prima facie case and declined to defend the charges.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; probation extended by one additional year, consecutive to the 2018 probation (all prior terms continue), with 40 hours/year of additional education, prescribing practices course, and cost recovery of $6,092.50; probation monitoring costs.

narrative: The psychiatrist had previously been on seven years' Board probation (2013-2020) after admitting to a federal felony conviction for unlawful distribution of controlled substances, having sold non-legitimate prescriptions for Adderall, Xanax, and Norco; during that probation he twice received citations for missed biological fluid tests. After a hearing, an administrative law judge found two new grounds for discipline, both arising while he was still on probation. First, in December 2018 he was found passed out at the wheel at a freeway off-ramp with the engine running and a blood alcohol concentration of 0.17 percent, leading to a misdemeanor "wet reckless" conviction. The ALJ found this was excessive use of alcohol and a substantially related conviction, and noted that he continued drinking, without treatment, until the Accusation was served in 2021.

Second, in December 2017 he wrote a letter on practice letterhead, given by his patient to a family court judge, stating his "strong impression" that the patient's wife suffered from borderline personality disorder, that people with the disorder can create "completely false stories," that she was a risk to her children, and that the domestic violence accusation against the patient was "very likely false." He had met the wife once for no more than 10 minutes as collateral; she had refused to be a patient and never authorized any disclosure, and the patient had just been arrested for domestic violence and was subject to a restraining order. Relying on the Board's expert and the APA's Goldwater Rule, the ALJ found the letter an extreme departure (gross negligence) and unethical, rejected the claim that an "impression" is not a diagnosis, found no repeated negligence (a single act), and concluded that the psychiatrist lacked insight and that revocation was necessary.
cases.outcome: License revoked; costs of $6,000 may be ordered as a condition of any reinstatement.

cases.type: Public reprimand / public letter of reprimand
narrative: The Board issued a one-page Public Letter of Reprimand stating that its investigation revealed that the psychiatrist deviated from the standard of care by failing to maintain adequate and accurate medical records, failing to obtain proper informed consent, and improperly discontinuing a patient's medications. The letter gives no further details about the patient, the medications, or the circumstances.
cases.outcome: Public Letter of Reprimand; required to complete a medical record keeping course and a prescribing practices course.

narrative: The psychiatrist settled a First Amended Accusation charging repeated negligent acts, inadequate records, and general unprofessional conduct in the outpatient care of two patients. He did not contest that a prima facie case could be established and made no admissions. Patient A, a 41-year-old woman whose son had died, came to him in October 2018 with depression and insomnia after ketamine infusions. She reported taking Zoloft, Pristiq, Xanax 0.5 mg, and Adderall 20 mg three times daily. He diagnosed major depressive disorder and ADHD and continued Adderall 20 mg three times daily while adjusting antidepressants over about 20 monthly visits through June 2020. The Accusation alleged that he never assessed or documented her substance use history or suicide risk, did not check CURES until at least February 2019, and never documented vital signs or physical examinations.

Patient B, a 60-year-old woman, began care in August 2016, 51 days sober after alcohol rehabilitation and with hepatitis C, a blood clot, and hypertension. She was treated through February 2019 with Ambien 10 mg at bedtime, citalopram, and gabapentin 600 mg four times daily. Dexedrine was added in mid-2017 after a relapse, manic symptoms, and a bipolar diagnosis. The Accusation alleged that he never adequately took her substance use history, never ordered urine drug screens, and did not check CURES until February 2019. It alleged that he kept prescribing Ambien after obstructive sleep apnea was diagnosed and while opioids were also being prescribed. It also alleged that the Ambien fills did not match his records: 17 thirty-day supplies at four pharmacies in 2018, some from another prescriber. He was also said to have failed to assess suicide risk. The Accusation cited a 2012 probation for doctor-patient boundary violations as a disciplinary consideration.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; three years' probation with 40 hours/year of education, prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, clinical competence assessment program, practice monitor, prohibition on supervising PAs, and cost recovery of $17,820.25.

narrative: In December 2022 the Board issued a Complaint and Notice of Proposed Disciplinary Action proposing a reprimand, a $10,000 civil penalty, a six-month suspension, a restriction prohibiting all intravenous therapies, and hearing costs of up to $30,000. The Notice charged conduct that does or might endanger patient health or safety, willful performance of treatment contrary to medical standards, administration of unnecessary treatment and failure to obtain consultations consistent with the standard of care, making statements the psychiatrist knew or should have known were false or misleading about the efficacy or value of treatment he prescribed or administered, and gross or repeated negligence. The Notice is not attached, so the treatments, patients and statements are not described; both the proposed sanctions and the final order restrict intravenous (parenteral infusion) treatments.
In the Stipulated Order he neither admitted nor denied the matter, but the Board found that his conduct as described in the Notice violated each of those provisions.
cases.outcome: Reprimand; $5,000 civil penalty; prohibited from personally administering or directing others to administer parenteral infusion treatments to any patient; random no-notice chart audits and office visits.

narrative: The psychiatrist, in outpatient practice, admitted only that the Board could establish a prima facie case. The Accusation alleged repeated negligent acts and inadequate records with four young or middle-aged men treated between 2016 and 2020, and incompetence with one. For all four, handwritten notes across 20 to 34 visits were short and hard to read, and for two patients there were no notes at all for the early months of treatment. Patient A, 31, with longstanding bipolar disorder, was diagnosed with bipolar II and prescribed lamotrigine, citalopram, trazodone, and Xanax, later also Klonopin, for about a year without any CURES check; other prescribers were also supplying him benzodiazepines. He reported a new epilepsy diagnosis, but the psychiatrist never obtained the EEG or spoke to the neurologist. Only after the patient's mother wrote that he was abusing benzodiazepines from several doctors, had been violent, and had recently overdosed did the psychiatrist check CURES; he then stopped Xanax without referring the patient for detoxification or dual-diagnosis care. Patient B, 29, with eight years of opioid addiction, disclosed ongoing heroin use while on Suboxone, yet was prescribed Klonopin, Suboxone, and later Adderall and Xanax with no trial of non-controlled medication, no referral to an addiction specialist, and no drug testing.

Patient C, 29, twice described childhood physical abuse and sexual abuse by his brother's friend; the psychiatrist did not explore or document whether it had been reported or whether the abuser still had contact with minors and did not consult law enforcement or child welfare, later telling investigators the abuse was long ago. Patient D, 54, 15 years sober from alcohol, was continued on Xanax 2 mg four times daily with Valium, and at times lorazepam, without first-line anxiety agents, non-medication treatment, or addiction referral. The Accusation also cited 2014 Board probation, terminated early in 2019, for sexual misconduct and negligence involving one patient.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 5 years' probation with patient disclosure of probation status, 40 hours/year of education, medical record keeping course, professionalism (ethics) program, and practice monitor; prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; costs of $20,000.

narrative: After a three-day contested hearing, an administrative law judge found that the psychiatrist, in outpatient private practice, committed gross negligence with one patient and repeated negligent acts, prescribing without appropriate prior examination, and inadequate records with two. Patient 2, a woman of 69 with hypertension, cardiac symptoms (palpitations, chest pain), a history of diabetes, and arthritis treated with long-term opioids (hydrocodone and Opana ER) by a pain specialist, was treated from 2016 for depression, PTSD, panic disorder, and anxiety. The psychiatrist prescribed Adderall (raised from 5 mg to 30 mg twice daily within two months), Lexapro, and both Klonopin and Xanax, later adding diazepam, while relying solely on the patient's own reports. In four years she never took a vital sign, did no baseline examination or medication reconciliation, and made no documented effort to contact the primary care physician (despite a signed release), cardiologist, or pain specialist. When the cardiologist suggested switching from Adderall to modafinil and insurance declined, she resumed Adderall at 30 mg twice daily without consulting the cardiologist, and she did not coordinate with a new pain physician who was tapering the patient off opioids. The judge credited expert testimony that these were extreme departures, including prescribing benzodiazepines to an elderly patient on opioids without collaborating with her other physicians.

For Patient 1, a 28-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder who transferred care in 2018, the psychiatrist continued Vyvanse, lamotrigine, and escitalopram, added Xanax, and later prescribed Cymbalta, but never obtained a baseline or follow-up pulse or blood pressure and did not document warning about Xanax dependence. The judge noted these lapses occurred while she was on Board probation (2012-2018) for prescribing controlled substances to family and friends without examination, during which she had failed a clinical competence program once and passed on retesting with significant deficiencies. Concluding further probation would not protect the public, the judge recommended revocation, and the Board adopted it.
cases.outcome: License revoked. (Petition for reconsideration denied; effective date stayed from August 14 to August 24, 2023.)

narrative: The psychiatrist, licensed since 1999, did not contest that the Board could establish a prima facie case and accepted a public reprimand. The First Amended Accusation concerned one woman with bipolar disorder, a substance-abuse history, and long QT syndrome whom he attended at an inpatient behavioral health center in August 2017. After emergency visits for abdominal pain, she was admitted voluntarily for depression and anxiety, and on his evaluation she reported continuing suicidal thoughts. He did not review her emergency department records or reconcile his medication list with a different list recorded by the nurse practitioner. Later that day she reported an unwitnessed loss of consciousness and the nurse practitioner sent her for medical clearance still on voluntary status, without a psychiatric risk assessment or a 72-hour involuntary hold; she left the emergency department against advice. When he learned she had been discharged, he took no steps to confirm her safety or to give law enforcement information supporting a hold. The next day she overdosed on 50 Tylenol tablets.

She was readmitted on an involuntary hold under his care, with liver pain, and a nurse practitioner prescribed hydromorphone 4 mg every six hours as needed. The next day he added clonazepam 1 mg three times daily without reviewing records from the outside hospital, without reconciling medications or considering her liver condition and the opioid, without a documented informed-consent discussion, and without increasing vital-sign monitoring or ordering a sedation protocol. After a further overnight emergency visit at which she received IM morphine and lorazepam, she returned to the unit, received her ordered medications, and slept through the morning, snoring; at about 11:30 a.m. he found her pulseless and not breathing, and she did not recover. The Accusation alleged gross negligence in the repeated failure to review records and reconcile medications and in inadequate informed consent, and negligence in the discharge risk assessment and respiratory monitoring.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand; prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, and 40 hours of approved education; costs of $25,815.94.

narrative: This public letter of concern addresses obstetric care, not psychiatric practice. Patient A, a 25-year-old woman with maternal obesity and a family history of hypertension, received routine prenatal care from the physician in her first pregnancy. At 37 weeks 5 days (November 2016) her blood pressure was 122/92, but no further workup was done and she was told to return in a week; at that visit it was 160/110 (repeat 146/90), and she was sent to the hospital and admitted that evening for induction of labor for gestational hypertension. Overnight, nurses reported recurrent late fetal heart rate decelerations and their resuscitative measures; the physician told them to hold further Cytotec until a morning evaluation. Decelerations continued; Pitocin was started at noon and stopped at 1:00 p.m. for continued decelerations, and at 1:40 p.m. the physician read the tracings as Category II and ordered amnioinfusion. During pushing from 6:00 p.m. the tracings were disrupted and hard to interpret, but no fetal scalp electrode was placed. The infant was born at 7:40 p.m. with an Apgar score of 1, coded about 10 minutes later, was resuscitated and airlifted to a Level IV NICU, and died just over a week later.

An independent reviewing expert found that the care may have failed to conform to prevailing standards, criticizing the lack of further evaluation of the diastolic pressure of 92, no documented consideration of cesarean section despite a persistent Category II pattern after 2:00 a.m., no fetal scalp electrode, no magnesium for seizure prevention, and untimely documentation of the induction in a late-entry note. The Board expressed concern that the care may have fallen below the standard, declined formal proceedings, and does not consider the letter disciplinary; the physician consented to it.
cases.outcome: Public letter of concern (non-disciplinary); no formal proceedings.

narrative: According to the Administrative Complaint, Patient B.S., a 52-year-old man with schizophrenia who had been taking clozapine for at least ten years and was also on Prozac, was admitted to a hospital in late February 2022 in part for suicidal ideation and anxiety. The psychiatrist treated him on several occasions between February 28 and March 8, 2022. During the hospitalization both clozapine and Prozac were stopped. Nursing staff documented over the following days that he was paranoid (believing everyone was after him to kill him), bizarre and not redirectable, disorganized, anxious, having trouble sleeping, skipping groups, needing to be coerced to take medication, and making inappropriate sexual comments to staff; on the day of discharge he was described as anxious and agitated. The psychiatrist discharged him on March 8 with a full 30-day supply of Elavil (amitriptyline). He died the next day, and an autopsy attributed his death to acute amitriptyline intoxication.

The Complaint alleged that the standard of care required the psychiatrist to verify the patient's medication history, including his long-term clozapine; to confirm that he was safe for discharge or consider alternatives such as involuntary examination under the Baker Act; and to refrain from giving a 30-day supply of amitriptyline to a patient who was paranoid, anxious and had expressed suicidal ideation. It charged medical malpractice. In the Settlement Agreement adopted by the Board's Final Order, the psychiatrist neither admitted nor denied the allegations.
cases.outcome: Letter of Concern; $8,000 fine; costs of $13,046.61 (both payable within 180 days); 5 hours CME in risk management and 5 hours CME in treatment of patients in a psychiatric setting, within one year.

narrative: This Consent Order resolved the psychiatrist's application to reinstate his North Carolina license; he made admissions and the Board made findings. He had not practiced since June 2021 and had a disciplinary history with the Board, primarily for substandard care in prescribing controlled substances and other medications to his psychiatric patients. A 2009 Consent Order suspended his license for two years, all but 45 days stayed, and barred him from prescribing Schedule II and III controlled substances and buprenorphine, while still allowing Schedule IIN and IIIN drugs. A 2017 Consent Order indefinitely suspended his license, stayed on numerous conditions, and limited his supervision of advanced practice providers to two facilities. A follow-up chart review under the 2017 order found that four patients with serious mental health or psychiatric problems received care that departed from accepted standards, that he continued to make poor diagnostic decisions without adequately documented medical justification, and that the substandard care was the same as or similar to that in the earlier orders. He voluntarily surrendered his DEA registration in 2020, and in 2021, after a hearing, the Board indefinitely suspended his license based on the care of those four patients.

He acknowledged that he had not practiced for the two years before applying, that his conduct was unprofessional conduct including departure from prevailing standards, and that his prior discipline was itself a ground for action. The Board agreed to reinstate the license with practice restrictions and monitoring. He later received a reprimand for resuming practice without the required approvals (Case 216).
cases.outcome: License reinstated with conditions: no controlled-substance prescribing (may petition once DEA registration is restored); Board-approved reentry plan, practice site, and onsite physician mentor/monitor with quarterly reports before resuming practice; practice limited to adult psychiatry (age 18+); NCPHP monitoring contract; no solo practice or practice where he is the only physician on site; no supervision of advanced practice providers.

narrative: The psychiatrist, who had previously been placed on probation in 2016 for failing to perform an adequate suicide assessment in a patient who later died by suicide, was charged with gross negligence, repeated negligent acts, incompetence, and inadequate records in the outpatient care of 11 patients between roughly 2013 and 2022. The First Amended Accusation alleged a pattern of sedative and stimulant polypharmacy without documented indication, risk counseling, or CURES review. Patient 2 received three benzodiazepines at once (clonazepam 2 mg twice daily, temazepam 30 mg, and alprazolam 1 mg four times daily), later with armodafinil, while another physician prescribed hydrocodone; the psychiatrist reportedly saw no risk in the combination and had no mental status examination documented for about five years. Patient 1 had temazepam 30 mg and eszopiclone refilled for months with no visits. Patient 3, documented as overusing Adderall, was prescribed Adderall 40 mg three times daily (120 mg/day, above the FDA maximum) despite bipolar II and schizoaffective diagnoses, and when she reported recent suicidal urges in 2020 no suicide risk assessment was done and the plan was unchanged. Patient 11, an older woman whose husband reported she was wandering off and getting lost, was diagnosed with bipolar disorder without consideration of cognitive decline and continued on zolpidem 12.5 mg/day (more than twice the 5 mg recommended for older women) plus alprazolam.

Other allegations included no metabolic monitoring for a patient on Latuda, alprazolam and other sedatives for a 65-year-old patient on opioids from another prescriber who reported multiple falls, clonazepam 4 mg/day with zolpidem 10 mg in a woman also receiving ketamine elsewhere, and widespread incomplete mental status examinations and medication-list or dose errors (including a note documenting a CURES check that was not done). The psychiatrist did not contest that a prima facie case could be established; there were no findings or admissions.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; four years' probation with standard terms (notification of hospitals/insurers, obey all laws, quarterly declarations, probation monitoring costs); cost recovery of $35,000.00.

narrative: The Accusation arose from two complaints to the Board. Patient A, a 36-year-old man with schizoaffective disorder, was the son of a family the psychiatrist knew socially. In April to May 2018, at the family's request, the psychiatrist made three undocumented home visits while the patient was hallucinating, burning the carpet, and taking hours-long showers; he recommended emergency evaluation (the family declined) and handed out unspecified sample medications. His June 2018 office note (cariprazine and bupropion) omitted the home observations, the samples, and any risk assessment despite the dangerous behavior. A month later he saw the patient again outside the office, where the patient refused medication and a referral; according to the Accusation, the psychiatrist did not document this, assess decision-making capacity, discuss risks or involuntary hospitalization with the family, or formally terminate care, and simply withdrew.

Patient B, a 61-year-old man in an adult residential facility with a psychotic/bipolar disorder diagnosis, was treated from 2016 to 2020. The Accusation alleged that for about 18 months (late 2016 to May 2018) the psychiatrist did not see him yet authorized lorazepam, divalproex, aripiprazole, and escitalopram with refills; never checked liver function or blood counts on divalproex; started lithium (900 mg/day) without baseline kidney or thyroid tests or a timely level; did not act on a level of 1.3 mmol/L; and wrote lithium after the last documented visit. Charges were gross negligence, repeated negligent acts, and inadequate records. The Accusation noted a 2012 public reprimand and 2018 probation (completed 2022), both for negligence and recordkeeping. In the stipulated settlement the psychiatrist agreed a prima facie case could be established and gave up the right to contest; no findings were made.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 5 years' probation with prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, clinical competence assessment program, practice monitor, notification of Decision and Accusation to required parties; prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; cost recovery of $51,290.75.

narrative: In April 2024 the Investigative Committee of the Nevada Board filed a First Amended Complaint alleging five counts of malpractice (Counts I, III, V, VII and IX), five counts of failure to maintain complete medical records (Counts II, IV, VI, VIII and X), and one count of charging for services not rendered (Count XI). The Complaint is not attached to the Settlement Agreement, which gives no facts about the patients, the care, or the billing involved, or how the matter came to the Board's attention. In the agreement the psychiatrist stated generally that he was not admitting the claims had merit and was settling to avoid the cost of a hearing, but specifically admitted two counts of malpractice (Counts I and III) and all five counts of failure to maintain complete medical records, and agreed the Board could enter an order finding conduct that is grounds for discipline. The remaining malpractice counts and the charging-for-services-not-rendered count were dismissed with prejudice. Stating that he intended to retire, he agreed to voluntarily surrender his license effective January 17, 2025, and not to apply for reinstatement for ten years. The Board approved the agreement on December 13, 2024.
cases.outcome: Voluntary surrender of license effective January 17, 2025, with no application for reinstatement for 10 years; Public Letter of Reprimand; $11,000 fine; costs of $13,037.91; Counts V, VII, IX and XI dismissed.

narrative: The psychiatrist, whose specialties are psychiatry and addiction medicine, issued patients wallet cards titled 'Kentucky Medical Cannabis' that bore the Commonwealth's seal and his name and license number and stated that the patient had a medical condition qualifying for cannabis possession. He began around January 2023, after a November 2022 executive order by the Governor granted a conditional pardon for possession of medical cannabis bought legally in another state to people holding a written certification, from a provider with a bona fide provider-patient relationship, that they had a qualifying condition. The state Board of Pharmacy notified the Board in June 2024. The psychiatrist reported issuing cards to about 1,292 patients and said he had dropped the seal after recognizing it could suggest the card was state-issued; a subpoenaed list showed about 1,399 patients.

A Board consultant reviewed ten randomly selected charts, each documenting a single visit, and found a pattern of failure to conform to acceptable practice and of gross ignorance or gross negligence: no psychiatric, medical, family, social or substance-use histories; diagnoses of PTSD and chronic pain without documented trauma history, current symptoms, pain onset or physical findings; no consideration of other diagnoses (one patient with 'mania without psychosis' was on an antidepressant); inadequate or undated mental status examinations; no vital signs, labs, urine drug screens or consistent KASPER checks; no counseling about addiction risk for patients with prior addiction; and unaddressed polypharmacy (one patient apparently on three antipsychotics). The psychiatrist responded that these were not treatment relationships but single visits to confirm that a diagnosis by another provider met the executive order's criteria. In the Agreed Order the parties stipulated to these facts and to conclusions that his conduct violated the Medical Practice Act. The order also recites a 1998 Agreed Order, expired in 2001, over his controlled-substance prescribing and documentation for two patients.
cases.outcome: Five years' probation: clinical skills assessment (CPEP or LifeGuard) with any recommended education plan; CPEP ProBE ethics program with an unconditional pass; Board access to patient records for consultant review at his expense; no modification for five years.

narrative: The Accusation concerned three patients seen by the psychiatrist between 2018 and 2021 on templated, largely blank or copied-forward progress notes. Patient A, an 83-year-old woman with Alzheimer-type dementia in an assisted living facility, was seen about a dozen times over three years on mirtazapine 45 mg/day, quetiapine 50 mg twice daily, and clonazepam 0.5 mg twice daily as needed (filled near-monthly per CURES); the notes differed only by a sentence or two of patient quotes, the regimen never changed, and there was no medication-specific informed consent, no attempt to taper or try alternatives despite the quetiapine black-box warning for dementia-related psychosis and the Beers Criteria for benzodiazepines, no metabolic or tardive dyskinesia monitoring, and no attention to her chronic kidney disease, hyperlipidemia, or vitamin D deficiency. For Patient B, a 61-year-old woman with generalized anxiety, notes left history and examination sections blank, routinely checked 'side effects discussed' even when no medications were listed, and recorded the alprazolam, clonazepam, and other medications only in addenda written in 2021, years after the visits; quetiapine was started 'for sadness' without metabolic monitoring, and paranoid beliefs the psychiatrist later described to investigators were never documented. Patient C, a 60-year-old man with HIV, prior stroke, chronic kidney disease, and a substance-use history, was maintained on paroxetine and quetiapine 100 mg without bloodwork, coordination with his primary care physician, or documentation of his medical or substance-use history.

The Accusation charged gross negligence (inadequate records for all three patients and inadequate quetiapine consent and monitoring for Patients A and C), repeated negligent acts, and failure to maintain adequate records. In the stipulated settlement the psychiatrist did not contest that a prima facie case could be established; there were no findings or admissions.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; three years' probation with 40 hours/year of education, prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, and practice monitor (or professional enhancement program); prohibited from supervising PAs and from supervising APNs other than the one already under his supervision; cost recovery of $50,854.31.

narrative: The psychiatrist was already on five years' probation (effective 2021) from an earlier Board decision based on a substantially related criminal conviction and general unprofessional conduct. A combined Accusation and Petition to Revoke Probation charged gross negligence, repeated negligent acts, incompetence, and inadequate records in the care of five outpatients from about 2016 to 2022, and violation of the probation condition to obey all laws. Representing herself, the psychiatrist admitted the truth of every charge and allegation and surrendered her license.

The pattern across all five patients was long-term controlled-substance prescribing with no initial evaluation note, no documented diagnosis or rationale, no informed consent, controlled-substance agreement, urine drug screens, or documented CURES checks, and largely illegible handwritten notes. Patient A, a 39-year-old man whose intake form listed heroin and opiate use, daily drinking, hepatitis C, PTSD, and ADHD, received amphetamine salts above the FDA daily maximum together with diazepam (later also lorazepam and alprazolam) for nearly two years without confirmation of the ADHD diagnosis or substance-use assessment. Patient B, a 49-year-old woman, received temazepam and hydrocodone-acetaminophen, with no documented counseling about combining them with alcohol and no naloxone, and much of it prescribed by the psychiatrist's physician assistant at her request without a signed delegation agreement, protocols, or chart review; the psychiatrist also treated this patient's thyroid disease and a "platinum" chelation regimen without testing or documentation. Patient C, 35, received high-dose diazepam or alprazolam plus Adderall for anxiety, with no suicide-risk assessment despite reported depression, possible bipolar disorder, an eating disorder, and daily cannabis use. Patient D, 68, with 29 years' sobriety from alcohol and cocaine, received lorazepam, diazepam, and oxycodone-acetaminophen together, plus testosterone and other non-psychiatric drugs. With Patient E, besides stimulants, benzodiazepines, and codeine, the psychiatrist sent an excessive number of inappropriate texts, solicited a ride from the patient, disclosed details of her own psychiatric treatment, and let the patient socialize with a family member.
cases.outcome: License surrender accepted effective June 30, 2025; costs of $26,674.50 payable before any new or reinstated license; any reapplication treated as a petition for reinstatement with the Accusation/Petition's allegations deemed admitted.

narrative: The psychiatrist, board-certified and licensed since 1987, worked for about twenty years as a county-employed psychiatrist in a county jail until 2020. She settled the Accusation without admitting the allegations, acknowledging only that the charges, if proven, would constitute cause for discipline. The Accusation charged gross negligence (for two patients), repeated negligent acts, and inadequate records, all centered on delays in starting medications for incarcerated patients in 2019.

According to the Accusation, at each of four initial jail visits the psychiatrist diagnosed the patient, recommended specific psychotropic medications, and obtained informed consent, but did not actually enter the prescriptions for one to more than three weeks. Patient 1, a man in his early thirties with prior methamphetamine use, presented in moderate to severe distress with panic symptoms, nightmares, and insomnia, said he had submitted many sick-call slips to be seen, and was diagnosed with PTSD, adjustment disorder, and amphetamine use disorder; mirtazapine, escitalopram, and diphenhydramine were recommended on July 22 but not prescribed until August 14. Patient 4, a man in his forties with depressive disorder, had buspirone, sertraline, and venlafaxine recommended on July 18 and filed an inmate grievance on August 1 that he had not received them; they were prescribed August 5, even though a planned 10-day venlafaxine titration could have been completed in that time. Patients 2 and 3 (one a recently bereaved man with a childhood suicide attempt who had stopped paroxetine and amitriptyline a week before incarceration) waited 11 and 7 days. For three patients, progress notes were signed into the record 7 to 11 days after the visit. The Accusation emphasized that antidepressants take weeks to work and that the jail setting increases the risk of decompensation while symptoms go untreated.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 35 months' probation with 40 hours/year of education, prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, professionalism (ethics) program; no solo practice; notification of facilities/insurers; prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; costs of $24,836.76.

narrative: In November 2024 the Board issued a Notice of Proposed Disciplinary Action charging the psychiatrist with repeated acts of negligence. The Notice proposed a reprimand, a 30-day suspension, a permanent practice restriction, comprehensive educational courses in psychotherapy, psychopharmacology and medical record keeping, a $10,000 fine, and hearing costs of up to $40,000. The Notice itself is not attached, so the specific patients and clinical failures are not described. The preceptorship the Board imposed is directed specifically at his psychotherapy practice.
In the Stipulated Order the psychiatrist neither admitted nor denied the matter, but the Board found that his conduct as described in the Notice constituted repeated acts of negligence.
cases.outcome: $10,000 civil penalty ($2,500 held in abeyance pending compliance); CPEP educational plan (already completed); Board-approved preceptor in psychiatry/psychotherapy, monthly meetings for five years with review of 50% of psychotherapy charts for six months, then possibly 25%, and quarterly reports; random no-notice chart audits and office visits.

narrative: The psychiatrist provided consultation-liaison care to medically hospitalized patients and then continued to supervise their psychiatric care after they were transferred to a skilled nursing facility. According to the Accusation, the care of three patients between 2020 and 2023 involved diagnoses that were assigned and changed without a documented evaluation to support them. Patient A, a 42-year-old man with intellectual disability and intermittent explosive disorder admitted for a femur fracture, was seen in March 2022; the consultation note for the first visit was largely unintelligible (including the mental status section), and at the second visit the psychiatrist diagnosed schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, without documentation substantiating it, while continuing lamotrigine, citalopram, benztropine, melatonin, and risperidone. Patient B, a 68-year-old woman hospitalized in late 2020 for altered mental status, confusion, and agitation, was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia with acute exacerbation (with Depakote and Seroquel added), and over the following month her documented diagnosis shifted repeatedly among paranoid schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder (bipolar type), and major depressive disorder with psychotic features while her symptoms were described as essentially unchanged, with no explanation of the reasoning; a note dated after two prior encounters was labeled an initial psychiatric evaluation. Patient C, a 69-year-old man admitted for joint swelling and referred to rule out depression with psychotic features, was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia with acute exacerbation without an adequate documented evaluation.

The Accusation charged repeated negligent acts and failure to maintain adequate and accurate records. The case was resolved by stipulated settlement; the psychiatrist did not admit the allegations but agreed that the Board could establish a factual basis for the charges at a hearing.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 3 years' probation with an education course (20 hours/year), professionalism (ethics) program, and practice monitor (or professional enhancement program); limited to supervising a total of two PAs/advanced practice nurses; cost recovery of $33,334.50.

narrative: The psychiatrist worked part time as a child psychiatrist providing medication support within a team-based community mental health agency serving low-income children, with visits held by telephone during the COVID-19 pandemic. Patient A, a boy who entered care at age eight with autism, ADHD, anxiety, and a history of statements about wishing to be dead, was treated by the psychiatrist from October 2020 to April 2022 with fluoxetine, later sertraline, and methylphenidate; his mother repeatedly gave the stimulant without the anxiety medication. On May 10, 2022, his therapist reported that the boy had said he would rather die than go to school and wanted to hurt himself, and the team asked for an urgent same-day visit, for which an opening existed. The psychiatrist emailed that she would not see him because the mother was not following medication directions and she would not "reward" the mother; she sent medication changes by email, did not join the video session despite a supervisor's request for help assessing his safety, and offered to see him at month's end. A therapist rated him at high acute risk that evening. The agency terminated her two days later and filed an 805 report. For about three months afterward she refilled psychotropic medications for former agency patients who contacted her (90-day supplies for several), with no medical record, until the agency told her to stop.

After a hearing, the administrative law judge found gross negligence for failing to perform a suicide risk assessment during the May 10 crisis and for failing to document her post-termination treatment, and on that basis repeated negligent acts and inadequate records. The judge did not find continued prescribing itself negligent, since the physician-patient relationships had not been ended, and did not find missed suicide assessments at routine visits, though her charting ("no safety concerns," cut-and-paste content) was inadequate. The judge noted she took no responsibility.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 3 years' probation with professionalism (ethics) program, education course (40 hours/year), prescribing practices course, and medical record keeping course; no practice monitor or supervision restriction; cost recovery reduced to $15,000.

narrative: According to the Second Amended Administrative Complaint, the psychiatrist, practicing in an outpatient psychiatry group, treated Patient DB, a 30-year-old woman with a history of panic disorder, bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder, from about May 2022 through March 2023, initially weekly and later every two weeks. The complaint alleged that on multiple occasions during the treatment period he sent inappropriate text messages to the patient, and that sending inappropriate text messages to a patient is a boundary violation and below the standard of care for a psychiatrist; it was charged as medical malpractice. The complaint does not describe the content of the messages.

The case had been referred for an administrative hearing but was resolved by a Settlement Agreement in which the psychiatrist neither admitted nor denied the allegations of fact, admitting only that they would constitute violations if proven. As a term of the agreement he agreed to communicate with patients only through a professional communication system, never through personal text messaging or personal email, and represented that he had already made that change; the agreement credits a three-day professional boundaries course he completed in January 2024.
cases.outcome: Reprimand; $10,000 administrative fine; Department costs of $25,000; 24 hours of in-person CME on professional boundaries within 6 months (a previously completed boundaries course satisfies this); pass EBAS evaluations in boundaries, unprofessional conduct and professional standards within 6 months; restriction requiring all patient communications through a professional communication system rather than personal text or email.

narrative: In a Consent Order, the psychiatrist made the admissions set out in the order and the Board made findings; she acknowledged that the conduct was unprofessional conduct, including a departure from acceptable and prevailing medical practice. From March to August 2018 she treated Patient A, a 38-year-old woman with a history of depression and anxiety who sought psychiatric evaluation and medication management for stress, irritability and brain fog. Patient A was taking escitalopram 20 mg daily; the psychiatrist diagnosed poorly controlled chronic depression and added aripiprazole 2.5-5 mg daily as adjunctive treatment. The order states that the standard of care requires a physical examination for extrapyramidal side effects (EPS) and tardive dyskinesia (TD) when an antipsychotic is started, when the dose is increased, when the antipsychotic is changed, and when the patient reports or shows possible side effects. She did none of these: no baseline examination at initiation or at the two-week visit when she raised aripiprazole to 5 mg; none when Patient A reported occasional jaw and hand muscle tension four weeks later; none in July 2018 when she switched to brexpiprazole 0.5-1 mg; and none in August 2018 when Patient A showed significant psychomotor impairment that should have raised the possibility of EPS. The Board also found that she concluded the depression was treatment-resistant without sufficient evidence, did not prioritize a trial of bupropion, which had worked for Patient A before, and did not document consulting Patient A's psychotherapist despite recommending intensive outpatient treatment. Patient A's next psychiatrist noted that brexpiprazole had caused akathisia, restlessness and sedation, and prescribed bupropion.

A November 2024 clinical assessment by CPEP, by which time she practiced only in a TMS and esketamine clinic, noted lapses in judgment and reasoning, at times an incomplete gathering of history needed for differential diagnosis, and diagnostic and treatment planning that was not sufficiently comprehensive; CPEP recommended structured education with external oversight.
cases.outcome: Reprimand; must work with a Board-approved educational preceptor in psychiatry (with esketamine/TMS and general psychiatry expertise) for regular case and documentation review, coaching on physician-patient communication, and CME in CPEP-identified areas, with semi-annual preceptor reports; may be required to repeat a record-keeping course; may seek relief no sooner than one year.

cases.type: Public reprimand / public letter of reprimand
narrative: According to the Board's Public Letter of Reprimand, an investigation by the Medical Board revealed that the psychiatrist failed to document discussions of medication side effects and risks with patients. The letter characterizes this as a violation of the medical records provision of the Business and Professions Code.
cases.outcome: Public Letter of Reprimand; no additional requirements stated.

narrative: The investigation began with a 2016 online complaint from a parent alleging that the psychiatrist, in outpatient practice, was prescribing her daughter alprazolam and amphetamine. The Board then obtained records for three long-term patients and charged gross negligence, repeated negligent acts, prescribing without appropriate examination or indication, clearly excessive prescribing, failure to consult CURES, inadequate records, and unprofessional conduct. Patient A, a 65-year-old woman with generalized anxiety disorder, COPD on home oxygen, and cardiac disease, received clonazepam and alprazolam (which her primary care physician had become reluctant to prescribe) while another physician prescribed carisoprodol; the psychiatrist contacted the primary care physician and reduced her doses over time. Patient B, about 55, with anxiety, panic, OCD, and ADHD, received lisdexamfetamine 70 mg, alprazolam 1 mg (#75 per 25 days), bupropion, and aripiprazole while other clinicians prescribed him opioids; the psychiatrist tracked his elevated liver enzymes and advised him to stop drinking. Patient C, 49, with generalized anxiety and panic disorder with agoraphobia and insomnia, received diazepam, alprazolam, lorazepam, and sublingual zolpidem monthly while also filling occasional opioid prescriptions from others.

After a five-day hearing, the administrative law judge, finding the Board's expert biased and the defense expert more persuasive, found that the benzodiazepine prescribing was reasonable and not excessive, that mental status examinations were performed, and that CURES checks were not mandatory before October 2018 (after which he checked CURES for all three). The only violation found was that he did not document informed-consent discussions of the risks and benefits of the controlled substances he prescribed; the judge credited his testimony that those discussions occurred and found this a records violation, not a departure from the standard of care. All other causes were dismissed, and a public reprimand was imposed below the guideline minimum, citing good care, no prior discipline, and improved record keeping.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand, conditioned on completing a Board-approved medical record keeping course within 90 days.

narrative: The psychiatrist worked at an inpatient psychiatric hospital. According to the Accusation, in May 2017 he assumed care of Patient A, a minor girl with recurrent major depressive disorder admitted on an involuntary hold after statements of self-harm. When her father asked for her discharge, the psychiatrist, believing she was not ready, placed a second 72-hour hold, and a certification review hearing upheld continued involuntary treatment. The Accusation alleged that the physician's orders and legal-holds sections of the chart were inconsistent and at times did not accurately show whether she was voluntary or involuntary, and that although the chart showed her parents were separated and her mother lived out of state, there was no documentation of custody or of the mother's consent, and he failed to identify and document who could consent to treatment for the minor.

In 2019 he treated Patient B, admitted on a grave-disability hold in a manic, disorganized state with hypertension, abnormal liver and renal tests, and an alcohol detoxification protocol, who twice needed transfer to the emergency department. She was diagnosed with schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, and repeatedly refused antipsychotics; the psychiatrist obtained two court orders permitting involuntary medication (including quetiapine, haloperidol, risperidone, chlorpromazine, ziprasidone, and lithium).
