The Accusation alleged his physician's orders did not reflect her changing legal status or the first court order authorizing involuntary medication, there were no physician's orders at all for several days, and he failed to diagnose or document alcohol withdrawal, including in the discharge summary when she left against medical advice. It charged gross negligence, repeated negligent acts, inadequate records, and unprofessional conduct, including intentional violation of involuntary inpatients' rights. He did not admit the allegations but agreed a prima facie case could be established; the public reprimand states that he failed to consistently and accurately document pertinent medical and legal information for both patients.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand (issued upon completion of coursework) with 40 hours of education, medical record keeping course, and professionalism program (ethics course); must cease practice if courses are not completed on time.

narrative: The Board entered this Consent Agreement in lieu of formal proceedings. No charging document is attached; the facts come only from the psychiatrist's admission. He treated three minor patients for various conditions, including attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. He admitted that, although his choice of medications was generally sound, there were deficiencies in his documentation of medication adjustments and of the patients' responses to medications. He also admitted deficiencies in the degree to which he considered lab and test results as part of the treatment plans.

The Board treated this as a failure to maintain minimal standards in the selection or administration of drugs and a departure from minimal standards of care. The agreement gives no specific medications, doses, or test results. The required courses (controlled-substance prescribing, medical records, and pediatric ADHD prescribing) suggest that the treatment involved stimulant prescribing for children, but the agreement does not name the drugs.
cases.outcome: Reprimand; $5,000 fine; probationary terms until completion (within one year) of courses on controlled-substance prescribing, medical recordkeeping, and pediatric ADHD prescribing, each with a written report; required reporting to employers, hospitals, and other licensing authorities.

narrative: The psychiatrist agreed that the Board could establish a prima facie case for the charges in the First Amended Accusation, which alleged repeated negligent acts and inadequate records in the outpatient medication management of three patients between 2015 and 2021. According to the Accusation, nearly every visit note lacked a narrative interval history and clinical assessment; the subjective entries were brief "provider notes" or chief complaints that the psychiatrist said nursing staff recorded, and after an electronic record change the treatment plan routinely read "continue current medications" even at visits where medications were changed. CURES review was never documented, and prescriptions the patients received from other physicians were not recorded.

The Accusation described benzodiazepine prescribing alongside opioids from other prescribers without documented risk discussion. Patient A, treated for depression and anxiety, was switched to alprazolam 0.5 mg twice daily with no follow-up for two months, then increased to 1 mg three times daily without a documented risk assessment, while CURES showed she had been filling monthly hydrocodone and tramadol from other prescribers since January 2016; this was first noted in 2019, when her pain physician asked why she was on Xanax, and alprazolam was stopped without a documented taper plan. Patient B, with bipolar depression and insomnia, received temazepam 15 mg (up to 60 per month) for years while filling hydrocodone elsewhere, with no documented discussion of opioid or alcohol interactions and no reconsideration after a fall requiring emergency back surgery. Patient C's alprazolam was raised to 1 mg twice daily while she was taking morphine and later OxyContin and oxycodone, with no documented discussion of combining a benzodiazepine with two opioids.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand (relating to medical record keeping) with 40-hour education course, medical record keeping course, and prescribing practices course; cost recovery $5,708.75.

cases.type: Public reprimand / public letter of reprimand
narrative: According to the Board's Public Letter of Reprimand, an investigation by the Medical Board of California revealed that the psychiatrist deviated from the standard of care by failing to adequately document complete mental status examinations and by providing courtesy refills for an inappropriate time or frequency. The letter gives no further facts about the patients, setting, or medications involved.
cases.outcome: Public Letter of Reprimand issued under the Board's authority to resolve a matter with a public reprimand; no probation terms stated.

narrative: The psychiatrist, practicing for about 45 years with no prior discipline, treated mostly Medi-Cal and Medicare outpatients in a psychiatric medical group. The case began with a complaint from a patient's husband that he kept prescribing Xanax after being warned she was abusing it. After a four-day hearing on charges involving four patients, an administrative law judge found that gross negligence was not proven. The judge did find inadequate records and, on that basis, repeated negligent acts. The judge found that he responded to the husband's call by stopping Xanax when Patient 1, a 30-year-old woman with depression and anxiety, had already tapered herself off. He restarted it six months later after she reported abstinence from alcohol, and he had been pasting CURES reports into the chart. The judge did not find that he failed to assess substance use, and found that contacting the husband without consent would have raised confidentiality concerns. He did not, however, document any discussion of alcohol with Xanax.

The judge found documentation failures for every patient. His notes were copied from prior visits and repeated the same boilerplate treatment plan and goals at every visit for four very different patients over years. Medication changes had no recorded rationale. For Patient 2, an 86-year-old man with dementia, he gave no documented rationale, monitoring, or alternatives for long-term concurrent Restoril and Ativan. For Patient 3, an obese 32-year-old with ADHD and anxiety, he raised Adderall from 80 to 120 mg/day after a phone call he never documented, while the chart said concentration had improved. He also continued Xanax 3 mg/day for years without documenting a rationale or a discussion of SSRI/SNRI alternatives. For Patient 4, he documented no rationale for Latuda and Seroquel and no counseling about combining Xanax and Ambien while she also filled Norco from another prescriber.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand (public reproval) with a Board-approved medical record keeping course within 60 days and cost recovery of $13,302 (reduced 50% from the $26,604.25 requested).

narrative: The psychiatrist, licensed since 1971 and in outpatient practice, admitted only that the Board could establish a prima facie case and accepted a public reprimand stating that between 2009 and 2020 he prescribed controlled substances to three patients while keeping sparse and incomplete records. According to the Accusation, his handwritten notes for all three women were short, hard to read, and rarely recorded examination findings, assessment, interventions, or goals. Patient A, 33 at intake in 2009, was treated for bipolar disorder, attention deficit disorder, and insomnia; from mid-2017 to early 2020 he provided monthly prescriptions for zolpidem, Vyvanse, and amphetamines while documenting only about five or six visits, including a gap of nearly 17 months between visits, which the Accusation alleged was gross negligence.

Patient B, 20 at intake in 2013 with ADHD, anxiety, and panic disorder, reported taking Xanax a few times a week; he added clonazepam in late 2017 and prescribed both benzodiazepines from 2018 to 2019 with no documented reason for either the new prescription or the combination. Patient C, 44 at intake in 2012 with depression, suicidal thoughts, an eating-disorder history, migraine, and later bipolar disorder and ADD, was on multiple medications including lurasidone, lamotrigine, methylphenidate, clonazepam, eszopiclone, and zolpidem. Although he knew she was also seeing a psychologist, neurologist, and pain physician and she had signed a release, the chart held no records from them and no documented coordination. In 2020 he wrote four prescriptions for 15 Percocet tablets each with no documented reason. The Accusation also cited 1989 Board discipline (60-day suspension and probation, terminated in 1996).
cases.outcome: Public reprimand; prescribing practices course and medical record keeping course; costs of $15,426.

narrative: The Accusation concerned two older women whom the psychiatrist treated, largely for general medical problems, while prescribing controlled substances. Patient 1, a 90-year-old woman seen in 2018-2019 for COPD, bronchitis, osteoarthritis, hypothyroidism, and epigastric pain, was prescribed promethazine with codeine from September to December 2018 at the same time as lorazepam and temazepam, plus pregabalin. Patient 2, a 71-year-old woman seen from 2017 to 2020, was already on clonazepam when the psychiatrist began prescribing it in February 2017. She later developed breast cancer and worsening anxiety and depression. The psychiatrist kept her on escitalopram and raised clonazepam from 1 mg three times daily to 1 mg four times daily in mid-2019 and again in 2020. The Accusation alleged that the standard of care for long-term benzodiazepines calls for routine urine toxicology to confirm adherence and rule out diversion, along with monitoring of clinical response and CURES. The psychiatrist said she had reviewed CURES but did not document it, and she ordered no urine toxicology screens.

For both patients, every electronic record entry listed a different physician as the provider because of an apparent system defect, and the psychiatrist added signed handwritten notes. Several entries showed "error message" in place of medication reconciliation, and others carried forward medication lists that had not been updated. The Accusation charged repeated negligent acts and inadequate records and cited prior discipline from 2011: a stayed revocation with seven years' probation for gross negligence, repeated negligent acts, prescribing without examination, inadequate records, and excessive prescribing. In the stipulated settlement the psychiatrist did not contest that a prima facie case could be established; she made no admissions. The reprimand states that from 2017 to 2020 she kept incomplete and unclear records for two patients to whom she prescribed controlled substances.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand with prescribing practices course and medical record keeping course; cost recovery $18,000.

narrative: The Accusation concerned two outpatients to whom the psychiatrist prescribed benzodiazepines. It stated that the prescribing itself was appropriate and faulted only the documentation of informed consent. Patient 1 was treated for anxiety from July 2019 to November 2020. The psychiatrist continued clonazepam that another provider had started and, in October 2020, added temazepam 30 mg at bedtime. Patient 2, first seen in November 2018 and diagnosed with bipolar disorder and depression, was started on alprazolam 0.5 mg three times daily as needed for panic attacks in April 2020. For both patients, the Accusation alleged that he did not document an informed consent discussion covering the risks, benefits, and alternatives before prescribing these controlled substances, and it charged this as repeated negligent acts and inadequate records. It also cited a 2018 Public Letter of Reprimand for failing to obtain baseline laboratory tests for a patient, failing to justify in writing a maintenance medication dose above the manufacturer's recommended dose, and omitting important documentation.

In the stipulated settlement the psychiatrist did not contest that the complainant could establish a prima facie case or factual basis for the charges and gave up his right to contest them; he made no admissions. The reprimand states that in 2020 he failed to document informed consent when prescribing benzodiazepines to two patients.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand with medical record keeping course; cost recovery $8,000.

narrative: In March 2024 the Investigative Committee of the Nevada Board filed a Complaint alleging malpractice (Count I), failure to maintain appropriate medical records (Count II), and continual failure to exercise skill or diligence (Count III). The psychiatrist had changed his Nevada license to inactive status in 2022. The Complaint is not attached to the Settlement Agreement, which gives no facts about the patients or care involved or how the matter came to the Board's attention. In the agreement he stated generally that he was not admitting the claims had merit and was settling to avoid the cost of a hearing, but specifically admitted Count II, failure to maintain appropriate medical records, and agreed the Board could enter an order finding conduct that is grounds for discipline. The malpractice and skill-or-diligence counts were dismissed with prejudice. The required continuing education was in best practices in prescribing, and both that requirement and payment of costs were stayed until he applies to return to active status. The Board approved the agreement on December 13, 2024.
cases.outcome: Public Letter of Reprimand; 4 hours of CME on best practices in prescribing and costs of $4,741.93, both stayed until he applies for active license status; Counts I and III dismissed.

cases.type: Public reprimand / public letter of reprimand
narrative: According to the Public Letter of Reprimand, a Board investigation found that between 2019 and 2023, for three patients, the psychiatrist made insufficient entries in the psychiatric records and finalized chart entries late, did not document the required CURES database checks, and failed to document medication informed-consent discussions and medication monitoring. The Board characterized this as repeated negligent acts and failure to maintain adequate records.
cases.outcome: Public Letter of Reprimand with conditions: complete a medical record keeping course and reimburse costs of $11,382.

narrative: The psychiatrist permanently surrendered a Maryland license by a Permanent Letter of Surrender while under Board investigation. The letter acknowledged that the Board had received multiple complaints from patients who had difficulty obtaining their medical records from the psychiatrist's office, and that during the investigation the psychiatrist informed the Board that all patient records had been shredded. It further acknowledged a January 2025 complaint from another healthcare practitioner alleging that patients transferred from the psychiatrist's office were on inappropriate and dangerous medication regimens requiring extensive benzodiazepine tapering. No individual patients, medications, or doses are described.

The psychiatrist surrendered to avoid further investigation; no charges were issued and no hearing was held. The psychiatrist did not contest the allegations and agreed that, for licensure purposes, they supported conclusions of unprofessional conduct in the practice of medicine, failure to provide patients' medical record details on proper request, and failure to notify the Board of a change of name or address within 60 days. The psychiatrist affirmed that copies of records would be provided to patients 'to the extent that such medical records currently exist.'
cases.outcome: Permanent surrender of license (no right to reapply); surrender of state controlled dangerous substance registration.

narrative: The psychiatrist permanently surrendered a Maryland license by a Permanent Letter of Surrender while under Board investigation. The letter acknowledged that the Board had received a mandated 10-day report from a hospital stating that the psychiatrist's privileges had been suspended because of concerns about the psychiatrist's documentation for outpatient work and about meeting the statutory requirements when prescribing controlled substances. The letter gives no further detail about the patients, medications, or specific documentation or statutory deficiencies involved.

The psychiatrist stated that the surrender was made to avoid further investigation and prosecution and because of impending retirement. No charges were issued and no hearing was held. The psychiatrist did not admit the allegations but chose not to contest them, and agreed that for all purposes relevant to medical licensure they would be treated as proven and supported conclusions that the psychiatrist had failed to meet appropriate standards of quality medical care and had failed to keep adequate medical records.
cases.outcome: Permanent surrender of license (no right to reapply); surrender of state controlled dangerous substance registration.

narrative: In a public letter of concern, the Board said it had investigated concerns about documentation and release of medical records. Patient A, whom the psychiatrist was treating for addiction, complained that he failed to provide a complete copy of her record, refused to complete Division of Motor Vehicles evaluation paperwork, and charged a $150 office fee to pick up her buprenorphine prescription when there was no visit. The Board said his responses to those allegations were appropriate, but its review of the record found entries that were overly repetitive and appeared cloned, and no documentation of patient phone calls; it cautioned him against heavily templated notes and advised documenting every attempted or successful patient communication. The Board also stated that during the investigation he failed to adequately respond to its requests for documents and information, a violation of the Medical Practice Act: over one year it issued four Orders to Produce and four Requests for Additional Information and tried repeatedly to reach him, delaying resolution by almost a year. The Board declined formal proceedings and does not consider the letter disciplinary; the psychiatrist consented to it and agreed not to contest its contents.
cases.outcome: Public letter of concern (non-disciplinary); no formal proceedings.

narrative: The psychiatrist owned an outpatient clinic, later converted to a federally qualified health center where he worked as an independent contractor. He also worked long shifts, often 12 or 24 hours, as a psychiatrist at a state prison. According to the Accusation, from 2017 to 2019 a physician assistant trained in family and internal medicine provided much of the monthly medication-management care for three clinic patients. Each had major depressive disorder with psychotic features and PTSD and was treated with antipsychotics (quetiapine, aripiprazole), antidepressants, and in one case zolpidem. For dozens of visits, the charts were electronically signed by the psychiatrist on days when his prison time records showed he was on shift and could not have been at the clinic, which he confirmed. Pharmacy records showed the physician assistant had sent the refill prescriptions, but the assistant's signature appeared nowhere in the charts. Some refills were duplicated days apart or sent on dates with no chart entry.

The Accusation described the notes as largely cloned from visit to visit, with unexplained short-interval return visits and contradictory data, such as one patient's height recorded as 67, 61, and 64 inches and a 15-pound weight swing with no comment. When asked, the psychiatrist could not produce a delegation of services agreement or drug formulary for 2017-2019 and signed a new one only in 2022. He said he did not know why the assistant had not signed the charts and thought he was co-signing them. The assistant's psychiatric training consisted of shadowing him for about two weeks, with no documented education or competency assessment. The Accusation charged repeated negligent acts, inadequate records, and failure to have a delegation of services agreement. In the stipulated settlement he did not contest that a prima facie case could be established and gave up his right to contest the charges; he made no admissions.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 5 years' probation with 40 hours/year of education, prescribing practices course, medical record keeping course, professionalism program (ethics course), practice and billing monitor, solo practice prohibition, notification of hospitals/facilities/insurers, and prohibition on supervising PAs/APNs; cost recovery $31,075.75.

narrative: The Board issued a Public Letter of Concern after investigating concerns of substandard care and inappropriate supervision of an advanced practice provider; it states that it is not a disciplinary action. In August 2022 the Board received a complaint about the administration of testosterone, a Schedule III controlled substance, to patients at a practice the physician owned and operated. The investigation found, and the physician admitted, that he had himself received bioidentical hormone replacement therapy by testosterone pellet insertion from a physician assistant (Provider A) whom he supervised. The letter states that this prescribing violated the Board's rule barring a physician assistant from prescribing controlled substances for the supervising physician's own use, and was contrary to the Board's position statement on supervision; it recognizes that he addressed the issue once it was raised.

An independent expert also reviewed two patients cared for predominantly by Provider A, and the letter reminds the physician of his responsibility as supervising physician. For Patient A, the expert considered that the testosterone dose exceeded recommended dosing and relied on calculations more aggressive than typical, failing to meet prevailing standards; the Board acknowledged that dosing opinions can differ. For Patient B, the electronic records duplicated the history, examination, diagnoses, and treatment plan from note to note with addenda, which the letter said can make records hard to follow and increase inaccuracy; the expert concluded the standard requires an accurate, current list of complaints, assessments, and plans.
cases.outcome: Public Letter of Concern (expressly non-disciplinary and not a restriction on the license or on supervising advanced practice providers); physician agreed to complete eight hours of Category I CME in hormone replacement therapy within six months.

narrative: The psychiatrist, whose only training was in psychiatry and who worked full-time elsewhere as an employed psychiatrist, admitted the truth of every charge and allegation in the Accusation, which charged unprofessional conduct and gross negligence arising from a medical aesthetics clinic he co-owned and nominally directed.

According to the admitted allegations, the psychiatrist and his then-wife, a registered nurse, jointly owned a cosmetic clinic offering Botox and dermal filler injections, thread lifts, laser hair removal, and skin tag removal, and he served as its chief executive officer and medical director while working off-site. The nurse was the only person who treated patients; the psychiatrist never saw, examined, or consulted on any patient there, had no training or knowledge of the procedures, established no policies or procedures, and acknowledged that she practiced unsupervised. From 2018 to 2021 she treated patients without supervision, and from August 2018 to May 2019 on an expired nursing license. The matter came to the Board through a 2019 complaint from a patient who alleged that the nurse injected Botox into her and a friend with the same needle, that a thread lift left scarring, and that the products used were not what was claimed; the clinic said it had misplaced her records. In the records of six other patients, the psychiatrist's stamped signature appeared on consultation notes for patients he had never met, some of whom were former hospital co-workers. In a 2023 Board interview he could not describe a medical director's duties, said he had told the nurse to hire another physician for examinations but did not know whether she had, and called it his error for trusting her.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 4 years' probation with 40 hours/year of education, medical record keeping course, professionalism (ethics) program; no solo practice; prohibited from performing dermal fillers, Botox, Juvederm, threading, and laser hair and skin tag removal, and from serving as an off-site medical director, with patient notification; prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; costs of $40,919.25.

narrative: From 2018 to 2024 the psychiatrist was supervising physician for Nurse Practitioner A under a collaborative practice agreement that authorized her to provide psychiatric and substance-use treatment, including opioid agonist medications for opioid use disorder, but not general medical care or chronic pain management. Supervision began when they worked at the same treatment facility and continued after she left in late 2019. In 2021 she opened a solo practice where, without his knowledge, she also saw general medical and chronic pain patients, sharing only psychiatric and substance-use cases with him. Her records showed high-dose oxycodone prescribing: Patient A, who had multiple substance problems including daily alcohol use, received oxycodone ten times in 2024 at 90 to 193 MME, and up to 180 tablets a month at times since 2019; other patients received 120 to 225 tablets at 180 to 450 MME, one getting three 225-tablet prescriptions with no documented encounters. Positive screens for THC, alcohol or cocaine went uninvestigated and some patients also received benzodiazepines. Her care fell below standards, including failing to check the controlled substances reporting system and failing to consult her supervising physician before starting or renewing opioids as the state's STOP Act requires; the Board of Nursing reprimanded her in December 2025.

The Board found that the psychiatrist kept supervising her without adequately questioning her opioid prescribing and without amending the agreement to restrict opioids after she left the shared practice. Quality-improvement meetings were held only annually or semiannually or when she called, recent ones concerned only renewing the agreement, after 2023 six months could pass without contact, and the meetings were not adequately documented as Board rules require. As a psychiatrist he lacked the training to supervise primary or chronic pain care. He knew of only one of her opioid patients, and only after a report to the Nursing Board, and ended the agreement in September 2024. In the Consent Order he made admissions and the Board found unprofessional conduct (departure from prevailing standards) and violation of a law relating to the practice of medicine.
cases.outcome: Reprimand.

narrative: The psychiatrist had been placed on five years' probation effective May 2015 under a stipulated settlement in which he admitted the allegations of a 2014 Accusation: after his license had lapsed into delinquent status, he faxed a state hospital's medical staff office a pocket license whose expiration date had been altered to appear current, and he signed a medical staff application listing that false expiration date and attesting that his license had never been not renewed; he renewed the license only after the hospital learned from the Board that it was delinquent.

The Petition to Revoke Probation alleged that he failed to pay the annual probation monitoring costs required by his probation. At the hearing, which proceeded by default because he did not appear, the administrative law judge found that he had been told in 2015 that costs (then $4,106 per year) were due each January 31, that a $400-per-month payment plan was arranged in late 2016 after he had made no payments, and that he made a $400 payment in March 2017 but did not keep up payments. He did not pay $15,473 by a February 2020 deadline, and by May 2020 he owed $21,904; he acknowledged to his probation inspector that he was behind and understood that nonpayment could lead to further discipline. The judge noted he was otherwise compliant apart from some late quarterly reports. Finding a violation of the cost-payment condition and no mitigating evidence, the judge set aside the stay and imposed the revocation.
cases.outcome: Probation revoked; stayed revocation imposed and license revoked.

narrative: The psychiatrist was already on three years' probation under a 2019 stipulated settlement resolving an Accusation for dangerous use of alcohol and a criminal conviction. According to that Accusation, in 2016 police followed a trail of radiator fluid from a telephone pole that had been struck by a car to the psychiatrist's home, where they found him lying on the ground near his damaged car; he admitted drinking several alcoholic beverages before driving, showed signs of intoxication, and preliminary breath tests showed a blood alcohol content of roughly 0.26% to 0.29%. He pleaded no contest to driving with a blood alcohol content of 0.08% or more and admitted a special allegation that it was 0.15% or greater. Probation terms included complete abstinence from alcohol and controlled substances, biological fluid testing, a professionalism (ethics) program, psychiatric evaluation, and psychotherapy.

The Petition to Revoke Probation alleged that he violated the condition requiring complete abstinence from alcohol: a biological fluid sample collected in July 2021 tested positive for phosphatidylethanol, consistent with ingestion of alcohol, and he admitted having consumed an alcoholic beverage within a week before the sample. A Cease Practice Order was issued in August 2021. In the stipulated surrender, the psychiatrist did not admit the allegations but agreed that the complainant could establish a factual basis for the charges and gave up his right to contest them.
cases.outcome: License surrendered; if he ever petitions for reinstatement, the Petition to Revoke Probation allegations will be deemed true and admitted.

narrative: Under a July 2020 Stipulated Order, the psychiatrist was required to remain enrolled in, and compliant with, his monitoring agreement with the state's Health Professionals' Services Program (HPSP); the order does not say what that earlier order was for. In September 2020 the Board opened a new investigation after receiving credible information of a possible violation of the Medical Practice Act, and in June 2021 he entered an Interim Stipulated Order withdrawing from practice and placing his license on inactive status pending the investigation. The order does not describe the underlying events.

In the Stipulated Order he neither admitted nor denied the matter, but the Board found that he engaged in unprofessional or dishonorable conduct, impairment, and willful violation of a Board order or rule, specifically the July 2020 Stipulated Order and the Board's rule governing the monitoring program. The order states that he failed to comply with the 2020 Stipulated Order.
cases.outcome: Surrendered Oregon license while under investigation; may not reapply for at least two years; the July 2020 Stipulated Order and June 2021 Interim Stipulated Order terminated.

narrative: The psychiatrist, a child and adult psychiatrist, had her license revoked in 2005 for cocaine use and impairment after relapses in the Board's diversion program and residential treatment. The license was reinstated on five years' probation in January 2019, with complete abstinence from alcohol and random biological fluid testing. After a three-day hearing on a First Amended Petition to Revoke Probation, an administrative law judge found that she committed major probation violations. She drank champagne at a wedding in June 2019, failed to test when selected while traveling in June 2021 (the site she went to was closed), and had positive alcohol tests in July 2021 (blood PEth 45.1) and October/November 2021. The July 2021 result followed drinking beer and possibly vodka during a period of grief over her brother's death. The October 2021 result was attributed to rum in a birthday pie. As aggravation, the judge found the 2005 revocation, a missed test in June 2019, and ten positive tests between January and September 2019, many at very low levels and attributed to rum cake, liqueur in coffee, food, and a vaginal wipe. Those 2019 results had already led to a cease-practice order and two citations with fines.

The judge found no evidence of cocaine use since 2014. A Board-ordered clinical diagnostic evaluation found cocaine use disorder in remission, major depressive disorder, no alcohol use disorder, and that she could practice safely. It also found that her alcohol use showed poor insight and judgment. The judge found that she had 22 months of negative tests, completed an outpatient program, added Soberlink monitoring, and had been in psychotherapy and TMS for depression. Revocation was rejected, but probation was restarted for a full five years, with an ethics course and psychotherapy added.
cases.outcome: Probation revoked and stayed revocation imposed, then stayed again; new five-year probation with abstinence from controlled substances and alcohol, biological fluid testing, 10 hours of community service, professionalism (ethics) program, psychotherapy, medical evaluation and treatment, and prohibition on supervising PAs and advanced practice nurses.

narrative: This short Agreement for Surrender of License concerns a psychiatrist who was already on Board probation. According to the agreement, an Accusation had been filed against him in February 2021, and an August 2021 decision revoked his license, stayed the revocation, and placed him on three years' probation with standard terms and conditions. That probation order allowed him to request voluntary surrender if he stopped practicing because of retirement or health reasons or was otherwise unable to satisfy the terms and conditions of probation. Invoking that condition, he agreed to surrender his license, wallet and wall certificates, and any California DEA registration, and the Board accepted the surrender in February 2023. The agreement does not describe the conduct underlying the 2021 Accusation, does not state which probation terms he could not meet, and does not allege any probation violation; at the time, his address of record was outside California.

Earlier decision (summarized in this document as Case 182): the 2021 probation was reciprocal discipline. After a hearing, an administrative law judge found that another state's medical commission had disciplined him for failing, as medical director of outpatient substance use disorder clinics, to prevent his signature from being used to order medically unnecessary urine drug testing billed to insurers, and for prescribing buprenorphine-naloxone and benzodiazepines to a friend and colleague without checking the prescription monitoring program while the friend was receiving opioids from six other providers.
cases.outcome: License surrender accepted; any future application for relicensure or reinstatement to be treated as a petition for reinstatement of a revoked license, with Board investigation reports admissible and time-based defenses waived.

narrative: The psychiatrist, a geriatric psychiatrist licensed in 2000, had been on Board probation for over ten years. In 2012 she admitted gross and repeated negligence while employed by a large medical group, including failing to properly manage patients' medications, assess a patient's psychosis in relation to her medical status, take adequate histories, and manage patients with substance abuse; she was placed on four years' probation with a billing monitor and courses. In 2016, after an Accusation alleging that in private practice she pressured patients to pay for multiple assessment sessions, failed to keep records of an examination, and had no written billing or payment policies, her probation was extended by 35 months with conditions including a billing monitor and a cap of two years of non-practice, with a clinical training program required after 18 months of non-practice.

After a hearing, an administrative law judge found that she went about six months without a billing monitor before enrolling in a professional enhancement program, which suspended her in August 2019 because she had submitted no patient lists since March 2019 and no chart notes or billing information for that year. The Board issued a cease-practice order in November 2019, and she did not practice for two years. When she then enrolled in a clinical competence program, it required a psychiatric fitness-for-duty evaluation, and the evaluators reported she was not fit for duty, so she did not complete the program. The judge found violations of the billing-monitor and non-practice/clinical-training conditions. A separate Accusation alleging she was unsafe to practice because of mental illness was dismissed because the evaluators did not testify and their report was hearsay; her own evaluator found her fit. The judge noted that she denied the original misconduct, blamed her probation monitors, and gave no assurance of future compliance.
cases.outcome: Petition to revoke probation granted; license revoked. Accompanying Accusation (mental-illness impairment under B&P 822) dismissed.

narrative: This is a short agreement for surrender of license made while the psychiatrist was on Board probation. An Accusation had been filed in June 2022, and a Decision in October 2023 revoked the license, stayed the revocation, and placed the psychiatrist on 35 months' probation with standard terms. That probation order allowed a request to surrender if the psychiatrist stopped practicing for retirement or health reasons or was otherwise unable to meet the probation terms. Shortly after the order, the psychiatrist used this provision to surrender the license, and the Board's Executive Director accepted it.

The agreement does not describe the conduct alleged in the underlying Accusation, does not say why the psychiatrist could not meet the probation terms, and does not allege any probation violation. No findings or admissions about patient care appear in this document.
cases.outcome: License surrender accepted; may no longer practice in California; must surrender wallet and wall certificates and any California DEA certificates; any future application treated as a petition for reinstatement of a revoked license.

narrative: This is a short agreement for surrender of license made while the psychiatrist was on Board probation. An Accusation had been filed in September 2022, and a Decision in August 2023 revoked the license, stayed the revocation, and placed the psychiatrist on three years' probation with standard terms. That probation order allowed a request to surrender if the psychiatrist stopped practicing for retirement or health reasons or was otherwise unable to meet the probation terms. A few months into probation, the psychiatrist used this provision to surrender the license, and the Board's Executive Director accepted it.

The agreement does not describe the conduct alleged in the underlying Accusation, does not say why the psychiatrist could not meet the probation terms, and does not allege any probation violation. No findings or admissions about patient care appear in this document.

Earlier decision (summarized in this document as Case 84): the 2023 probation resolved an Accusation alleging years of benzodiazepine and other controlled-substance prescribing to three women despite ongoing drinking, overdoses, early refills, and opioids from other prescribers, with almost no CURES checks or drug screens, no suicide risk assessment despite documented self-harm, and poorly legible records. He did not contest that a prima facie case could be established.
cases.outcome: License surrender accepted; may no longer practice in California; must surrender wallet and wall certificates and any California DEA certificates; any future application treated as a petition for reinstatement of a revoked license.

narrative: The psychiatrist had previously been disciplined under a June 2021 Final Order adopting a settlement of allegations that he inappropriately prescribed opioids and benzodiazepines to chronic pain patients at a pain management clinic. That order required him, within one year, to pay a $20,000 fine and $12,806.24 in costs and to document completion of risk-management continuing medical education. The Administrative Complaint in this case alleged that he did none of these within the year, violating a lawful order of the Board.

The psychiatrist was personally served with the Complaint but did not file an election of rights or otherwise respond, and so waived his right to a hearing. He did not appear at the Board meeting. On the Department's motion, the Board adopted the Complaint's allegations as its findings of fact and found the violation established.
cases.outcome: Reprimand; $5,000 fine; costs of $520.97; license suspended until he demonstrates full compliance with the June 2021 Final Order.

narrative: This is a short agreement for surrender of license made while the psychiatrist was on Board probation. An Accusation had been filed in December 2020, and a Decision in December 2021 revoked the license, stayed the revocation, and placed the psychiatrist on five years' probation with standard terms. That probation order allowed a request to surrender if the psychiatrist stopped practicing for retirement or health reasons or was otherwise unable to meet the probation terms. About two years and three months into probation, the psychiatrist used this provision to surrender the license, and the Board's Executive Director accepted it.

The agreement does not describe the conduct alleged in the underlying Accusation, does not say why the psychiatrist could not meet the probation terms, and does not allege any probation violation. No findings or admissions about patient care appear in this document.

Earlier decision (summarized in this document as Case 41): the 2021 probation resolved an Accusation alleging that a mental illness impaired the psychiatrist's ability to practice safely. According to that Accusation, a Board-approved evaluator reported that she had admitted to an inappropriate relationship with a patient and did not understand doctor-patient boundaries; the probation barred her from practicing until she completed a professional boundaries program and was found mentally fit. She did not admit the allegations, agreeing only that a prima facie case could be established.
cases.outcome: License surrender accepted; may no longer practice in California; must surrender wallet and wall certificates and any California DEA certificates; any future application treated as a petition for reinstatement of a revoked license.

narrative: This is a short Agreement for Surrender of License signed while the psychiatrist was on probation. It recites that a Second Amended Accusation had been filed against her in March 2020 and that an October 2020 Decision revoked her license, stayed the revocation, and placed her on 35 months' probation with standard terms. That probation order allowed her to request surrender if she stopped practicing for retirement or health reasons or was otherwise unable to satisfy the probation terms, and she used that provision to surrender. The document does not describe the conduct behind the original Accusation or any specific probation violation, and it contains no findings or admissions about the underlying allegations. By its terms, any future application for licensure would be treated as a petition for reinstatement of a revoked license.

Earlier decision (October 2020; it predates the newsletter volumes covered here and was retrieved separately from the Board's Winter 2021 newsletter): the probation resolved a Second Amended Accusation prompted by a complaint that she might be excessively prescribing controlled substances to a family member. It alleged that she prescribed stimulants (Adderall, dextroamphetamine, and Vyvanse) to three patients diagnosed with ADD without any comprehensive evaluation supporting the diagnosis, including supratherapeutic Adderall doses combined with Vyvanse without documented justification, and that she kept inadequate records. It also cited a 2015 Texas Medical Board agreed order, in which she admitted prescribing controlled substances and other medications to a person with whom she had a close personal relationship without a documented immediate need, resulting in a public reprimand in Texas. In the California settlement she admitted the Texas discipline and denied the other charges.
cases.outcome: Surrender of license accepted by the Executive Director on behalf of the Board (under a probation term allowing surrender when unable to satisfy probation); any future application to be treated as a petition for reinstatement; no cost recovery stated.

narrative: The Investigative Committee of the Nevada Board issued an Order of Summary Suspension and Notice of Hearing, an interim action taken without a prior hearing, based on information Board staff presented to it. The order stated that the psychiatrist's license had been inactive while she sought treatment for substance abuse, and that in June 2024, in recovery, she appeared before the Board to return to active status. The Board granted her license with conditions, requiring her to complete a 12-month preceptorship under a senior psychiatrist at the facility where she would work, who agreed to report any concerning pattern in her work performance, attendance, documentation or clinical decision-making. The order stated that the preceptor then reported that on January 3, 2025, she arrived late to work appearing to be in an altered state, entered the monthly staff meeting seemingly disorganized, and was observed by coworkers to smell of alcohol; that evening she texted the preceptor that she had relapsed. By January 6, 2025 she no longer worked at the facility and the preceptor reported the preceptorship terminated. The Committee found that by failing to complete the preceptorship she had willfully and knowingly violated the Board's order, and that this put the public at risk of imminent harm, and suspended her license immediately pending a hearing. The matter was resolved by a settlement in June 2025 (Case 215); an earlier, unrelated 2021 settlement is Case 200.
cases.outcome: License summarily suspended until further order of the Investigative Committee or Board; hearing on continuation of the suspension noticed.

narrative: In April 2025 the Investigative Committee of the Nevada Board filed a Complaint alleging one count of failing to comply with a lawful order of the Board. The Complaint is not attached and the Settlement Agreement recites no facts; the related Order of Summary Suspension (Case 214) states that she had been granted her license with conditions in 2024, after a period of inactive status during treatment for substance abuse, and that the required preceptorship ended in January 2025 after she reported relapsing. At the time of the settlement her license was in suspended status under that January 14, 2025 summary suspension, which the parties had stipulated on January 16, 2025 would remain in effect pending resolution. In the Settlement Agreement the psychiatrist stated generally that she was not admitting the claims had merit, but specifically admitted Count I, failing to comply with a lawful order of the Board, and agreed the Board could enter an order finding conduct that is grounds for discipline. The Board approved the agreement on June 6, 2025. Under its terms the summary suspension was lifted and her license placed in inactive status, and she must appear before the Board for any further change in license status. An earlier 2021 settlement against the same physician is Case 200.
cases.outcome: Public Letter of Reprimand; costs of $361.50; summary suspension lifted and license placed in inactive status; must appear before the Board for any further change in license status; remaining claims dismissed.

narrative: The psychiatrist had been placed on four years' probation by a 2023 stipulated settlement of an Accusation alleging gross negligence, repeated negligent acts, and inadequate records. That earlier Accusation, attached to this decision, alleged that he closed his outpatient private practice of roughly 50-60 patients in 2020 by mailing (uncertified) termination letters that gave no referrals or resources, no instructions for obtaining records, and no crisis guidance, without facilitating transfer of care. It also alleged that on an inpatient unit he started a 23-year-old woman with psychosis on Clozaril at 50 mg daily and tripled the dose to 150 mg after two days (the labeling recommends starting at 12.5-25 mg with 25-50 mg increments), repeatedly failed to document which medications and doses she was receiving, and that she later had a new-onset seizure.

The Accusation and Petition to Revoke Probation in this case alleged that the psychiatrist failed the clinical competence assessment program required by his probation: in September 2024 his performance was rated "Fail - Category 4," not meeting the minimum standards for safe patient care, with inadequate knowledge of care and treatment recommendations for several common psychiatric concerns, including omissions that could have harmed patients. The Board issued a cease-practice order. In the stipulated settlement he gave up the right to contest that a prima facie case could be established; there were no findings or admissions.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; three years' probation, concurrent with existing probation (whose terms remain in effect); must complete a clinical competence assessment program before resuming practice (cease-practice order remains until then), practice monitor (or professional enhancement program), prohibited from supervising PAs/APNs; cost recovery of $6,500.00.

narrative: The psychiatrist was already on probation: after an Accusation filed in August 2022, a May 2024 Board decision revoked her license, stayed the revocation, and placed her on three years' probation with standard terms and conditions. This document does not describe the conduct underlying that earlier discipline. Relying on the probation condition that allows a licensee who stops practicing for retirement or health reasons, or who is otherwise unable to satisfy the terms and conditions of probation, to request surrender, the psychiatrist signed an agreement to surrender her license, which the Board accepted. No new misconduct or probation violation is alleged in the document, and nothing was found or admitted.

Earlier decision (summarized in this document as Case 92): the 2024 probation resolved an Accusation alleging that, over about three years, she prescribed medications including modafinil, zolpidem, lorazepam, and tramadol to three adult relatives without appropriate examinations or medical records; the probation prohibited her from treating family members. She did not contest that a prima facie case could be established.
cases.outcome: License surrendered; any future application will be treated as a petition for reinstatement of a revoked license.

narrative: The psychiatrist had been placed on 35 months' probation by a Board decision effective November 20, 2025, resolving an Accusation filed in 2023 (summarized separately as Case 129, concerning delayed prescribing and late documentation for jail patients). Under the standard probation condition allowing a probationer who stops practicing for retirement or health reasons, or who is otherwise unable to satisfy the terms and conditions of probation, to request surrender, she signed an Agreement for Surrender of License, which the Board's Executive Director accepted. The agreement does not allege any new misconduct or any specific probation violation, and it does not state why she was unable to comply with the terms.
cases.outcome: Surrender of license accepted under the probation surrender condition; wallet certificate, wall license, and any California DEA registration surrendered; any reapplication treated as a petition for reinstatement of a revoked license, with investigation reports admissible and time-based defenses waived.

narrative: The psychiatrist entered a Consent Order in which he made admissions and the Board made findings. He had a disciplinary history primarily for substandard care in prescribing controlled substances and other medications to his psychiatric patients, including a 2009 partial suspension with prescribing restrictions, a stayed indefinite suspension in 2017, surrender of his DEA registration in 2020, and an indefinite suspension after a hearing in 2021. In September 2024 the Board reinstated his license by a Consent Order (Case 224) that required him, before resuming practice, to obtain practice-site approval from the Board's Office of Medical Director and to have an onsite physician mentor and monitor approved.

In or about April 2025 he began working for a Critical Access Behavioral Health Agency without having obtained site approval. Records the Board obtained from the agency showed he was performing patient evaluations, taking histories, reconciling medications, performing mental status examinations, and documenting impressions and recommendations, which the Board found constituted the practice of medicine. The Board, through his counsel, instructed him to stop evaluating patients there or otherwise practicing. The Board concluded that his failure to comply with the site-approval and mentor/monitor provisions of the 2024 order was unprofessional conduct.
cases.outcome: Reprimand; $2,500 administrative fine within 30 days; all conditions of the 2024 reinstatement order remain; may not resume practice until the fine is paid and practice-site and onsite mentor/monitor approvals are obtained.

narrative: The physician, licensed in another state since 1984 with experience in laboratory medicine and addiction medicine, held a California license only to serve as medical director of a laboratory serving California clients. From 2014 to 2017 he was paid medical director of several outpatient substance use disorder clinics in the other state. That state's medical commission, in a stipulated agreed order in August 2020, found that an owner of some of those clinics ran a scheme requiring patients in intensive outpatient treatment to undergo twice-weekly urine drug tests sent for definitive testing of many substances regardless of medical need, billed to insurers as ordered by the physician; that he either knew or should have known his signature was being used to authorize the unnecessary testing, and was otherwise deficient in his duty as medical director to set and oversee laboratory testing policy. It also found that from 2015 to 2019 he treated a friend and colleague (the owner of a behavioral health agency where he had been medical director) for back pain with buprenorphine-naloxone, later adding zolpidem, alprazolam, and lorazepam, without checking the prescription monitoring program or documenting a detailed history, and kept prescribing while the patient received oxycodone and hydrocodone from six other providers; the commission called this a boundary violation and below the standard of care, while noting it did not cause the patient's 2019 death.

The Board sought reciprocal discipline. After a hearing, an administrative law judge found the out-of-state discipline was for conduct that is also unprofessional in California (facilitating insurance fraud and unsafe prescribing). The physician acknowledged he should have prevented the fraud and let a personal relationship affect his judgment; the judge credited his testimony that he did not knowingly participate in or profit from the fraud and acted to stop it when he learned of it, and noted his completion of a competence assessment and the out-of-state courses. Probation mirroring the other state's order was imposed rather than revocation.
cases.outcome: Revocation stayed; 3 years' probation with partial controlled-substance restriction (limited to Schedules III-V and naloxone; no marijuana recommendations), controlled-substance record log, 40 hours/year education, prescribing practices course, professionalism/ethics program, practice and billing monitor, and prohibition on supervising PAs/APNs.

narrative: This was reciprocal discipline based on an Alabama action. In November 2020 the Alabama State Board of Medical Examiners issued a Consent Order, under a joint settlement with the physician, imposing discipline 'related to the excessive prescription of controlled substances.' The Alabama order indefinitely restricted his controlled-substance authority there: no pain management services; no narcotics, opioids, carisoprodol or codeine cough syrups, except buprenorphine/naloxone for opioid use disorder up to 16 mg a day; no central nervous system depressants (sedative-hypnotics, gabapentinoids, sedating anti-emetics and similar) for any patient on more than 45 MME a day for chronic pain; no benzodiazepines for patients taking opioids; a benzodiazepine cap of 7 lorazepam milligram equivalents a day after 120 days; referral of chronic pain patients to a board-certified pain specialist within 120 days; and reporting of controlled-substance-related deaths, overdoses and hospitalizations within 14 days. The Georgia Public Consent Order recites the Alabama action and its terms but gives no facts about the underlying prescribing (no patients, drugs, doses or dates). The physician agreed to the findings of fact, and the Georgia Board concluded that the Alabama action was sufficient grounds for discipline.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand; Georgia controlled-substance restrictions largely mirroring Alabama's: no pain management services; no opioids/narcotics, carisoprodol or codeine cough syrups except buprenorphine(/naloxone) for opioid use disorder up to 16 mg/day; for three years no CNS depressants for chronic-pain patients on more than 45 MME/day and benzodiazepines capped at 14 lorazepam-mg equivalents/day; refer chronic pain patients to a pain specialist; report controlled-substance adverse events within 14 days; may not petition to lift sanctions until all Alabama sanctions are lifted.

narrative: The Administrative Complaint was based on action by the Colorado Medical Board, where the psychiatrist also held a license. According to the Complaint, in January 2023 the Colorado board issued an order in response to reports that she possessed a large amount of marijuana and ecstasy pills and that she had qualified patients for medical marijuana cards in Michigan by diagnosing them with qualifying conditions without seeing them. That order required her to contact the Colorado physician health program by a set date in January 2023, submit to a mental or physical examination, and cooperate with the program's recommendations. When the program reported that she had not made contact by the deadline, the Colorado board suspended her license indefinitely in February 2023, until she complied with the program, was appropriately evaluated, and the board reviewed a request to lift the suspension. The Florida Complaint charged her with having her license acted against by another jurisdiction.

The psychiatrist was served by certified mail but did not file an election of rights or otherwise respond, and so waived her right to a hearing; she did not appear before the Board. On the Department's motion, the Board adopted the Complaint's allegations as its findings of fact and found the violation established.
cases.outcome: $5,000 fine; costs of $289.79; license suspended until she shows that her Colorado license is unencumbered and free of restrictions or conditions, with the Board retaining jurisdiction to impose probation or other terms on reinstatement.

narrative: The California case was based entirely on discipline imposed by the Illinois medical licensing agency, where the psychiatrist practiced. According to the Accusation and the attached Illinois Consent Order (August 2021), the Illinois agency received information that the psychiatrist had prescribed controlled substances without renewing her Illinois controlled substance license, and, while that matter was pending, that she failed to appropriately evaluate and treat a patient in her practice who was experiencing an acute psychiatric episode. The Illinois order does not describe the patient or the episode further. In Illinois the psychiatrist neither admitted nor denied the allegations; she was placed on indefinite probation for a minimum of one year with a practice monitor reviewing ten charts per quarter, 10 hours of CME in psychiatric emergencies and 10 hours in professional responsibility, and a $5,000 fine.
California charged discipline by another state. In the stipulated settlement the psychiatrist did not contest that a prima facie case could be established; there were no findings or admissions.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand; professionalism program (ethics course) within one year; cost recovery of $10,636.31.

narrative: The psychiatrist, board-certified in psychiatry and licensed in Maryland since 2023, self-reported to the Board in January 2025 that another state's medical board had reprimanded him in December 2024 under a consent order. According to the Maryland Consent Order's findings, the other state's discipline was for failing to disclose, on his 2023 new-license application, several disciplinary actions taken against him during residency, and for failing to report disciplinary actions from residency and medical school to the Federation Credentials Verification Service. The undisclosed residency actions included a verbal warning in 2019 after a complaint about unprofessional conduct; a 2020 written warning finding his professionalism, patient care, and interpersonal and communication skills on an internal medicine rotation unacceptable and below the starting level of a PGY-1; a 2020 reprimand for unprofessional conduct and language at work; a three-workday unpaid suspension in 2021 for offensive language and creating a disturbance; and a four-workday unpaid suspension in 2022 for abusive, offensive, or unprofessional language or conduct and quarreling. In medical school he had been placed on academic leave and repeated his second year, and repeated his fourth year because of academic difficulty and difficulty with professional conduct.

In the Consent Order, Disciplinary Panel B found these facts and concluded that he had been disciplined by another state's licensing authority for acts that would be grounds for discipline in Maryland, namely fraudulently or deceptively obtaining or attempting to obtain a license and willfully making a false representation on a licensure application. The psychiatrist signed the Consent Order and waived any right to contest its findings.
cases.outcome: Reprimand.

cases.type: Public reprimand / public letter of reprimand
narrative: According to the Board's Public Letter of Reprimand, the psychiatrist was reprimanded in another state (Rhode Island) on January 10, 2024. The letter states that this out-of-state discipline constitutes a violation of the California provisions on discipline imposed by another state and unprofessional conduct. It does not describe the conduct underlying the Rhode Island reprimand.
cases.outcome: Public Letter of Reprimand; no additional requirements stated.

narrative: The Administrative Complaint was based on discipline in New York, where the psychiatrist also held a license. According to the Complaint, in August 2023 the New York State Board for Professional Medical Conduct issued a Consent Order suspending his New York license for 18 months, with the entire suspension stayed, and placing him on three years' probation with conditions including practice under an approved monitor and keeping a prescription log. The New York action stemmed from allegations that, from about 2011 through about 2021, he failed to render or document appropriate care and treatment for three patients and prescribed medications to those same patients in an inappropriate manner. The Florida Complaint does not describe the patients, medications or prescribing problems further. It charged him with having his license acted against by another jurisdiction.
In the Settlement Agreement adopted by the Board's Final Order, the psychiatrist neither admitted nor denied the allegations.
cases.outcome: Letter of Concern; $2,000 fine; costs of $2,108.65; probation for as long as his New York license remains on probation, practicing only under indirect supervision of a Board-approved board-certified psychiatrist monitor who reviews 10% of active patient records quarterly with office visits; tri-annual reports and Probation Committee appearances.

cases.type: Public reprimand / public letter of reprimand
narrative: The Medical Board of California issued a Public Letter of Reprimand because the psychiatrist was reprimanded in the State of New Jersey on October 31, 2023. The letter does not describe the conduct underlying the New Jersey action.
cases.outcome: Public Letter of Reprimand.

narrative: On or about September 3, 2024, the Alabama State Board of Medical Examiners issued an Order Denying Application for Alabama Certification of Qualification, refusing the physician's application for Alabama licensure based on a finding that his answers on the application were 'false, misleading, and untruthful.' The Georgia Public Consent Order does not say which questions were answered falsely or what information was involved. It noted that he fully cooperated with the Georgia investigation, had no prior discipline by the Georgia Board, and that neither the Alabama action nor the Georgia matter involved direct patient harm. He admitted the findings of fact.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand; $5,000 fine within 90 days; 10 hours of CME in professionalism and 10 hours in ethics within 90 days, not counted toward renewal.

narrative: According to the Administrative Complaint, Florida law requires every licensed physician to pay an annual $250 assessment, due around January 1, to the state's Birth-Related Neurological Injury Compensation Association (NICA). The Complaint alleged that the psychiatrist failed to pay the assessments for five consecutive years, 2017 through 2021, and that in July 2022 NICA obtained a default final judgment against him in county court based on those unpaid assessments. The Department charged this as a failure to perform a statutory or legal obligation placed on a licensed physician. No clinical conduct was alleged. In the Settlement Agreement adopted by the Board's Final Order, the psychiatrist neither admitted nor denied the allegations.
cases.outcome: Letter of Concern; costs of $609.05; 5 hours CME in laws, rules and ethics within one year.

narrative: According to the Administrative Complaint, on or about August 4, 2022, the psychiatrist closed or relocated his office practice and was no longer available to patients there. A Board rule requires a physician who terminates or relocates a practice to notify patients by publishing a notice once a week for four consecutive weeks in the newspaper of greatest general circulation in the county and in a local newspaper serving the practice area, giving the date of the closure or move and an address where patients can obtain their records, and to send a copy of the notice to the Board within one month. The Complaint alleged that he did neither. No clinical conduct was alleged.

The psychiatrist was personally served with the Complaint but did not file an election of rights or otherwise respond, and so waived his right to a hearing; he did not appear before the Board. On the Department's motion, the Board adopted the Complaint's allegations as its findings of fact and found the violation established.
cases.outcome: License revoked; costs waived.

narrative: In April 2025 the Oregon Medical Board's Executive Director issued a one-page Order of Immediate License Suspension suspending the psychiatrist's Oregon medical license, effective immediately. The order states that the Executive Director is authorized to issue final orders of suspension that occur by operation of law, and it cites a range of state statutes outside the Medical Practice Act as the basis for the suspension. The order contains no factual findings, describes no clinical or professional conduct, and states no conditions for reinstatement.
cases.outcome: License suspended immediately by operation of law (order of the Executive Director); no other terms stated.

narrative: The psychiatrist, who practiced psychiatry in North Carolina, entered a Consent Order in which he made admissions and the Board made findings. Beginning November 22, 2024, Board staff sent him four emails about his annual license renewal; the first was delivered but never opened, the second and third (December 2024 and January 2025) drew no response, and the fourth, sent January 22, 2025, was not opened until April 23, 2025. A certified letter mailed to his address of record in February 2025 was returned as undeliverable. Because he did not register on time, his license was made inactive on April 9, 2025.

After he realized his license was inactive, he continued to treat patients, including prescribing controlled substances, until about July 14, 2025. Through counsel he asked that the license be reactivated retroactively to April 9, 2025. The Board concluded that his conduct was unprofessional conduct and a failure to respond within a reasonable time and in a reasonable manner to Board inquiries.
cases.outcome: Reprimand; license retroactively reactivated to April 9, 2025; two hours of Category I CME in ethics/professionalism within six months; obey all laws, investigative interviews and compliance information on request.

narrative: In July 2022 the Board issued a Complaint and Notice of Proposed Disciplinary Action against the psychiatrist, proposing revocation. It charged unprofessional or dishonorable conduct that did or might endanger patients or the public or was contrary to recognized ethical standards, and misrepresentation in applying for a medical license. It also charged failure to report an adverse action taken against the psychiatrist by a peer review body, health care institution, or governmental agency, and failure to self-report within 10 working days an official action based on a finding of unprofessional conduct. The Stipulated Order does not describe the underlying facts, and the Notice is not attached.
The psychiatrist neither admitted nor denied the allegations, but the Board found that the conduct described in the Notice violated each of the cited provisions.
cases.outcome: $2,500 civil penalty; Board-approved ethics course and professionalism course within three months; ongoing therapeutic relationship with a Board-approved healthcare provider who reports to the Board quarterly; practice-site and contact-change reporting.

narrative: The psychiatrist was selected for a Board audit of his continuing medical education for January 2021 to January 2023. He did not respond to three email notices in September and October 2023. In December 2023, Board staff spoke with him by phone. He said he would provide the documentation and then asked for more time because he was moving out of state. Staff gave him the extension and asked for an update within 30 days. A further request in January 2024 went unanswered, and he never submitted the documentation.

The Board issued a Notice of Opportunity for Hearing in March 2024. He did not open the emailed notices, and the Board served him by newspaper publication. He then called the Board twice but never submitted the required written hearing request. A Hearing Examiner reviewed the evidence without a hearing. The Board adopted the Hearing Examiner's findings that he violated the Board's rule on evidence of continuing medical education. The Hearing Examiner noted that the move was the only mitigating circumstance offered and that there was no evidence it prevented him from producing the documentation after the extension was granted.
cases.outcome: Indefinite suspension; $4,500 fine; reinstatement conditioned on documentation of 50 hours of CME for the 2021-2023 period (plus 50 hours for each period while suspended) and payment of the fine; CME documentation for further periods after reinstatement.

narrative: The psychiatrist, whose Oregon license was on inactive status, became the subject of a Board investigation in April 2025 after the Board received credible information that she might be unable to practice medicine safely and competently because of impairment. In October 2025 the Board issued an Order for Evaluation requiring her to complete a competency evaluation. According to the Stipulated Order, she did not propose an evaluator within the 15 days the Order required, had still not proposed one, and had not completed the Board-ordered evaluation.

In the Stipulated Order she neither admitted nor denied the matter, but the Board found that she engaged in conduct violating the Medical Practice Act, specifically willful violation of a Board order (the Order for Evaluation). The Board made no finding on the underlying impairment question; the order states that if she reapplies she must comply with the Order for Evaluation and demonstrate medical competency.
cases.outcome: Retired Oregon license while under investigation; may not reapply for at least two years, and on any reapplication must complete the Board-ordered evaluation and demonstrate medical competency.

narrative: The Public Consent Order found that on or about August 17, 2016, the psychiatrist referred a male patient to another physician in order to pursue a non-professional, personal relationship with him. She noted in the chart that she had verbally told the patient she would no longer be his treating physician, and sometime after that entry began a personal relationship with him that lasted until October or November 2016. Before the personal involvement began, she did not terminate the doctor-patient relationship in writing as the Board's rules require. The order found that this departed from minimum standards of acceptable practice and was unprofessional conduct. It does not describe the nature of the relationship beyond 'personal', the patient's diagnosis or treatment, or how the matter reached the Board. In mitigation, the Board found that she fully cooperated with its inquiry, had voluntarily completed a boundaries course at her own expense, had no other known boundary violation in her career, and was genuinely remorseful. She agreed to the findings of fact.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand; $3,000 fine within 30 days; CME course on sexual boundaries within six months, in addition to renewal CME.

narrative: In April 2022 the Investigative Committee of the Nevada Board filed a Complaint alleging one count of malpractice (Count I) and one count of violation of patient trust and exploitation of the physician-patient relationship for financial or personal gain (Count II). The Complaint is not attached to the Settlement Agreement, which gives no facts: it does not identify the patient, describe the relationship or the gain involved, or say how the matter came to the Board's attention. In the agreement the psychiatrist stated generally that he was not admitting the claims had merit and was settling to avoid the cost of a hearing, but specifically admitted Count II, violation of patient trust and exploitation of the physician-patient relationship for financial or personal gain, and agreed the Board could enter an order finding conduct that is grounds for discipline. The malpractice count was dismissed with prejudice. As a condition he had to pass all five sections of the Ethics and Boundaries Assessment Services (EBAS) examination. The Board approved the agreement on September 16, 2022.
cases.outcome: Public Letter of Reprimand; $2,500 fine; costs of $1,506.08; must pass all five sections of the EBAS ethics and boundaries examination within 60 days, at his own expense; Count I dismissed.

narrative: The psychiatrist, board-certified in psychiatry with a subspecialty in geriatric psychiatry, worked at a hospital. The Board opened an investigation after the hospital filed a mandated 10-day report in March 2024 stating that in early February he had begun behaving erratically and sending messages of a problematic nature to hospital employees, and that he had been placed on administrative leave. According to the Order for Summary Suspension, on February 2, 2024 his supervisor notified him that the hospital was taking disciplinary action after determining that he had fostered a hostile work environment. Around February 6 he sent messages to the supervisor and several employees that contained numerous expletives and statements such as threats to have the supervisor arrested, that they would get into trouble, that he does not lose, a reference to what he used to do in the military, and 'see you on the other side.' The supervisor and an employee obtained a temporary and then a final peace order, to which he consented, directing him to stay away from the hospital, not to contact them, and not to possess firearms; the Board found that he had kept a firearm at his residence before the order. His medical records, which he authorized the Board to obtain, showed that around February 7 he was diagnosed with a medical condition requiring treatment that impacts his ability to practice safely.

These are investigative findings that Disciplinary Panel B had 'reason to believe' were true, issued without a prior hearing; the Panel concluded that the public health, safety, or welfare imperatively required emergency action. This was an interim action, with a post-deprivation hearing scheduled.
cases.outcome: License summarily suspended (interim) pending a post-deprivation hearing; option to request an evidentiary hearing before an ALJ.

narrative: On or about April 11, 2023, Patient M.P., a woman seeking psychiatric services as a victim of trauma, had an initial assessment with the psychiatrist. The Public Consent Order states that she had, among other traumas, experienced a sexual assault, and found that the psychiatrist compared her trauma to 'a car accident.' The order further found that, after some delay, he sent the Board a response letter notarized on or about November 18, 2024, and that his signature on M.P.'s records indicated he signed them on November 11, 2024, roughly nineteen months after the assessment and one week before his response to the Board. He admitted the findings of fact. The order does not say how the matter reached the Board, whether M.P. continued in his care, or what else the records showed; the required coursework in recordkeeping, ethics and trauma-informed counseling reflects the three issues described.
cases.outcome: Public reprimand; $3,000 fine within 90 days; within six months, Board-approved CME of 5 hours in recordkeeping, 5 hours in ethics and 10 hours in trauma-informed counseling, not counted toward renewal.
